commits.pr_title: [Perf][DSv4.1] Extend the latency_specialized decode on NVIDIA
commits.pr_body:
## Overview This PR makes the `latency_specialized` decode from #61868 faster for DeepSeek-V4.1 on NVIDIA GPUs. Most of the work is in the decode step's kernels: larger batches now stay on the low-latency paths, more of each step overlaps, and the indexers split their work across the TP ranks. "What changed" below goes through each part. On one GB300 tray with DSpark, the decode step takes 5.9–17.0% less time than on `main` at batch 1 to 32, and AgentX P90 interactivity is 4–26% higher at concurrency 1 to 32, with slightly higher throughput. ![Decode step and AgentX, main against this PR](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yaoyaoding/vllm/93d0aafb7e0d32b440d597fa680476b5de27d5f9/pr3_perf.png) Left: three ABBA sets at `0cdfc566`, 12 measurements per arm and batch. Right: AgentX at `0cdfc566`, both arms of each concurrency on one tray. ## Validation This branch includes #63914 (merged into this branch), which keeps the specialized decode's FlashInfer paths on `main`'s FlashInfer 0.7.2.post1; this PR's two further paths on FlashInfer internals follow the same rule. The runs below are from before this branch merged `main`: `main` at `76518259` on that commit's wheel with FlashInfer 0.7.2, against this PR at `0cdfc566`, except compute-sanitizer, which ran at `5ab5ef9e`, the commit before it (`0cdfc566` adds only a start-up requirement, no runtime weight updates, a test option, a comment and documentation). After the merge, on `main`'s wheel at `ed1a7307` with FlashInfer 0.7.2.post1, four GB300: these GPU tests pass at `b7bb822b` (`test_kernels.py`, `test_all_gather.py`, `test_decode_topk.py`, `test_sparse_mla_cute.py`, `test_numerics.py`, `test_layers.py`, `tests/kernels/test_engram.py`, `tests/distributed/test_custom_all_reduce.py`; all but `test_kernels.py` ran at `d7fcb755`, which differs only in that file), and a TP4 server with `decode_backend: latency_specialized` starts with the specialized decode on and no fallback warning, and answers a completion and a chat request correctly. FlashInfer 0.7.2.post1's MoE finalize adds the top-k products in a different order at small batches, so `b7bb822b` lets one test's finalize comparison allow FP32's reordering error. ### Correctness | Task | `main` | This PR | | --- | ---: | ---: | | GSM8K, strict match (1,319, c8, real verification) | 0.9742 | 0.9735 | | GPQA-Diamond (198 × 16, c32) | 0.789 | 0.791 | | AIME25 (30 × 16, c32) | 0.983 | 0.985 | | RULER NIAH (`single_2`, `multikey_2`, `multikey_3`; 32K, 128K, 256K; 40 samples each), concurrency 8 | 1.000 in all nine cells (40 of 40 each) | 1.000 in all nine cells (40 of 40 each) | | RULER NIAH, same, concurrency 32 | 1.000 in all nine cells (40 of 40 each) | 1.000 in all nine cells (40 of 40 each) | | GSM8K with `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error` | | 0.9719, no GPU↔CPU sync reported | | GSM8K with `decode_backend` unset (stock decode) | | 0.9704 | | All-gather stress: CUDA graphs of three back-to-back gathers of different sizes, some with the ranks skewed, replayed 2,000,000 times in a seeded random order on four GPUs; every word encodes its rank, gather and replay, checked on the GPU (`test_all_gather.py` as a module; `--custom-all-gather` replays the same graphs on vLLM's custom all-gather) | custom all-gather: 392 stale words | 0 bad words (6,000,000 gathers) |
Tests ```bash # One SM100-family GPU: the new kernels against FlashInfer, cuBLAS or torch references .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_kernels.py tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_decode_topk.py tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_sparse_mla_cute.py tests/kernels/test_engram.py -v # Four GPUs: the all-gather, AllReduceMHC's LL and two-shot protocols, TP4 numerics .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_all_gather.py tests/distributed/test_custom_all_reduce.py tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_numerics.py -v # The all-gather stress run (four GPUs), then the same replays on vLLM's custom all-gather .venv/bin/python -m tests.models.deepseek_v41.nvidia.specialized_decode.test_all_gather --replays 2000000 .venv/bin/python -m tests.models.deepseek_v41.nvidia.specialized_decode.test_all_gather --replays 2000000 --custom-all-gather # Four GB300: five-layer model at TP4 with DSpark, switch on vs off .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_layers.py -v ``` | Check | What it covers | Result | | --- | --- | --- | | Kernel tests | Routed experts against FlashInfer up to 192 rows, eagerly, in graphs and over 500 replays with alternating inputs (bitwise); the front against the stock chain; pinned and wide low-latency MXFP8 GEMMs; the replicated embedding lookup; the metadata graph against eager builds, with slow clamping builders | 299 passed (with `tests/kernels/test_engram.py`), 1 skipped | | Decode top-k (CuTe DSL) | An exact top-k of the BF16 logits against `torch.topk`, k 512 and 2048, 1–64 rows: sampled and direct paths, crowded, constant and rising values, NaN and infinities, a sample that misses the top values, the wide 16-CTA rows, CUDA graphs; block mode against the stock `select_candidate_blocks` | 77 passed | | Sparse MLA (CuTe DSL) | Against an FP32 reference: widths of 1–5 chunks (128 to 640 columns), masked columns, a token with no active column, as many tokens as the GPU holds clusters for, with and without sinks, CUDA graph replay | 33 passed | | All-gather | Against NCCL, bitwise: int32, BF16 and FP32 inputs of 1 pack to the full 4 MiB, growing and shrinking from call to call, one rank late each call; the sentinel word; CUDA graphs of three gathers of different sizes, some with the ranks skewed, replayed in a random order with new contents each replay, 4 GPUs | Passed; the stress run: 0 bad words in 6,000,000 gathers | | `AllReduceMHC` | Shrinking and growing batches in one mailbox with LL only, two-shot only (to 200 rows) and both in turn; the two protocols give the same bits, 4 GPUs | 61 passed (the whole file) | | Numerics, layers (4 GB300) | TP4 collectives through the new paths, including the logits and the row-sharded indexer at 1, 2, 5, 8 and 32 requests through the new all-gather; with the switch on the executor runs, embeds from the replicated table and replays its graphs | Both passed | | compute-sanitizer | memcheck and synccheck over the new kernels' single-GPU tests | memcheck and synccheck: 0 errors each (199 tests: 110 in the two new test files, 89 selected from `test_kernels.py`; at `5ab5ef9e`) | | pre-commit | All hooks | Passes | **CI.** The new test files (the all-gather's among them), the `AllReduceMHC` tests (`test_custom_all_reduce.py -k all_reduce_mhc`) and `test_engram.py` join the nightly 4×B200 DeepSeek-V4.1 step. Three tests need hardware that step does not have, and skip there: `test_pinned_mxfp8_mm` and `test_wide_low_latency_mxfp8_mm` (the tactics are pinned for GB300, SM103) and the layers test (four GB300).
### Performance All runs: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on one GB300 tray (TP4), DSpark (5 draft tokens), Model Runner V2, FULL CUDA graphs for decode. The decode step and AgentX use DSpark's synthetic acceptance (length 3.51, as InferenceX runs AgentX); the accuracy runs above verify for real.
Server command and clients Both arms ran the same command, on `main`'s wheel with either `main`'s or this PR's source: ```bash VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 VLLM_HTTP_TIMEOUT_KEEP_ALIVE=900 vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --attention-config '{"backend":"FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41","indexer_kv_dtype":"mxfp4","indexer_sparse_logits":true}' \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","enable_adaptive_verification":false}' \ --engram-config '{"cpu_offload":true,"use_thp":true}' \ --kernel-config '{"enable_flashinfer_autotune":true}' \ --additional-config '{"decode_backend":"latency_specialized"}' \ --compilation-config '{"mode":"VLLM_COMPILE","cudagraph_mode":"FULL_AND_PIECEWISE","cudagraph_capture_sizes":[5,6,12,18,24,30,36,48,60,72,96,120,144,192,240,288,384,480,576,768,1020,1536,2046,3072,4092]}' \ --max-cudagraph-capture-size 4092 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 64 \ --max-model-len 1048576 --language-model-only \ --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 --tool-call-parser deepseek_v41 --reasoning-parser deepseek_v41 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice ``` - Decode step and AgentX: the speculative config adds `"rejection_sample_method":"synthetic","synthetic_acceptance_length":3.51`. - GSM8K: InferenceX's lm-eval GSM8K (5-shot, temperature 0, all 1,319 questions), 8 requests in flight, one run per cell. - GPQA-Diamond and AIME25: zero-shot through lm-eval, reasoning effort high, temperature 0.6, 16 samples of every question, 32 requests in flight, as for #61868. GPQA-Diamond is InferenceX's task (the last standalone A–D letter, 16,384 output tokens); AIME25 is lm-eval's with DeepSeek-R1's math prompt (65,536 output tokens). - RULER NIAH: lm-eval's RULER generator and scorer for `niah_single_2`, `niah_multikey_2` and `niah_multikey_3` at 32K, 128K and 256K tokens, 40 seeded samples per task and length (upstream lm-eval draws 500), 128 output tokens, thinking off, one run per cell. - AgentX: InferenceX's AgentX scenario (AIPerf, the 393-trace corpus), closed loop at a fixed concurrency for 3,600 s. - Decode step: one server per block. A block runs batch 1 (a 524K-token context), batch 8 and batch 32 (84K–648K tokens a request) twice each. The requests are prefilled one at a time, then sent together for 3,000 tokens each, so they decode from the prefix cache. The step is the client-side window in which every request decodes, divided by its chunk count.
**AgentX.** The InferenceX AgentX trace corpus (393 traces), 3,600 s per concurrency, closed loop, DSpark at the synthetic acceptance length 3.51 as InferenceX runs it, at `0cdfc566`. Both arms of a concurrency ran on the same tray, one after the other (the first arm alternates with the concurrency). Each cell reads `main` → this PR. | Concurrency | P90 interactivity (tok/s/user) | Change | Total tok/s/GPU | Change | TPOT p50 (ms) | TTFT p50 (s) | E2E p50 (s) | Requests | | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 1 | 817.7 → 852.0 | +4.2% | 7,856 → 8,016 | +2.0% | 1.110 → 1.050 | 0.984 → 0.783 | 2.10 → 1.52 | 341 → 395 | | 4 | 666.3 → 808.7 | +21.4% | 10,336 → 10,477 | +1.4% | 1.110 → 1.040 | 0.434 → 0.431 | 1.13 → 1.09 | 764 → 769 | | 8 | 539.6 → 678.7 | +25.8% | 16,813 → 17,198 | +2.3% | 1.280 → 1.110 | 0.414 → 0.434 | 1.26 → 1.16 | 1,443 → 1,456 | | 16 | 431.1 → 536.2 | +24.4% | 29,316 → 29,922 | +2.1% | 1.520 → 1.230 | 0.496 → 0.448 | 1.30 → 1.11 | 2,715 → 2,748 | | 32 | 225.0 → 258.2 | +14.8% | 61,858 → 63,312 | +2.3% | 2.210 → 1.640 | 0.829 → 0.671 | 2.30 → 1.80 | 4,869 → 4,966 | Some trace turns ask for one output token. When that token ends the reasoning, the response has no content, and the client records the request as an error: 0–1 such requests a run for `main` and 0–1 for this PR.
TTFT: API server and engine AgentX TTFT is mostly the API server's single-threaded work before the engine sees the request: chat-template rendering and tokenization of the whole conversation. aiperf's per-request `request_ack_ns` separates that work from the engine's (acknowledgement to first token). This PR changes only worker-side code, and the engine part stays within 18 ms of `main` at every concurrency; the TTFT differences in the table are in the API server: | Concurrency | API server p50 (s) | Engine p50 (s) | | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 1 | 0.693 → 0.479 | 0.267 → 0.249 | | 4 | 0.215 → 0.219 | 0.177 → 0.167 | | 8 | 0.237 → 0.244 | 0.150 → 0.153 | | 16 | 0.284 → 0.239 | 0.158 → 0.162 | | 32 | 0.503 → 0.354 | 0.214 → 0.213 |
**Decode top-k.** `decode_topk` against vLLM's opt-in DeepSelect and the stock path (FP32 upcast + `cooperative_topk`), k = 512, µs per call: Random BF16 logits; "valid" is the share of each row's columns before its end. One GB300, a CUDA graph of 20 back-to-back calls, median of 20 replays. Each cell: `decode_topk` / DeepSelect / stock. With row sharding, a rank selects 12 rows at batch 8 and 48 rows at batch 32 (6 rows a request, over 4 ranks). - Up to 12 rows, `decode_topk` is faster than DeepSelect at every shape but two: 65,536 columns with 1/8 valid (7.3–7.7 against 4.2–4.3 µs), and 1,048,576 columns with 1/8 valid at 12 rows (17.1 against 16.5). - From 24 rows, DeepSelect is faster when 1/8 of the columns are valid (65,536 columns at 48 rows: 17.1 against 4.3 µs) and at 65,536 columns from 48 rows and 524,288 all-valid columns from 48 rows (44.2–44.1 against 46.1–44.7 µs). `decode_topk` stays faster with all 262,144 columns valid (11.8–22.5 against 26.1–26.2 µs). - Above 12 rows, `decode_topk` does not take 1,048,576-column rows, so they use the stock path (81.7–289.3 µs against DeepSelect's 16.6–76.6). - In block mode `decode_topk` is faster at every size (5.9–12.7 against 9.3–80.0 µs). - Against the stock path `decode_topk` is faster at every shape it takes, except 65,536 columns with 1/8 valid (7.3–17.4 against 6.7–12.9 µs; equal at 24 rows).
All shapes | Columns, valid | 1 row | 6 rows | 12 rows | 24 rows | 48 rows | 64 rows | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 65,536, 1/8 | 7.3 / 4.2 / 6.7 | 7.4 / 4.2 / 7.0 | 7.7 / 4.3 / 7.4 | 8.9 / 4.3 / 8.9 | 17.1 / 4.3 / 11.3 | 17.4 / 4.3 / 12.9 | | 65,536, all | 9.0 / 10.8 / 11.5 | 9.3 / 10.7 / 12.2 | 9.4 / 11.0 / 14.1 | 10.3 / 11.0 / 15.7 | 17.9 / 11.0 / 21.4 | 20.2 / 11.0 / 23.3 | | 262,144, 1/8 | 7.4 / 8.2 / 11.1 | 7.9 / 8.2 / 13.2 | 8.0 / 8.2 / 17.0 | 9.9 / 8.3 / 22.3 | 19.3 / 8.3 / 35.9 | 19.6 / 8.4 / 54.6 | | 262,144, all | 9.5 / 25.8 / 14.6 | 11.3 / 25.9 / 18.6 | 10.1 / 26.0 / 29.7 | 11.8 / 26.1 / 34.9 | 20.8 / 26.2 / 62.0 | 22.5 / 26.2 / 80.7 | | 524,288, 1/8 | 8.7 / 11.0 / 11.8 | 9.0 / 11.1 / 17.2 | 9.3 / 10.9 / 23.8 | 15.5 / 11.0 / 36.3 | 28.5 / 11.0 / 81.4 | 35.0 / 11.1 / 102.6 | | 524,288, all | 12.4 / 16.8 / 18.0 | 11.5 / 17.0 / 29.7 | 28.9 / 43.9 / 49.3 | 37.0 / 44.0 / 63.2 | 46.1 / 44.2 / 130.0 | 44.7 / 44.1 / 151.9 | | 1,048,576, 1/8 | 9.4 / 11.8 / 14.3 | 10.1 / 12.0 / 23.9 | 17.1 / 16.5 / 39.4 | – / 16.6 / 81.7 | – / 16.7 / 149.9 | – / 16.8 / 190.7 | | 1,048,576, all | 12.1 / 20.9 / 27.0 | 12.4 / 21.1 / 49.1 | 27.3 / 76.1 / 90.1 | – / 76.2 / 129.9 | – / 76.4 / 246.8 | – / 76.6 / 289.3 | Block mode (the candidate source: top 2,048 blocks of 8 columns; DeepSelect over the block maxima), 1/8 valid, `decode_topk` / DeepSelect: | Columns | 1 row | 6 rows | 12 rows | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 524,288 | 5.9 / 9.3 | 6.2 / 24.5 | 6.3 / 42.7 | | 1,048,576 | 6.3 / 13.3 | 6.5 / 43.6 | 12.7 / 80.0 |
**Memory and start-up.** The replicated embedding table takes 1.32 GB per GPU and the all-gather's mailbox 48 MiB, which the KV cache gives up (106,281,697 → 105,286,588 KV-cache tokens on the tray, −0.9%). Engine start: the engine's init (profile, KV cache, warm-up) took 98.8–103.0 s (`main`) and 98.8–108.9 s (this PR) with warm compile caches, three starts each; a tray's first start, with cold caches, took 680–748 s in either arm. ## Details **Duplicate-work check.** No open PR extends the DeepSeek-V4.1 specialized decode. Related open PRs: - #62633 adds a swap-AB CuTe DSL decode attention to the FlashMLA mega-attention layer. This PR's sparse-MLA kernel replaces the TRTLLM-gen decode of the `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41` backend, which the specialized decode requires. - #62172 lets `cooperative_topk` read BF16 logits, and #57109 adds FlashInfer's sampled `gvr_2` as an opt-in indexer top-k. `decode_topk` serves only this model's decode indexers. It also selects the candidate source's blocks, and it covers the 1M-wide rows on 16 CTAs. The comparison with DeepSelect is above. - #62635 fuses the finalize with the shared-expert add where the fused all-reduce + mHC does not take it. This PR's MoE finalize stays deferred into that fused kernel.

They were measured one at a time, on a moving base that also held DSpark-draft changes not in this PR, so they do not add up exactly. | Change | Why | Measured when added | | --- | --- | --- | | Pinned CuTe DSL MXFP8 tactics for the attention projections above 8 rows | The autotuner sometimes picked an unclustered `wo_b` tactic (15.3 against 5.9 µs at 48 rows), about 310 µs a step at batch 8, depending on the server start | Batch 8 −7.3% | | The next layer's mHC coefficients on the side stream at every executor step (was up to 48 rows) | They ran inline above 48 rows | Batch 32 −3.9% | | Low-batch routed experts up to 64, then 192 rows: a fused front, a routing-record prefix, the router's padding mask | Above 8 rows the stock FlashInfer chain ran (routing, sort, GEMMs, finalize) | Batch 2 −8.6%, batch 4 −7.0%; 12 cold layers at 80–128 rows 10–13% under FlashInfer | | Low-latency MXFP8 projections up to 48 rows | FlashInfer's block-scaled GEMMs, 13.5 µs for the three projections at 12 rows against 4.3 µs of HBM time | Attention sublayer at batch 2 50.4 → 48.5 µs | | Dense indexers row-sharded from two requests; Engram WKV run ahead; candidate expansion overlapped | Every rank scored every row of the indexers | Batch 2–21 −0.6% to −4.7% (all separated) | | Two-shot all-reduce + mHC from 64 rows, adapted from FlashInfer's MNNVL two-shot all-reduce | Each rank read four contributions per value; the owner now sums them once | Batch 21 −1.0%, batch 28 −0.9%; 192 rows 15.7 → 12.1 µs per call | | The dense indexer planned before the index-key wait | 6.6–7.2 µs of reset, schedule and cast waited for the keys without reading them | About −25 µs a step at batch 2, −50 at batch 8 (profile) | | Embedding from a replicated table into the hyper-connection streams | Sharded lookup + all-reduce + copy | Not measured on its own: it was added in a set of four changes, which together gave batch 4 −1.6% and batch 21 −1.4%. commits.pr_title: [Perf][MoE] Skip the combine staging copy in flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

`flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided` copies the whole expert output into FlashInfer's symmetric workspace before every combine (`moeA2APrepareCombineKernel`). This PR hands the experts the workspace combine region through the existing `allocate_fused_expert_output` hook, as `allgather_reducescatter` already does with its combine input, so FlashInfer detects the workspace-backed payload and skips the copy. Follow-up to #54268.

## Claims

- Removes the staging copy of every received row before combine. On B200 EP4 with Qwen3.5-397B shapes the copy costs 163 us per MoE layer at 16K tokens per rank (~0.5 GB read + 0.5 GB write of HBM).
- One-sided dispatch + combine microbenchmark: −6 / −43 / −161 us at 1K / 4K / 16K tokens per rank.
- End-to-end prefill throughput on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-NVFP4 (DP4 + EP, 4× B200): +1.4% to +3.2% across ISL 512–32K, faster at every ISL, ~10M input tokens per point. gsm8k unchanged.
- No change when the hook cannot apply: experts that do not reduce top-k themselves, outputs that are not bf16/fp16, or a shape/device mismatch keep vLLM's own buffer and the existing copy.

## Validation

Hardware: one DGX B200 node (8 GPUs on NVSwitch), FlashInfer 0.7.2, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, NCCL 2.29.7. Baseline is `main` at 51c6dfd8c8, the parent of this change.

### Unit tests

```bash
python -m pytest tests/distributed/test_mnnvl_alltoall.py -v
python -m pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_moe_layer.py -k flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided -v
```

- `test_mnnvl_alltoall.py`: 5 passed, 13 skipped. The multi-GPU tests are skipped by `requires_ptrace` on this bare-metal host (no `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`), so `test_one_sided_manager_lifecycle`, `test_one_sided_manager_workspace_grow` and the new `test_one_sided_expert_output_in_workspace` were also run directly on 2 GPUs (bypassing only the marker): all 3 passed.
- `test_one_sided_expert_output_in_workspace` dispatches through `FlashInferNVLinkOneSidedManager`, writes the expert output into the buffer returned by `allocate_fused_expert_output`, runs the real `finalize()`, and checks that combine got `payload_in_workspace=True` and the output is exact.
- `test_moe_layer.py -k flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided`: 2 passed, 8 skipped (no supported config / EPLB requires EP).

### Microbenchmark (communication only)

EP4 on B200, hidden 4096, top_k 10, 512 experts, NVFP4 dispatch, bf16 combine, random routing. `flashinfer.testing.bench_gpu_time_with_cupti` with cold L2 and CUDA graphs, 100 iterations, median of the slowest rank. The "with copy" case passes a separate expert-output tensor (current vLLM), the "no copy" case passes the buffer from `get_combine_input_buffer()`. No expert GEMM in either case, so the difference is the removed copy.

| tokens/rank | AGRS (us) | one-sided, with copy (us) | one-sided, no copy (us) | delta |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1024 | 169.2 | 97.9 | 92.0 | −5.9 |
| 4096 | 357.8 | 324.5 | 281.4 | −43.1 |
| 16384 | 982.3 | 1195.3 | 1034.4 | −160.9 |

p10–p90 of the one-sided medians stays within ±1.5%. nsys shows `moeA2APrepareCombineKernel` at 13.4 us (1K) and 163.3 us (16K) per call, matching the 4K/16K deltas.

### End-to-end

One server at a time on the same GPUs 0–3 of the node: the full sweep on the baseline server, then the server is stopped and this PR is started on the same GPUs and runs the same sweep. Load comes from the Rust benchmark client (`vllm-bench` 0.1.0), which starts in milliseconds, so the measured window is not affected by client startup:

```bash
vllm serve nvidia/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-NVFP4 \
  --data-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel \
  --all2all-backend flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 32768 --max-model-len 40960 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --moe-backend flashinfer_trtllm \
  --language-model-only --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache --max-num-seqs 512 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85

# prefill-bound: ~10M input tokens per point, 1 output token, all requests at once
vllm-bench --backend vllm --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8101 \
  --model nvidia/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-NVFP4 --tokenizer <local snapshot> \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len $ISL --random-output-len 1 \
  --random-range-ratio 1.0 --num-prompts $((10 * 1048576 / ISL)) \
  --request-rate inf --ignore-eos --seed 10
```

One run per ISL and server, after a 1024-prompt warmup. Both servers got the same prompts (same seed, identical input token counts) and no request failed.

| ISL | prompts | baseline input tok/s | this PR input tok/s | ratio | baseline duration (s) | this PR duration (s) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 512 | 20480 | 130205 | 134084 | 1.030x | 80.4 | 78.1 |
| 1024 | 10240 | 133693 | 138033 | 1.032x | 78.3 | 75.9 |
| 2048 | 5120 | 135770 | 138764 | 1.022x | 77.2 | 75.5 |
| 4096 | 2560 | 134813 | 137933 | 1.023x | 77.7 | 76.0 |
| 8192 | 1280 | 132550 | 134780 | 1.017x | 79.1 | 77.8 |
| 16384 | 640 | 128228 | 129970 | 1.014x | 81.8 | 80.7 |
| 32768 | 320 | 117129 | 119326 | 1.019x | 89.5 | 87.9 |

The ~2% at long ISL matches what the removed copy predicts. With 32K batched tokens per rank the copy costs ~0.33 ms per MoE layer, ~20 ms over the model's 60 MoE layers, against a prefill step of ~1.1 s (4 × 32K tokens at ~117K tok/s).

gsm8k (5-shot, `lm_eval --model local-completions`, 1319 questions):

| | flexible-extract | strict-match |
|---|---:|---:|
| baseline | 0.8135 ± 0.0107 | 0.7930 ± 0.0112 |
| this PR | 0.8211 ± 0.0106 | 0.7998 ± 0.0110 |

## Details

**Root cause.** Combine in the one-sided backend is pull-based: each rank reads its tokens' partial results directly from the owners' workspace over NVLink, so the expert output must live in the symmetric workspace. `FlashInferNVLinkOneSidedPrepareAndFinalize` did not override `allocate_fused_expert_output`, so the modular kernel gave the experts a buffer from vLLM's workspace manager and `finalize()` passed that buffer to `combine()`. FlashInfer then launched `moeA2APrepareCombineKernel` with `ep_size * tokens_per_rank` CTAs to copy every received row into the combine region. `NaiveDPEPPrepareAndFinalize` (AGRS) already overrides the hook, so AGRS never paid an equivalent copy.

**Change.** `allocate_fused_expert_output` returns `communication.get_combine_input_buffer(dtype)`, a `[ep_size * tokens_per_rank, hidden]` view of this rank's combine region. `finalize()` is unchanged: `NVLinkOneSidedAlltoAll.combine()` compares the payload pointer with that buffer and passes `payload_in_workspace=True`, and FlashInfer reduces the copy kernel to a single CTA that only bumps the round flag. The hook returns `None` (old behavior) unless the experts reduce top-k themselves (`TopKWeightAndReduceNoOP`), the dtype is bf16/fp16 (the combine region is sized for 16-bit rows), and shape and device match.

**Why it is safe.**

- The combine region starts after the last dispatch payload region (cacheline aligned), so experts can read the dispatched activations while writing their output.
- Peers may still be reading a rank's combine region right after its combine returns. The next layer's experts write that region only after the next dispatch, which waits for completion flags that every peer sets after its own combine. This is the same point where the staging copy writes today.
- The view is valid between dispatch and combine. The modular kernel calls the hook from `_fused_experts`, after `_prepare` (dispatch) and before `_finalize` (combine). The address depends only on the workspace base and `runtime_max_tokens_per_rank`, so CUDA graph capture is unaffected.
- No new host-device synchronization: the hook only builds a tensor view.

**Duplicate check.** No open or closed PR touches `allocate_fused_expert_output` or `get_combine_input_buffer` for this backend (`gh pr list --search` on both names, "nvlink one sided combine copy", and `flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided`). Related but different: #59134 (dispatch sizing for experts that quantize their own inputs).

**AI assistance.** This change, its tests, the benchmarks and this description were prepared with AI assistance (Claude). The submitter has reviewed every changed line and the results above.

---

commits.pr_title: [Test][UMBP] Cover end-to-end restore while the embedded DRAM pool is evicting
commits.pr_body:
- Let the `umbp_llm` fixture take pool options through indirect parametrization.
- Add `test_restore_under_pool_eviction` on a 64 MiB pool: the newest prompt restores exactly, the oldest is evicted.

The existing end-to-end UMBP tests never fill the pool, so the connector and scheduler path under eviction never runs, and `test_mori_embedded_gpu.py` only overfills it at the runtime level. Prompts run one at a time so MORI's LRU commit order is deterministic, and the pool size assumes Qwen3-0.6B KV on MORI's 64 KiB pages. On MI350X with MORI v1.2.3.post1 built with UMBP, `pytest -v -s -rs v1/kv_connector/umbp_integration/test_mori_token_e2e.py` gave 3 passed and the new test passed 10/10 in a loop. With a 1 GiB pool the same flow restores the oldest prompt in full, so the miss comes from eviction. While probing this we found that equal watermarks, or a high watermark at or below MORI's default low of 0.7, silently disable eviction; that fix is a separate PR. No open UMBP PR covers end-to-end restore under eviction.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to draft this change. Every line was reviewed by the submitter.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Honor add_generation_prompt and continue_final_message in the DeepSeek V4.1 tokenizer
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Fixes #64431. Python-frontend part of #46256 on DeepSeek V4.1 (`vllm/tokenizers/deepseek_v41_encoding.py`).

The V4.1 encoder ignores `add_generation_prompt` and `continue_final_message`. When the last message is an assistant message, the prompt always ends at `<｜end▁of▁sentence｜>` without an `<｜Assistant｜>` turn prefix, so the model returns empty or garbled text with HTTP 200. With `continue_final_message=true`, the final message is still closed with EOS, so the reply cannot continue it.

This PR makes the V4.1 encoder honor both controls, and declares turn boundaries for the V4.1 parser so that the prompt-aware reasoning start from #61857 also applies to V4.1. It is the Python counterpart of the Rust-frontend fix in #62189 and uses the same semantics. The encoder change is a port of #57882 by @xijiaat (closed without review; credited as co-author of the commit) onto current `main` (after #60792, image order, and #62199, the 1017 reference encoding).

**Related, not duplicates:** #62199 (merged) and #62196 (open) sync turn handling with the 1017 reference encoder (tool-result turns) and do not touch the generation controls. #62459 (open) fixes a conversation whose final message is `system`; this PR leaves that case to it and only changes conversations that end with an assistant message. #62887 (open) fixes `continue_final_message` only, by setting `wo_eos` on the final assistant message; this PR also covers `add_generation_prompt`. #64493 (draft) makes the same change for V3.2.

**Behaviour change:** a conversation that ends with an assistant message now gets a new assistant turn by default (`add_generation_prompt=true`), as with Hugging Face chat templates and #62189. To continue the final assistant message, clients send `continue_final_message=true`. Callers that pass `add_generation_prompt=false` explicitly for a conversation ending with a user message now get a prompt without the assistant turn prefix (see Details).

## Claims

- `add_generation_prompt=true` (the default): when the final message is an assistant message, the prompt now equals the DeepSeek reference encoding of the conversation followed by the reference assistant turn prefix, `<｜Assistant｜><think>` in thinking mode and `<｜Assistant｜></think>` in chat mode. The comparison is token-for-token. Earlier assistant messages keep their EOS.
- `add_generation_prompt=false`: for a conversation that ends with an assistant message, the prompt is unchanged from before and equals the DeepSeek reference encoder output. For any other final message the prompt now ends without the assistant turn prefix, as the flag asks (before, the flag was ignored).
- `continue_final_message=true`: the final assistant message is left open (no EOS). If it ends inside its reasoning, the reasoning is left open as well. A request without a final assistant message is rejected with HTTP 400 (before, the flag was ignored and the request returned 200).
- With the default `add_generation_prompt=true`, prompts that end with a user, developer or system message are token-identical to before.
- A final assistant message that is already left open with `wo_eos` (only possible when calling `encode_messages` directly; requests cannot set it) gets no new assistant turn, so it renders exactly as before.
- With `turn_boundary_tokens` declared, the V4.1 parser starts in content when the current turn's prompt already closed reasoning (for example a continued answer after `</think>`). A `</think>` in an earlier turn does not count.
- Fixes empty and garbled replies on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with the Python frontend: 210/280 empty replies before this change, 2/280 after (both remaining ones hit `max_tokens` while still reasoning).

## Validation

Setup for all server-side checks: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 4×H200 with TP4, image `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly-e68efc68`, Python frontend (`VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=0`), `--tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 --reasoning-parser deepseek_v41 --tool-call-parser deepseek_v41`, speculative decoding with the model's built-in draft module (`--speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block","enable_adaptive_verification":false}'`). "Before" overlays the affected Python files from `main` @ `6e780d14` (the nightly predates #60792 and #62199); "after" overlays the same files with this PR. A fresh server for each side. These checks predate the rebase onto `main` @ `2eae56c4b`, which needed no conflict resolution, and the `wo_eos` check, which no request can reach (the E2E section below was run on the current head `3c8a7257`).

**Reference encoder.** The server's `/tokenize` output was compared, as token ids, with the updated reference `encoding/encoding.py` of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. Seven conversation shapes, each with thinking on and off:

| Shape | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| ends with user (2 shapes) | = reference | = reference (unchanged) |
| ends with assistant (5 shapes): plain, with `reasoning_content`, after a multi-turn history, with a system message, with `tool_calls` | = reference closed history (ends at EOS, no turn prefix) | = reference + `<｜Assistant｜>` + `<think>`/`</think>` |

**Unchanged paths render identically.** The exact lm-eval requests were re-rendered with both versions (sha1 of the token ids):

| Requests | identical |
|---|---|
| GSM8K 5-shot (1,319) | 1,319 / 1,319 |
| IFEval (541) | 541 / 541 |
| HumanEval-instruct, prefill **without** `continue_final_message` (164) | 0 / 164: each differs by exactly the 2 opener tokens (see Behaviour change) |
| HumanEval-instruct, prefill with `continue_final_message` (164) | 0 / 164: each is exactly 1 token shorter (the final EOS is no longer appended) |

Of 342 saved request bodies from our other end-to-end tests (tools, streaming, `reasoning_effort`, `json_schema`, multi-turn agent loops), 335 render identically; the 5 that end with an assistant message differ as described above (3 gain the 2 opener tokens, 2 that continue the final message lose its EOS); the 2 that use the `latest_reminder` role are rejected with HTTP 400 on both sides (that role is not supported by this renderer).

**End-to-end, final assistant message.** Each cell is 40 requests: 20 greedy (`max_tokens` 1024) and 20 with T=1.0, top_p=0.95 (`max_tokens` 4096).

| Request shape | before: empty replies | after: empty replies |
|---|---|---|
| `[user]` (control) | 1 | 0 |
| `[user, assistant(code prefix)]`, no flags | 40 | 0 (40 replies with code) |
| same, `continue_final_message=true`, `add_generation_prompt=false` | 40 | 0 (40 replies continue the code) |
| `[user, assistant(complete answer)]`, thinking on | 35 | 1 (hit `max_tokens`) |
| same, thinking off | 20 | 0 |
| `[user, assistant(code prefix)]`, content as a list of text parts | 40 | 0 |
| `[user, assistant(complete answer)]`, content as a list of text parts | 34 | 1 (hit `max_tokens`) |
| **total** | **210 / 280** | **2 / 280** |

Before the change, 4 replies also leaked special-token text; after it there are no leaks and no garbled starts, and the 2 empty replies spent all 1,024 tokens in reasoning (`finish_reason=length`). The `[user]` control renders the same prompt on both sides, so its one empty reply before is run-to-run variance. A conversation that ends with a system message is unchanged by this PR (0/40 empty on both sides). Server logs have no errors.

**End-to-end on the current head: generation flags** (added for review). Run on this PR's head `3c8a7257`. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 on 4×H200, TP4, image `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly-335dd77b` (= this PR's base `main` @ `2eae56c4b` plus one unrelated commit), Python frontend, the serve arguments listed above, plus `--moe-backend marlin` on both sides: this nightly's default MXFP4 MoE backend on Hopper (Humming) fails at startup for V4.1-Flash at TP4, which is #63793. "Before" is the image as is; "after" overlays this PR's 3 changed Python files. A fresh server for each side.

Prompt: server `/tokenize` (chat messages + flags) compared as token ids with the reference `encoding/encoding.py` of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. Expected = the reference encoding; a new assistant turn ends in `<｜Assistant｜>` + `</think>` (thinking off) or `<think>` (thinking on); `continue_final_message` leaves the final assistant turn open (no EOS). Every row was checked with thinking off and on, with the same result.

| Final message | `add_generation_prompt` | `continue_final_message` | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| user | True | false | = expected | = expected |
| user | False | false | assistant prefix still added (+2 tokens) | = expected |
| assistant (complete answer) | True | false | no new assistant turn (ends at EOS, −2 tokens) | = expected |
| assistant (complete answer, content as a list of text parts) | True | false | no new assistant turn (−2 tokens) | = expected |
| assistant (complete answer) | False | false | = expected | = expected |
| assistant (code prefix) | True | false | no new assistant turn (−2 tokens) | = expected |
| assistant (code prefix) | False | true | EOS still appended (+1 token) | = expected |
| assistant (code prefix) | True | true | HTTP 400 | HTTP 400 |

The last row is rejected by the chat API itself on both sides ("Cannot set both `continue_final_message` and `add_generation_prompt` to True").

Generation: 20 requests per cell, 10 greedy (`max_tokens` 1024) and 10 with T=1.0, top_p=0.95 (`max_tokens` 4096), for thinking off and thinking on. Each reply is put in the first class that matches, by how its `content` opens: **reasoning only** (`content` empty, the text is in `reasoning_content`; this is what the section above counts as an empty reply), **empty** (both empty), **user-voice line** (it opens as the user's next turn, e.g. `> Explain how it works.`; no special token is involved), **continues** (continues the code prefix, or the user's own text), **odd start** (opens with junk such as `-1`, `+++`, `@@`, `#include`, a base64 string or `<｜end▁of▁thinking｜>`), **answer** (a normal reply).

Thinking off:

| Final message, flags | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| user, `add_generation_prompt=True` | 20 answer | 20 answer |
| user, `add_generation_prompt=False` | 20 answer (the prompt still had the assistant prefix) | 17 empty, 2 continue the user's text, 1 answer |
| assistant (complete), `add_generation_prompt=True` | 14 user-voice line, 6 odd start | 20 answer |
| assistant (complete, list of text parts), `add_generation_prompt=True` | 15 user-voice line, 4 odd start, 1 answer | 20 answer |
| assistant (complete), `add_generation_prompt=False` | 11 user-voice line, 9 odd start | 11 user-voice line, 9 odd start |
| assistant (code prefix), `add_generation_prompt=True` | 17 continue the code after the EOS, 2 answer, 1 odd start | 18 answer, 2 continue the code |
| assistant (code prefix), `continue_final_message=true` | 18 continue the code, 1 answer, 1 odd start | 20 continue the code |

Thinking on:

| Final message, flags | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| user, `add_generation_prompt=True` | 20 answer | 20 answer |
| user, `add_generation_prompt=False` | 20 answer (the prompt still had the assistant prefix) | 20 continue the user's text in `reasoning_content`; 9 of them then also write a reply in `content` (see notes) |
| assistant (complete), `add_generation_prompt=True` | 16 reasoning only, 4 answer | 20 answer |
| assistant (complete, list of text parts), `add_generation_prompt=True` | 18 reasoning only, 2 answer | 20 answer |
| assistant (complete), `add_generation_prompt=False` | 19 reasoning only, 1 answer | 17 odd start, 1 user-voice line, 2 answer (see notes) |
| assistant (code prefix), `add_generation_prompt=True` | 19 reasoning only, 1 answer | 19 answer, 1 continues the code |
| assistant (code prefix), `continue_final_message=true` | 19 reasoning only, 1 answer | 20 continue the code |

Notes:

- With thinking on, "before" shows the same failure as the section above: the reply text ends up in `reasoning_content` and `content` is empty (19/20 for `continue_final_message=true`, 16/20 for a complete final answer; above: 40/40 and 35/40). With thinking off, a complete final answer gives a user-voice line or an odd start instead (14/20 and 15/20 user-voice lines); a code prefix is mostly continued even after the EOS (17/20 and 18/20), so for that shape the old prompt fails mainly with thinking on (the code-prefix rows above were run with thinking on, the server default). This run uses a newer nightly, `--moe-backend marlin`, and classifies replies by how they open, so its counts are not comparable one to one with the section above; both runs show the same direction.
- `add_generation_prompt=False` after a complete final assistant message: the prompt is identical on both sides and equals the reference (the conversation is closed at EOS), and 9 of the 10 greedy replies are the same text on both sides. What changes with thinking on is which field the text goes to. Before, the parser treats it as still inside reasoning (19/20 reasoning only); with this PR's `turn_boundary_tokens` it does not, so the same text is returned as `content`. Both are continuations after a closed conversation, not answers.
- `add_generation_prompt=False` after a user message: the prompt now has no assistant turn, as requested, so the model continues the user's own text. With thinking on, all 20 replies start by continuing the user's sentence inside `reasoning_content` (e.g. ` It should be ... handle large numbers efficiently.`); 11 stop there with empty `content`, and 9 then also write a reply in `content`. 8 of the 20 contain special-token text such as `<｜place▁holder▁no▁798｜>` (in `reasoning_content`), and 10 hit `max_tokens`. This combination is meant for `/tokenize` or scoring, not for chat generation. Elsewhere, special-token text appears in 2 "before" replies (`<｜end▁of▁thinking｜>`) and in no "after" reply.

commits.pr_title: [Core][CUDA Graph] Separate prefill (token) and decode (request) CUDA graph capture sizes
commits.pr_body:
## 1. Why this change A CUDA graph's batch size means different things for two kinds of step: - A prefill or mixed batch is sized by its **tokens**. - A uniform decode batch, where every request has the same query length `q = 1 + K`, is sized by its **requests** and `q`. On main, model runner V2 captures both from one token list (`cudagraph_capture_sizes`, capped at 1024 tokens on GB200). A decode graph must be a list entry divisible by `q`, so the larger K is, the fewer decode requests the graphs cover, and every mixed batch above 1024 tokens runs eagerly. Example: with the 1024-token cap and K = 7 (`q = 8`), decode graphs cover at most 128 requests. Uniform decode batches above 128 requests exceed main's FULL coverage. This is the "separate prefill/decode graph sizes" item of the Q4 roadmap (#61024). ## 2. What this PR changes This PR adds five configuration fields: a cap and a capture-size list for each kind of graph, plus a token budget for uniform decode graphs. Prefill coverage is configured in tokens; uniform decode coverage is configured in requests. | field | unit | controls | default on SM100 (GB200, B200) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `max_prefill_cudagraph_capture_tokens` | tokens | Maximum token count for prefill, mixed, and fallback decode PIECEWISE graphs | `min(8192, max_num_batched_tokens)` | | `prefill_cudagraph_capture_token_sizes` | tokens | Token counts at which those graphs are captured | Default prefill grid up to the cap: 54 sizes at 8192 tokens | | `max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests` | requests | Request-count cap for uniform decode FULL graphs, before applying the token budget | `max_num_seqs` | | `decode_cudagraph_capture_request_sizes` | requests | Request-count capture sizes, converted by each runner into `n × q` tokens | Default decode grid up to the cap: 64 sizes at 1024 requests, before applying the token budget | | `max_decode_cudagraph_capture_tokens` | tokens | Maximum token count of each uniform decode graph | 8192 | For either kind, setting only a cap generates the default grid up to that cap. An explicit list selects the capture sizes; if a cap is also supplied, the list must fit within it. An empty list disables that kind. The decode request grid is the starting point for capture planning. Each runner uses its own query length `q` and captures only shapes that fit its execution limits and token budget. At the default 1024-request cap, the target captures 64 decode sizes through 1024 requests for K ≤ 7, or 48 sizes through 512 requests for K = 15. Wider target decode batches try the prefill token graphs before falling back to eager execution. The token budget also bounds adaptive-verification graphs. It does not bound one-token draft decodes, which reach `max_num_seqs` whatever the decode caps are (only `[]` turns them off). On other GPUs, the prefill and target decode defaults stay as on main. **How the defaults were chosen.** Defaults trade padding and coverage against memory/startup cost; current padding measurements are in appendix A. The decode budget limits wide graphs (why 8192: section 5.1); explicit lists/caps support workload- and parallelism-specific tuning. The default configuration and tuned performance ceiling are separate evaluation targets.
Grids, other GPUs and edge rules Defaults on other GPUs: the prefill cap is the platform's `max_cudagraph_capture_size` (512 on H100 / H200) and the prefill sizes are main's list; the decode cap is main's reach, 512 / (1 + K) requests, with main's request counts; there is no decode token budget. | what you set for a kind | graphs captured for that kind | | --- | --- | | nothing | the default grid up to the default cap | | a cap only | the default grid up to that cap | | a list only | exactly those sizes | | both | the list; a size above the cap is an error | | `[]` | none | - **Grids.** - **Prefill** / mixed (tokens): 1, 2, 4, every 8 up to 64, four sizes per doubling up to 1024 (…, 512, 640, 768, 896, 1024), then multiples of 256 through 7680, followed by 8192 — **54 capture sizes** at the default cap. Between 64 and 1024 tokens, a mixed batch pads by at most 25%, reducing padding-induced crossings of a model's own shape threshold (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's decoder-replay trim at 768 tokens; DEP section). - **Decode (requests):** every count from 1–6; then 8–16 in steps of 2, 20–48 in steps of 4, 56–128 in steps of 8, 144–352 in steps of 16, and 384–1024 in steps of 32. **64 capture sizes before applying the decode-token budget**; the default 8192-token budget keeps all of them for K ≤ 7 and limits target K=15 to **512 requests / 48 sizes**. - **Adaptive verification (tokens):** 1, 2, 4, 8; then four additional sizes per doubling through 1024—for example, 10, 12, 14, 16, followed by 20, 24, 28, 32. Above 1024, use steps of 128 through 4096, then steps of 256. The cap is `min(decode request cap × (K + 1), max_num_batched_tokens, max_decode_cudagraph_capture_tokens)`; **K=5 with a 1024-request cap gives 64 sizes through 6144 tokens**. Adaptive verification picks its verify width from the captured sizes, so this grid is finer than the prefill grid. - Sizes above `max_num_batched_tokens` (prefill) or `max_num_seqs` (decode) are dropped with a warning. `[]` for both kinds turns decoder CUDA graphs off. Under `cudagraph_mode` FULL or PIECEWISE (no separate decode routine) every batch uses the prefill sizes; under FULL_DECODE_ONLY the prefill sizes are not captured and do not count toward the recorded maximum. - Setting one kind leaves the other kind's graphs unchanged. Exception: DSpark, DFlash, DFlash2 and LiLiCorr are also capped by the resolved `max_cudagraph_capture_size` divided by their `q`. That value is the largest token count over the language-model/drafter graphs: prefill sizes, target decode `n · q`, one-token draft decodes and adaptive-verification sizes. At the SM100 defaults with K ≤ 7 it is the 8192-token prefill cap. Off SM100 with an EAGLE-family drafter it is the one-token draft decode reach (`max_num_seqs`, 1024), above the 512-token prefill cap. - `cudagraph_capture_sizes` and `max_cudagraph_capture_size` are deprecated on model runner V2. Set alone, they seed both kinds as on main, with a warning; combined with the new fields, they raise. Adaptive verification, DSpark and one-token draft decodes do not reproduce main's graphs under them. Model runner V1 is unchanged and rejects the new fields. ```bash # Before: one cap for both kinds, in tokens. --compilation-config '{"max_cudagraph_capture_size": 1024}' # After: delete it to take the defaults, or set each kind in its own unit. --compilation-config '{"max_prefill_cudagraph_capture_tokens": 8192, "max_decode_cudagraph_capture_requests": 256}' # Prefill instance of a disaggregated deployment: no decode graphs. Adaptive verification # needs decode graphs and is rejected with this; a prefill instance never verifies, so disable it there. --compilation-config '{"decode_cudagraph_capture_request_sizes": []}' # Decode instance of a disaggregated deployment: FULL decode (and adaptive verification) only, no PIECEWISE graphs. --compilation-config '{"prefill_cudagraph_capture_token_sizes": []}' ```

The target and EAGLE-family draft step 0 see the 1 + K verified positions (`q = 1 + K`); later EAGLE-family steps add one token (`q = 1`); DSpark drafts K positions per round (`q = K`); DFlash, DFlash2, LiLiCorr and multi-module MTP draft K + 1 (`q = K + 1`). Dynamic SD changes the target's verification length. EAGLE-family drafters also shorten their drafting sequence, while DSpark and DFlash currently retain their maximum draft-block width (K = 7: all 1024 requests under the 8192-token budget). A graph for `n` requests holds `n · q` tokens, which is what the decode budget bounds. **The decode budget** applies to every FULL uniform-decode graph with `q > 1`: the target's, the drafter copies of it, DSpark, DFlash and multi-module MTP. DSpark and DFlash drafters have no PIECEWISE fallback, so a narrower budget runs them eagerly. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash DSpark K7 with adaptive verification this costs no steady-state throughput (8192 / 4096 budget: 0.990× / 0.998× / 1.002× at C512 / C768 / C1024 over 4 + 4 alternating launches on two nodes), but it makes each step depend on the host's launch speed: with 4096 tokens the step-time spread across launches is 3× larger, and a launch on a slow host loses 4.0 ms per step instead of 0.4 ms. A decode instance has no prefill grid, so without adaptive verification a decode step wider than the budget runs entirely eagerly, which is 1.6× / 1.2× slower at 6144 / 8192 tokens. Above 8192 tokens the budget stays: at K11 (12288 tokens) wider graphs cost 7.8 GiB more graph memory with no throughput gain, and above 14,527 decode rows DeepSeek-V4's FlashMLA sparse decode fails at capture. The cost of 8192 over 4096 is 0.8–3.3 GiB of graph memory (1–3% of KV on DeepSeek, 7% on GLM-5.3), measured directly in the table above. Users can lower `max_decode_cudagraph_capture_tokens` where KV capacity matters more.

### 5.2 DFlash graph memory and the MiMo limitation DFlash and DFlash2 drafters have no PIECEWISE fallback, so at K7–K8 the 8192-token budget gives their FULL graphs up to 8190 tokens (main: about 1024). On MiMo this adds 10.2 GiB of graph memory, from two sources. The target's widest prefill graph (8192 tokens) takes 5.4 GiB more than main's (1024 tokens), mostly FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE workspace. The DFlash drafter's widest graph (8190 tokens) takes 5.45 GiB, against 0.68 GiB on main, because it materializes full-vocabulary draft logits three times (the TP all-gather output, a contiguous copy and the vocabulary remap; about 2.07 GiB each). None of this is a leak. `graph_capture()` gives the target and the drafter separate capture streams, and the caching allocator keeps free graph-pool blocks per stream, so neither runner reuses the other's free blocks. Capturing every graph on one stream per device (#59537) brings MiMo from 14.16 to 12.84 GiB of graph memory; it also helps beyond DFlash: DeepSeek-V4-Flash DSpark K7 with AV 12.67 → 9.01 GiB, GLM-5.3 DFlash2 12.41 → 11.12 GiB, Qwen3-8B DFlash 5.75 → 4.77 GiB (main's MiMo: 3.93 → 3.76 GiB; one launch each, GSM8K unchanged). The order of capture then matters, because the graphs captured second reuse the free blocks of those captured first: capturing MiMo's drafter, its widest graphs, before the target brings MiMo to 9.89 GiB and lets the vLLM recipe command (`--max-model-len auto`, adaptive verification on) start at the full 1,048,576-token context, as on main, but costs 1.68 GiB on DeepSeek-V4-Flash DSpark and 0.26 GiB on GLM DFlash2, so it is not a default. With the shared stream alone, the recipe command still does not start: a 1,048,576-token request needs 15.06 GiB of KV cache and 13.96 GiB is left. **Known limitation:** with this PR, that recipe command (`--max-model-len auto`) fails at startup on 4x GB200. With the extensible KV cache, `auto` is fitted before CUDA graphs and warmup take their memory, and main only checks the fitted length afterwards. The error names the length that fits (`estimated maximum model length is ...`). An explicit `--max-model-len 524288` starts and passes GSM8K (93.8% / 94.5%). Lowering `max_decode_cudagraph_capture_tokens` to 4096 cuts graph memory to 11.05 GiB. Fitting `auto` again after warmup is a follow-up: CUDA graphs captured at the planning-time length would need recapturing, or must stop baking the length in. ## 6. Appendix A. How the grids were chosen **Data.** The rule was derived from traces on earlier PR heads; the padding cost in (c) is a current measurement. **The rule.** Each grid captures a graph wherever padding to the next size would cost more than a fixed share ε of the step's time. A batch runs on the smallest graph that holds it, and padded rows are not free, so the spacing between sizes follows how fast step time grows with batch size, regime by regime. **(a) Decode step rule.** - Padding a batch of `n` by δ costs about `e(n) · δ / n` of its step time, where `e(n) = n · c′(n) / T(n)`. - Bounding the mean cost by ε gives the local step `Δ(n) = 2εn / e(n)`. - One envelope over all measured models, `e ≈ n^(1/3) / 5`, gives `Δ(n) = 10 ε n^(2/3)`. Rounded down to a power of two, with ε = 0.065, that is the decode rule: 64 sizes at 1024. **(b) PIECEWISE rule.** PIECEWISE step time is flat below 1–4K tokens and linear above. The same rule with `e_PW(t) = min(1, t / 4096)` and ε = 0.035 gives the prefill grid: 39 sizes at 8192, which sum to 127,487 tokens (main: 35,335). The default now also caps the step at a quarter of the size below 1024 (at least 8), giving 54 sizes; it bounds small-size padding at 25% so a padded size cannot jump across a model's own threshold (DEP section). **(c) Current padding cost.** Single prefill (pure) or one prefill injected into 16 running decodes (mixed), no SD, no prefix cache, 8192 batched tokens; median of 15 per point, with the dispatch checked for each point. commits.pr_title: [ROCm][Perf][MiniMax-M3.1] Score DSpark 7 decode locally below 3 requests instead of via indexer CP
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

With `indexer_decode_cp` at TP4 (#64448), every DSpark 7 decode step scores through the context-parallel
push kernel (`m3_nvfp4_index_score_push_cp`), whatever the batch size. Its two cross-rank handshakes (index-q
exchange, then score push plus a four-rank done barrier) cost a fixed ~13 us per layer that does not shrink with
the batch, so at 1-2 requests the kernel spends its time waiting, while the single-head scorer
(`m3_nvfp4_index_score_decode_r8h1`, each rank scores its own head over the whole context, no cross-rank traffic)
takes 6-9 us. This PR scores steps of fewer than `CP_MIN_REQS = 3` requests (8 rows each) with the single-head
scorer, which is the path the scorer already takes when CP is off. Steps of 3 or more requests, and DSpark 3 (4 rows
per request), are unchanged.

Not covered by an existing PR: #64448 (merged) enables CP for DSpark 7 at any batch size; #65087/#65267 only touch the top-k.

## Root cause (kernel level)

Per-layer kernel durations from the torch profiler (rank 0, 120 decode steps per window, 150K-token real-text
contexts, DBO off, `VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM=0`), before / after this change:

| N requests | scorer before | scorer after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `m3_nvfp4_index_score_push_cp` 15.8 us avg (p50 13.0) | `m3_nvfp4_index_score_decode_r8h1` 7.0 us |
| 2 | `m3_nvfp4_index_score_push_cp` 14.9 us avg (p50 13.3) | `m3_nvfp4_index_score_decode_r8h1` 9.7 us |

(58 sparse layers per step: 0.92 -> 0.41 ms/step at N=1 and 0.87 -> 0.57 ms/step at N=2.)

Isolated, four ranks, CUDA-graph replay of 8 back-to-back calls with the L2 flushed before each replay, `max_seq_len`
1M as in the captured graph, 8 rows per request, context lengths uniform in [0.7, 1.3] x the stated mean; CP vs
single-head scorer, us per call. The scores of the two kernels are bit-identical in all 28 cells.

| requests | 30K: CP / single-head | 150K: CP / single-head | 400K: CP / single-head | 800K: CP / single-head |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 14.2 / 6.2 | 14.2 / 6.4 | 14.1 / 9.2 | 14.9 / 16.4 |
| 2 | 15.0 / 7.4 | 14.4 / 9.0 | 15.1 / 13.1 | 18.4 / 23.7 |
| 3 | 14.6 / 8.7 | 14.5 / 11.3 | 15.4 / 17.6 | 19.8 / 29.6 |
| 4 | 14.8 / 7.0 | 15.0 / 15.1 | 18.8 / 26.1 | 24.7 / 48.9 |
| 6 | 16.0 / 8.2 | 15.3 / 18.3 | 23.8 / 33.0 | 35.0 / 64.5 |
| 8 | 15.7 / 8.6 | 18.8 / 22.0 | 25.7 / 45.5 | 43.8 / 82.1 |
| 16 | 15.8 / 13.3 | 24.1 / 36.0 | 45.6 / 85.9 | 85.3 / 160.4 |

CP is a fixed ~14-15 us up to 4 requests; the single-head scorer grows with the pages it reads (one head, all
blocks) and loses once a step reads ~4-5K index pages in total (4 requests at 150K, 2-3 at 400K). The gate is on the
request count because under CUDA graphs `max_seq_len` is the model maximum, so the batch's context is not known when
the graph is captured. 3 requests at 150K would also win (11.3 vs 14.5 us) but loses at 400K (17.6 vs 15.4 us) and
showed no end-to-end gain, so the gate stops at 2 requests.

## End-to-end (decode step p50, ms; same server flags, only this change differs)

MI355X x4, TP4, `amd/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-Quark-MXFP4`, NVFP4 KV and NVFP4 indexer with `indexer_decode_cp`,
DSpark 7 with synthetic acceptance 4.04, DBO off, `VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM=0`, 150K-token prompts, N concurrent
decodes (`decode_bench.py <port> 150000 N`: p50 of the gap between streamed chunks once all N streams are
decoding, 900 output tokens, 3 passes per server, median of the passes). "base" is the mean of two server instances
(range in brackets); the change was measured on a third instance. The change was run with `CP_MIN_REQS = 4` (one
request more than this PR gates), which only affects the N=3 row; at N=3 this PR keeps CP, i.e. is the base.
Steps of 4 or more requests take the same code path as base, so their rows are a measure of server-to-server
noise (within +-0.6%).

Random-token prompts:

| N | base (S1_base,S3_base) | cp_gate_only (S6_cp) | cp_gate_only vs base |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10.27 [10.23-10.30] | 9.83  | -4.2% |
| 2 | 10.86 [10.84-10.87] | 10.61  | -2.3% |
| 3 | 12.34 [12.34-12.35] | 12.38  | +0.3% |
| 4 | 12.75 [12.72-12.77] | 12.70  | -0.4% |
| 5 | 14.35 [14.32-14.38] | 14.28  | -0.5% |
| 6 | 14.64 [14.57-14.71] | 14.64  | +0.0% |
| 8 | 16.14 [16.11-16.18] | 16.05  | -0.6% |
| 12 | 17.67 [17.54-17.80] | 17.62  | -0.3% |
| 16 | 19.52 [19.52-19.52] | 19.46  | -0.3% |

Real-text prompts (python sources; the model's attention is not uniform):

| N | base (S1_base,S3_base) | cp_gate_only (S6_cp) | cp_gate_only vs base |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 11.23 [11.21-11.25] | 10.88  | -3.1% |
| 2 | 12.50 [12.44-12.56] | 12.11  | -3.1% |
| 4 | 14.81 [14.80-14.82] | 14.80  | -0.0% |
| 5 | 16.64 [16.57-16.71] | 16.69  | +0.3% |
| 8 | 18.93 [18.92-18.94] | 18.92  | -0.0% |
| 12 | 20.57 [20.51-20.62] | 20.56  | -0.0% |
| 16 | 22.46 [22.43-22.49] | 22.48  | +0.1% |

## Correctness

* The scorer is not changed. The scores of the CP kernel and the single-head scorer are bit-identical (existing
  `test_index_decode_cp_push_matches_single_head` and the 28-cell sweep above), so the top-k ids and the attention
  output are bit-identical to the CP path: this change only picks which of the two bit-identical scorers runs.
* New `test_decode_cp_gate` (8 cases, unit test of `_decode_cp`).
* `pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_minimax_m3_nvfp4_index.py`: 182 passed (174 existing + 8 new) on MI355X.
* End-to-end sanity: "What is 17*23?" answers 391 at TP4 on a tree with this change (stacked with #65087 and a
  split-count change; greedy; the synthetic-acceptance recipe garbles some of the surrounding text with or without them).

## Limitations

* Measured at 150K contexts (and 30K-800K in the isolated sweep) on MI355X, TP4, DSpark 7 only. DSpark 3 keeps
  CP at every batch size; the crossover for 4-row requests was not measured.
* The gate is conservative for short contexts: at 30K the single-head scorer also wins at 3-16 requests (4 requests 7.0 vs
  14.8 us, 16 requests 13.3 vs 15.8 us). A context-aware choice would need it inside the kernel or two graphs per batch size.
* Requests of ~800K tokens or more at 1-2 requests are slower with the single-head scorer than with CP (800K:
  16.4 vs 14.9 us at 1 request, 23.7 vs 18.4 us at 2). Contexts that long are rare in the target agentic workload
  (30K-500K, mean ~150K).
* DBO on (the recipe): not measured for this change alone. Decode steps do not split under the recipe thresholds, so
  CP is used outside microbatches exactly as before; stacked with two other changes the step was 2-8% lower at N=1..16.
* Server-to-server variation of the decode step is +-0.6% within one machine state; the shared machine also had
  MoE kernel changes land between runs, so only runs from a frozen copy of the install (same state) are compared.

Related: #64448 (DSpark 7 CP), #57909 (indexer CP), #65087 (top-k, independent).

Test command and config (from /home/fai/profile_m31/run): `DBO=0 VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM=0 ./serve.sh 16 0,1,2,3 8000 20000`
= `vllm serve amd/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-Quark-MXFP4 --tensor-parallel-size 4 --attention-config
'{"indexer_kv_dtype":"nvfp4","indexer_decode_cp":true}' --block-size 128 --kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 --max-model-len 1048576
--max-num-batched-tokens 32768 --max-num-seqs 32 --moe-backend aiter --enable-prefix-caching
--disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark",
"num_speculative_tokens":7,"attention_backend":"TRITON_ATTN","kv_cache_dtype":"fp8","draft_sample_method":"probabilistic",
"rejection_sample_method":"synthetic","synthetic_acceptance_length":4.04}'` (+ the InferenceX recipe env:
`VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE=1 VLLM_ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4`),

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][Step5] Exercise the real CSA decode and engine paths in tests
commits.pr_body:
- test_amd_csa_paged.py: decode summary scores, region selection and gated sparse decode attention against FP32 references, on the TP1 (4x16) and TP8 (1x8) head layouts, for single-token decode and 4-row MTP verify, with BF16 and FP8 KV.
- test_amd_model.py: engine test on the reduced registry checkpoint (top-k 16, FP8 KV, block size 32, 300-token chunked prefill) that runs scored prefill and sparse decode end to end, checks that the scored-prefill warmup runs, and compares decode logprobs against a teacher-forced re-prefill.
- test_amd_fp8_kv_init.py: removed, the engine test covers the same FP8 KV and block-size check.

Follow-up to #61837. Most of the ROCm Step5 tests that came with it mock out the code they cover or only check dispatch, so nothing ran the CSA decode chain against a reference or drove the model through the engine. The kernel test is the numerical check: scores, scale, masks, paging and the gate against FP32. The engine test makes sure the real path runs through vLLM. With dummy weights its logits are nearly flat, so a decode wiring bug and a harmless rounding difference across GPUs both move a logprob by one bf16 step. Its logprob tolerance (1e-2) is therefore only a guard against gross breakage, which the docstring says.

On MI355X the Step5 CI step (`pytest -v -s models/step5` plus the Step5 `test_initialization` case), on this branch merged with main, passed 12/12 runs. Both files run in the existing Step5 CI step.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Accept an empty tools array like OpenAI
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Accept `tools: []` on `/v1/chat/completions` like an omitted `tools` field, matching what the OpenAI API does today. Supersedes #49346 (stale, conflicting) and reverses the check from #39780. The Rust frontend keeps its matching check from #63060; that is a follow-up.

## Claims

- `tools: []` with `tool_choice` omitted, `"none"`, `"auto"` or `"required"` now returns a normal chat completion (HTTP 200) instead of 400 `` `tools` must not be an empty array ``, as OpenAI does. Before, every empty array was rejected.
- `tools: []` with a named function still returns 400, and the message now names the function that is not in `tools` (also for non-empty lists), as OpenAI's does.
- Requests without a `tools` field, and with a non-empty `tools` list, are unchanged. `/tokenize` keeps accepting an empty list without its own workaround.

## Validation

**OpenAI today** (gpt-4o-mini, 2026-11-04): `tools: []` returns 200 with text for `tool_choice` omitted, `none`, `auto` and even `required`; a named function returns 400 `no function named 'f' was specified`. So the `empty_array` 400 that #39780 matched no longer exists upstream.

**Live before/after on one H200**, `vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --max-model-len 4096 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser hermes --no-enable-prefix-caching`, before = d8a13402fe (merge-base), after = this branch:

| request | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `tools: []`, no `tool_choice` | 400 `tools` must not be an empty array | 200, text, `finish_reason=length` |
| `tools: []`, `tool_choice: "none"` | 400 | 200, text |
| `tools: []`, `tool_choice: "auto"` (stream and non-stream) | 400 | 200, text, usage present |
| `tools: []`, `tool_choice: "required"` | 400 (param `tools`) | 200, text |
| `tools: []`, named function `f` | 400 (param `tools`) | 400 `` The tool `f` specified in `tool_choice` does not match any of the specified `tools` `` (param `tool_choice`) |
| no `tools`, `tool_choice: "auto"` | 400 | 400, unchanged |
| one tool, `tool_choice: "auto"` | 200, tool call | 200, identical output |
| `/tokenize` chat with `tools: []` | 200 | 200, identical |

```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"model":"Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello in three words."}],"max_tokens":30,"tools":[]}'
```

commits.pr_title: [Rust Frontend] Support --skip-tokenizer-init
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Support `--skip-tokenizer-init` in the Rust frontend: serve token IDs only, without loading a tokenizer, like Python's `skip_tokenizer_init`. The flag was declared unsupported, so `vllm-rs serve` with it exited at startup, and so did `vllm serve` with `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1`, where it arrives through `--args-json`. `tests/entrypoints/openai/completion/test_token_in_token_out.py` (a model directory without tokenizer files) is exactly this use case.

## Claims

| Input | Python | Rust after this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `/v1/completions` with a token-ID prompt | runs; `text` is `""`, token IDs returned on request | same |
| `/inference/v1/generate`, gRPC generate | runs | runs |
| text prompt, chat request, `/tokenize`, `/detokenize` | error | 400 ``"this request needs a tokenizer, which is not loaded when `--skip-tokenizer-init` is set"`` |
| `echo` of a token-ID prompt without `return_token_ids` | `AssertionError` (500) | 400 |
| structured outputs | 400 | 400 (the engine skips its tokenizer too, so it cannot compile grammars); the render server forwards them, since it does not configure the downstream engine |
| `stop` strings, `bad_words` | silently ignored | 400: neither can take effect without a tokenizer (vllm-project/vllm#46310 proposes the same for Python's stop strings) |
| completions `logprobs` | error when a token string is needed; `return_tokens_as_token_ids` works | 400 unless `return_tokens_as_token_ids` (request or server default) applies |
| token-ID range check | model vocab size (vllm-project/vllm#62911) | model vocab size |
| primary EOS | `None`; `generation_config` EOS ids become stop tokens | first `config.json` EOS id (the existing fallback when the tokenizer has no EOS); the rest stay stop tokens |

## Validation

Commands from `.buildkite/scripts/run-rust-frontend-cargo-ci.sh` (`style-clippy` and `test`), run from the repo root on this branch:

```
cargo fmt --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --all -- --check   # ok
cargo sort --workspace --check rust                          # ok
cargo deny --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --config rust/deny.toml check bans   # ok
cargo clippy --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings   # ok
cargo nextest run --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-features --locked --no-fail-fast
# 2417 tests run: 2417 passed, 13 skipped
```

- `vllm-text` `tokenizerless_backend_prepares_token_id_prompts_only`: a token-ID prompt lowers with detokenization off; text prompt, stop strings and `bad_words` are rejected; structured outputs survive `prepare` for the render server; the model vocabulary bounds token IDs.
- `vllm-text` `skip_tokenizer_init_loads_a_model_without_tokenizer_files`: file resolution and backend load ignore a missing `--tokenizer` source and an unparsable `tokenizer_config.json`; EOS comes from the model config.
- `vllm-chat` `skip_tokenizer_init_rejects_every_chat_request`.
- `vllm-server` `skip_tokenizer_init_serves_token_id_completions_only`: a token-ID completion with `return_token_ids` returns `text: ""` and the token IDs; text prompt, `echo`, `stop`, string-form `logprobs`, structured outputs, `/tokenize` and `/detokenize` are 400.
- `vllm-cmd` `skip_tokenizer_init_reaches_backends_and_managed_engine`: the flag from the CLI and from `--args-json`, forwarded to the managed engine.
- E2E on one GB200 GPU, `tests/entrypoints/openai/completion/test_token_in_token_out.py` (Qwen3-0.6B with the tokenizer files removed, dummy weights): with this branch's `vllm-rs` 1 passed; with `main`'s `vllm-rs` 1 error (the frontend rejects `skip_tokenizer_init` in `--args-json` at startup); Python frontend 1 passed. The test can join the Rust frontend CI step after this merges.

## Details

**Design.** The tokenizer is a null object, not an `Option`. Under the flag the text backend holds an `UnavailableTokenizer` whose text operations fail with `TokenizerError::Unavailable`, mapped to `vllm_text::Error::TokenizerUnavailable` (a request validation error, so 400). The `Tokenizer` interface and its consumers (prompt encoding, `tokenize_bad_words`, `/tokenize`, `/detokenize`, echo decoding) are unchanged and fail through their existing error paths. Only two places know the tokenizer is absent: loading, and one `TextBackend::has_tokenizer` flag for the checks that have no tokenizer call to fail.

- **Tokenizer (`vllm-tokenizer`).** `TokenizerError` becomes an enum, `Backend { message }` and `Unavailable`; the rest of this crate's diff is the mechanical rename of its error macro. `UnavailableTokenizer` reports the model vocabulary as its size.
- **CLI (`vllm-cmd`).** `skip_tokenizer_init` moves from the unsupported markers to `ModelArgs`, next to `--tokenizer`, `--revision` and `--hf-config-path`, because like them it decides which model files are read. `ModelArgs::python_args` forwards it to the managed engine, whose structured-output manager would otherwise load a tokenizer. The render server shares `ModelArgs`.
- **Loading (`vllm-text`, `vllm-chat`).** `ModelFileSources::skip_tokenizer_init` reads no tokenizer-side file (tokenizer, `tokenizer_config.json`, chat template; an explicit `--tokenizer` source is not opened), so a cached snapshot only needs `config.json`. `load_model_backends` builds a `TokenizerlessChatBackend` that rejects every chat request, since rendering and output parsing both need a tokenizer.
- **The flag.** `TextRequestProcessor::prepare` sets `detokenize = false`, which reuses the token-only output path and the stop-string rejection from vllm-project/vllm#63789. Structured outputs are rejected in `TextLlm` just before engine submission, since the engine skips its tokenizer too. Completions `logprobs` are rejected up front unless `return_tokens_as_token_ids` applies, because token strings would all be empty and collapse the candidate map instead of failing.
- `/tokenize` and `/detokenize` now map tokenizer errors through `text_submit_error` instead of a blanket 500, so request validation errors there (including prompt truncation) become 400.

**Differences from Python.**

- Stop strings and `bad_words` are rejected rather than silently ignored.
- gpt-oss chat is rejected too. Python's Harmony path happens to work without an HF tokenizer, but nothing tests or documents chat under `--skip-tokenizer-init`; a tokenizer-optional Harmony chat backend is a possible follow-up.
- Structured outputs are rejected even if an independently started engine has its own tokenizer: `skip_tokenizer_init` is one `ModelConfig` field shared by frontend and engine, and Python's frontend rejects them under it regardless of the engine.

Not a duplicate: no open PR implements `--skip-tokenizer-init` in the Rust frontend (searched open PRs for `skip-tokenizer-init` and `skip_tokenizer_init`). AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to prepare this change; the human submitter reviewed every changed line.

commits.pr_title: [Rust Frontend] Drop incomplete tool-call markup at the end of output like Python
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

When generation stops inside a tool call (`max_tokens`, a stop string, or EOS before the closer), drop the unfinished tool-call markup and keep the text before it, like the Python parser engine (vllm-project/vllm#47562, pinned by `tests/parser/engine/test_parser_engine.py::TestTruncatedToolOpenerStreamParity`). Today the Rust frontend returns the truncated markup as assistant `content`.

## Claims

- For Python's own test input `"Checking the weather. <tool_call>\n<function"` with `qwen3_coder`, Rust returned `content: "Checking the weather. \n<function"`; it now returns `"Checking the weather. "`, like Python. An output that is only a truncated call ends with no content.
- Applies to every Rust tool parser family and every finish reason, in streaming and non-streaming (chat completions and the Responses API share the path).
- Other finish errors (malformed but complete markup, e.g. Llama's `invalid Llama JSON`) still fall back to text as before.

## Validation

Commands from `.buildkite/scripts/run-rust-frontend-cargo-ci.sh` (`style-clippy` and `test`), run from the repo root on this branch:

```
cargo fmt --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --all -- --check   # ok
cargo sort --workspace --check rust                          # ok
cargo deny --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --config rust/deny.toml check bans   # ok
cargo clippy --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings   # ok
cargo nextest run --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-features --locked --no-fail-fast
# 2511 tests run: 2511 passed, 13 skipped
```

- `vllm-chat` `unified_stream_drops_incomplete_tool_parser_call_at_eos`: Qwen Coder through `CombinedParser`, Python's input, in four deltas and in one.
- `vllm-chat` `unified_stream_drops_incomplete_gemma4_tool_call_at_eos`: a unified parser, with an empty and a non-empty prefix. It replaces `unified_stream_recovers_incomplete_gemma4_tool_call_at_eos`, which pinned the old fallback.
- Red-green: without the new match arm both fail, with `"Checking the weather. \n<function"` and the full Gemma 4 markup as text. `unified_stream_finish_error_recovers_buffered_text` still pins the fallback for other finish errors.
- `vllm-parser`: the existing `*_finish_fails_incomplete_tool_call` snapshots now show the typed error's message.
- Python's seven `TestTruncatedToolOpenerStreamParity` cases were run against the Python parser engine for comparison.
- Second commit: `responses_streaming_emits_function_call_events` (from the stateless Responses API, vllm-project/vllm#63902) pinned the leaked trailing `}\n</tool_call` text as an extra message item after the function call; the stream now ends after the function call item.

## Details

- `ToolParserError::IncompleteToolCall { parser }` and `UnifiedParserError::IncompleteToolCall { parser }` replace the generic `ParsingFailed("incomplete … tool call")` at every "output ended inside a call" site: the JSON family (Hermes, Qwen3 JSON, Mistral, Phi-4-mini, InternLM2 through the shared parser; Llama JSON; Granite 4), DeepSeek V3/V3.1 JSON, DeepSeek DSML (V3.2/V4/V4.1), GLM-4.5/4.7, Kimi K2, Qwen Coder (and Seed-OSS, Step-5, MiMo through it), MiniMax M2/M3, HY, and the unified Gemma 4, Inkling, Kimi K3 and Muse parsers. `UnifiedParserError::is_incomplete_tool_call` covers both, including a tool parser's error carried through `CombinedParser`.
- `UnifiedParserState::finish` (`rust/src/chat/src/output/default/unified.rs`) drops the parser buffer on that error only. Events already emitted stand, so text before the call is kept. Before this change, every finish error reset the parser and re-emitted the buffer as text (added by vllm-project/vllm#47289 so a truncated-only output would not come back empty).
- Ownership: the parser alone knows it ended inside a call, so it reports a typed error; what to show the client is output policy in `vllm-chat`, so the drop sits in `UnifiedParserState::finish`, the one consumer of `UnifiedParser::finish`. Streaming and non-streaming agree by construction, since non-streaming assembles the same event stream.

**Differences from Python.**

- Python drops the markup for its parser-engine families and still returns raw content in non-streaming for legacy ones (e.g. `hermes`); Rust drops it for every family. Half a tool-call opener is neither text nor a call, and a client cannot act on it.
- A call whose header already streamed (`ToolCallStart`, partial arguments) before the cut stays in the response with truncated arguments, as streaming clients already saw it. Python's non-streaming path drops such a call; retracting a streamed call is a separate question.
- The `hf` and Beam template parsers are not changed: a tool-call region still open at EOF is closed and parsed by the template's content rules, and a parse failure already drops the body, so the markup never reaches the text.

Not a duplicate: vllm-project/vllm#62290 drops an incomplete DeepSeek DSML call at `max_tokens` only; this PR covers every family and finish reason. vllm-project/vllm#52886 recovers malformed Kimi K3 calls mid-stream, a different case; the two touch neighboring lines in `kimi_k3.rs` `finish`. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to prepare this change; the human submitter reviewed every changed line.
