commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Materialize DeepSeek V4.1 content iterators before deepcopy
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Fix DeepSeek V4.1 chat requests whose message `content` is an empty array. Before this change, both streaming and non-streaming requests can fail before generation:

```json
{
  "model": "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": []}],
  "stream": false
}
```

The non-streaming request returns HTTP 400; the streaming request emits an error SSE. The underlying exception is:

```text
TypeError: cannot pickle 'pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidatorIterator' object
```

After `ChatCompletionRequest` validation, `content=[]` can remain a Pydantic `ValidatorIterator`. DeepSeek V4.1’s message normalization deep-copies the messages, which raises this exception.

## Claims

- Materializing iterator-form `content` before the deep copy allows the affected request to render.
- Saving the resulting list in the message allows repeated rendering without consuming a one-shot iterator.
- The change is confined to the DeepSeek V4.1 tokenizer. General request validation and `tool_calls` handling are unchanged.

## Validation

- Reproduced the failure with streaming and non-streaming `content=[]` requests before the fix.
- Added regression coverage for empty content in both modes, text content parts, repeated rendering, and request JSON serialization.
- `python -m pytest --noconftest tests/tokenizers_/test_deepseek_v41.py -q` — **48 passed**.
- Ruff check and format check passed.

## Details

The fix converts `content` to a list only when it is an iterator, immediately before `_normalize_messages()` calls `copy.deepcopy(messages)`. Existing string and list content follows the previous path. Related materialization fixes for `tool_calls` do not cover this `content=[]` case.

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][HY4] Use breakable graphs without torch.compile
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Remove `torch.compile` support from the HY4 AMD backbone and use breakable HIP graphs by default, matching the NVIDIA execution approach. This follows #57526 while retaining graph capture for prefill and decode.

## Claims

- Retain HIP graph replay without compiling the AMD backbone.
- Improve output throughput by 18.7% and median TPOT by 15.6% in the measured C8 decode workload.

## Validation

Benchmarked public `tencent/Hy4-preview-FP8` on upstream `b91df5a9`, 8× MI355X, TP8/MRV2, BF16 activations/KV, identical prompts and serving settings, and no speculation or prefix caching. Ran compiled → no compile → compiled, three repeats per arm; the table compares medians of six compiled controls and three no-compile runs.
The client streams `/v1/completions` with seeded synthetic token prompts, temperature 0 and `ignore_eos=true`.

| Workload (concurrency; input/output tokens) | Compiled tok/s | No compile tok/s | Change | Compiled TPOT | No compile TPOT |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| C1; 1024/256 | 36.77 | 42.62 | +15.9% | 26.26 ms | 21.88 ms |
| C8; 4096/600 | 245.71 | 291.59 | **+18.7%** | 30.65 ms | **25.86 ms (−15.6%)** |
| C8; 4096/16 | 42.91 | 44.89 | +4.6% | 132.25 ms | 127.13 ms |
| C8; mixed 128–6144/32–256 | 181.30 | 206.61 | +14.0% | 36.76 ms | 31.68 ms |

The main C8 throughput ranges were 241.71–249.22 versus 286.54–293.28 tok/s. Mixed-workload TTFT increased 5.5% (555→586 ms).

Compilation freezes prefill-sized MXFP8 GEMM tiles into small-batch decode. Without it, graph capture selects decode-specific tiles: `_mxfp8_linear_kernel.kd` summed duration falls **7.534→2.437 ms per rank/step**, with the same 411 calls. Forcing prefill tiles back reproduces 69% of this kernel-time penalty. Both paths retain HIP graph replay; attention and communication barely change. These kernel sums are not wall-clock latency.

### GPQA-Diamond

Parent `f2ba523d67` versus patch `c4f150d739`, same checkpoint: all 198 questions, zero-shot chat, temperature 0.9/top-p 1.0, matched prompts and seeds, 65,536 output-token limit and concurrency 15. Scores use explicit final-answer exact match; blank/unextractable answers count as wrong.

| Dataset | Compiled | No compile | Difference |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| GPQA-Diamond | 91.92% (182/198) | 92.42% (183/198) | +0.51 pp |

Truncations decreased from 5 to 3. Other accuracy discrepancies remain under investigation; this GPQA result alone does not establish overall accuracy parity.

`.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/test_hyv4_rocm.py -v -s`: **6 passed** on AMD. The new default-graph regression fails on the unmodified parent and passes with this patch.

No duplicate removal PR was found during the HY4 compile/breakable-graph search. AI assistance was used for implementation and validation.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Quantization] Fix online MoE weight conversion `KeyError: 'weight_scale'` with Humming
commits.pr_body:
This failure is deterministic whenever generic online FP8, MXFP8, or MXFP4
MoE quantization selects Humming: its converter reads the layer before the
generated quantized weights and scales have been registered there.

## Purpose

Online FP8, MXFP8, and MXFP4 MoE quantization produces quantized weights and
scales as temporary tensors, then passes them to the selected backend's format
converter. Most converters consume those arguments directly. Humming instead
builds its conversion input from `layer.state_dict()`.

At that point, the layer still contains the full-precision weights used for
online loading and does not contain the newly generated weight scales. As a
result, selecting Humming for an online-quantized MoE model fails during model
loading. For example, online MXFP8 loading reaches Humming's ModelOpt schema
without `weight_scale` and raises:

```text
KeyError: 'weight_scale'
```

Stage the online-quantized weights and scales on the layer before invoking the
Humming converter. This gives Humming the same canonical quantized tensors that
the other converters receive as arguments. The normal post-conversion
replacement remains unchanged.

The fix covers all generic online MoE formats supported by Humming:

- FP8
- MXFP8
- MXFP4

The MXFP8 path also created two full-size FP8 tensors that were immediately
discarded before quantization. Remove those unused allocations. For the
Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE dimensions (128 experts, 2,048 hidden size, and 768 expert
intermediate size), this avoids 576 MiB of transient device allocations per
layer being processed.

## Reproduction

On the parent commit, the following command deterministically fails while
loading the first MoE layer with `KeyError: 'weight_scale'`:

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 \
  --quantization online \
  --quantization-config '{"moe":"mxfp8"}' \
  --moe-backend humming \
  --max-model-len 128 \
  --max-num-seqs 1 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \
  --enforce-eager
```

```
Mxfp8OnlineMoEMethod.process_weights_after_loading
→ convert_to_fp8_moe_kernel_format
→ convert_to_humming_moe_kernel_format
→ ModeloptMxfp8WeightSchema.convert_humming
→ KeyError: 'weight_scale'
```

`--quantization online` ensures that the generic online quantization path is
used, while the explicit MoE configuration selects MXFP8 for every routed
expert layer.

## Why this is not a duplicate

No open PR currently fixes this conversion boundary. PR #42997 adds Humming's
native online quantization path; it does not bridge the generic `online`
quantization methods to Humming's layer-based format converter. PR #51808
addresses online quantization configuration overrides and does not change
backend conversion.

## Test Plan

```bash
python -m pytest tests/quantization/test_online.py -q \
  -k 'stages_quantized_weights_for_humming'

pre-commit run --files \
  tests/quantization/test_online.py \
  vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/online/fp8.py \
  vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/online/moe_base.py \
  vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/online/mxfp4.py \
  vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/online/mxfp8.py
```

The regression tests exercise the shared FP8 setup path, MXFP8, and MXFP4 and
assert that Humming's converter observes the exact online-quantized weight and
scale tensors through `layer.state_dict()`.

The model-loading path was also validated on an NVIDIA A100 with
`Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507`, using online MXFP8 for MoE and Humming as the
MoE backend.

## Test Result

- Focused regression tests: 3 passed, 47 deselected.
- All changed-file pre-commit checks passed, including Ruff, formatting, mypy,
  SPDX, forbidden-import checks, and repository-specific validation.
- Before this change, the real model failed while processing the first MoE
  layer with `KeyError: 'weight_scale'`.
- After this change, all 16 weight shards and all 48 MoE layers completed
  Humming weight conversion. Weight loading used 30.78 GiB and completed in
  496.08 seconds; the original missing-scale failure did not recur.

## Compatibility

Weight staging is limited to the Humming branch of generic online MoE
quantization. Other MoE backends retain their existing conversion behavior;
the only shared change is removal of the unused MXFP8 allocations. No
user-facing configuration or documentation changes are required.

## AI-assisted contribution

This contribution was developed with AI assistance.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][ToolParser] Scan Kimi K3 streaming tool calls incrementally
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Kimi K3 streaming tool extraction rescanned the accumulated tools section and
redecoded completed calls on every delta. This change resumes parsing from the
last unfinished call boundary and decodes each completed call once.

## Claims

- Reduce CPU parsing time for native Kimi K3 tool streams, including `auto` and
  `required` tool choices.
- Preserve response content, tool-call timing, names, argument bytes, indices,
  types, and ID presence.
- Keep the optimization inside `KimiK3ToolParser` and reuse its existing call
  matching and decoding logic.
- This is separate from [#60882](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60882),
  which optimizes the generic JSON scanner for `tool_choice="required"`.
- [#50627](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50627) streams Kimi K3
  arguments before a call closes; this change preserves the existing
  announcement timing and removes repeated parsing after calls close.

## Validation

Five-run CPU parser medians after warmup, using four-character deltas and
alternating before/after order. Timings include text-history accumulation and
parsing, excluding parser construction.

| Workload | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 256-character string argument | 0.523 ms | 0.332 ms | 1.57x |
| 4,096-character string argument | 5.463 ms | 2.602 ms | 2.10x |
| 16,384-character string argument | 36.611 ms | 10.000 ms | 3.66x |
| 65,536-character string argument | 401.085 ms | 43.256 ms | 9.27x |
| Truncated 65,536-character argument | 398.718 ms | 42.784 ms | 9.32x |

Response-only parsing remains at baseline speed. These are CPU parser results and
do not establish GPU inference or end-to-end serving throughput.

- Differential replay: 16,540 streams and 189,754 deltas, with no differences.
- Composed `KimiK3Parser` replay matched across `auto`, `required`, and `none`,
  with and without reasoning.
- Relevant tests: 178 passed.
- Ruff, formatting, mypy, and `git diff --check` passed.

```bash
python -m pytest --noconftest -q \
  tests/tool_use/test_kimi_k3_tool_parser.py \
  tests/tool_parsers/test_kimi_k3_named_tool_choice.py \
  tests/reasoning/test_kimi_k3_reasoning_parser.py \
  tests/tool_parsers/test_structural_tag_registry.py -k kimi_k3
```

## Details

The existing call regex and decoder remain responsible for recognizing and
decoding calls. A call-close regex finds newly completed call blocks; the parser
then scans only the unparsed interval. Partial matching preserves close markers
split across deltas, including whitespace variants. Matched invalid call blocks
still advance the parsed span, so they do not affect later call indices.

The change adds two parser offsets and does not introduce a scanner class or a
second accumulated text buffer. Response extraction and tools-channel discovery
remain unchanged. The optimization reduces repeated tool-call work while the
existing caller-side history concatenation and full response/channel searches
remain. The existing K3 decoder remains responsible for decoding calls after a complete call boundary is found.

---

commits.pr_title: [Rust][Benchmark] Keep transport failures visible in measured requests
commits.pr_body:
## Overview


Measured workload requests currently retry connection reset, refused, and
timeout failures up to three times. A later successful attempt can hide an
overloaded or unstable service and report the sample as successful.

The retry also changes the workload being measured: failed attempts and
backoff are omitted from per-request latency, while they still extend the
overall benchmark duration and retain a concurrency slot. This can produce
normal-looking latency and failure counts alongside unexpectedly lower
throughput.

Remove automatic retries only from the measured request path so each
scheduled sample produces one HTTP attempt and one observable result.
Preparation-stage retries remain unchanged.



## Claims


- Report measured connection failures directly instead of replacing them with
  the result of a later attempt.
- Keep the scheduled request count, arrival behavior, and concurrency pressure
  consistent with the configured workload.
- Prevent failed attempts and retry backoff from being excluded from
  per-request latency while still affecting total benchmark duration.
- Preserve endpoint readiness and tokenizer preparation retries, which occur
  outside the measured workload.
- Add an entry-point regression test that resets the first connection, would
  accept a second request, and verifies that the benchmark sends only one
  workload request and reports it as failed.
- Document the measured-request behavior in the Rust benchmark README.



## Validation

```bash
cargo test -p vllm-bench test_measured_request_does_not_retry_connection_failure
cargo test -p vllm-bench
cargo clippy -p vllm-bench --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all -- --check
```



## Details

The previous loop used max_retries = 3 with an inclusive range, allowing one
initial request plus three retries. The concurrency permit remained held
throughout those attempts.

The request start time was recreated before every attempt, and only the final
attempt's output was retained. If a later attempt succeeded:

- the original connection failure disappeared from the failure count;
- E2EL latency represented only the successful attempt;
- retry backoff and earlier attempts still extended benchmark duration;
- the concurrency slot remained occupied during backoff;
- the server could receive more requests than the configured sample count.

Retries are useful for application clients, where completing an operation can
be more important than exposing a transient failure. For a benchmark, however,
the requests and arrival schedule define the workload. Retrying inside the
measurement changes that workload and makes overload less visible.

The Python benchmark provides a useful reference for this behavior: it invokes
the request function once per scheduled sample and returns transport errors as
failed outputs. Using the same one-attempt model avoids a Rust-only recovery
policy and supports meaningful comparisons between the two clients.



---

commits.pr_body:
## Overview

On gfx950, the MiniMax-M3.1 NVFP4 indexer picks the 16 best blocks of every decode row with one wave per row. This PR gives each decode row four waves and merges their top-16 lists exactly, so the ordered block ids are unchanged. No other kernel, flag or call site changes.

## Claims

- Decode top-k is 4.1x faster over the decode shapes of a served MiniMax-M3.1 AgentX run (18.9 -> 4.65 us per call, weighted by how often each shape occurs, real index scores); 4.07x in the live server (21.2 -> 5.2 us per call). With random scores the same shapes give 1.26x: the old kernel is much slower on real scores (see Details).
- End to end (TP4, 2 runs per arm): c16 +1.34% and c32 +2.47% tok/s/GPU, TPOT p50 -12.2% / -12.0%, p90 -8.3% / -8.2% (interactivity p50 +13.9% / +13.6%, p90 +9.0% / +8.9%).
- Same output as before: bit-for-bit equal to AITER's `pa_sparse_block_topk` and to the old kernel in 4,500 sweep cases (772,650 rows); eager and CUDA-graph replay agree. In a replay of the real served calls 1 of 2,816 decode rows differs, in a call with duplicate page ids where the old kernel's own output changes from run to run. GSM8K and spec-decode accept length are unchanged.
- **Costs:** With random scores a call is up to 12% slower when every row is under about 213k tokens; with real scores that only shows for calls in which no row triggers the old kernel's slow path. See Limits.

## Validation

**Microbench.** MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 10.0.0, torch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:minimax-m31-flash` with the two top-k files of this PR on top of main (7b77ed581d; the files are unchanged on main at 76c6f3f2a9, where the test file was re-run); stock = main's files. CUDA-graph replay of 16 back-to-back calls on distinct score buffers, 1 GiB memset (cold L2) before every replay, median of 20 replays per process, 6 fresh processes per arm; per-call us, median of the 6 (process-to-process range at most 0.07 us ours, 0.21 us stock). 1 index head, 4 rows per request, output equal in every process. Scores are the real output of the unchanged scorer on captured queries and index-K pages of a served run (grid cells: re-scored captured requests clipped to the cell's lengths; live lengths uniform in [max/2, max]). Rows = requests, columns = max sequence length (graph width). Not a repo benchmark (none exists for this op); the method is in the details block.

```python
K, QL = 16, 4

        fn(); torch.accelerator.synchronize()
        g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()

        ts = []
        for _ in range(20):
            flush.zero_(); a, b = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
            a.record(); g.replay(); b.record(); torch.accelerator.synchronize(); ts.append(a.elapsed_time(b) * 1000 / K)
        res[f"{nr}x{msl}"] = statistics.median(ts)
json.dump(res, open(sys.argv[1], "w"))
```

## Details

Each decode row is one workgroup that walks the row's block scores in windows, keeps a running top 16 and ranks the candidates. The old kernel did this with a single wave over windows of 1,664 blocks (213k tokens); rows longer than that serialize on the one wave. Now the workgroup has four waves, each walking every fourth window of 1,024 blocks with its own candidates and running top 16, and the lists are merged by an exact rank over (score, block id), which reproduces AITER's order including ties, NaN and infinities. A wave with no live window pads its list with dead entries, and a row of at most one window skips the merge. The lane-bound threshold uses 16 bits instead of 12 and falls back to all 32 bits when too many keys pass. Prefill compiles to the same code as before. The kernel name for decode changes from `..._w26` to `..._w16`.

Why real scores matter: the old kernel keeps the keys above a bound and ranks at most 64 of them per window; when more pass, it rebuilds the candidates, and with many near-ties it runs an exact bit search on one wave. Random scores never reach that. Real index scores sit in a narrow range, so the 12-bit bound lets more than 64 keys through in about a third of the rows (emulated on the captured rows: 33% of rows with the old bound and window size, 6% with the 16-bit bound), and a call takes as long as its slowest row. Calls in which no row overflows run at the random-score time. I did not build a 16-bit-bound-only or four-wave-only variant, so I cannot say how much of the 4x comes from each.

Limits:
- Slower in some calls: when every row is under about 213k tokens and no row overflows the old kernel's candidate buffer, a call is up to 12% slower (about 0.5 us on a 4 us call; random-score table, and the 0.88x-0.92x served calls there) and 8-9% slower at 100 requests under 131k tokens. In my real-score runs no cell (20 served calls, 32 grid cells, 6 cells of 131k-213k rows) is slower than stock (lowest 1.04x), but about 30% of single-request calls with 131k-213k rows have no overflowing row (emulation). The launch only sees the graph's `max_seq_len` (1M in serving), not the row lengths, so the host cannot choose between the two kernels.
- The real-score grid cells are re-scored captured requests, not replays of served calls; the max length 1M column is random-score only.
- E2E was run on the published ROCm image with the two files overlaid, not on a build of current main: the CI recipe (DBO with this multimodal model) does not start on main under Model Runner V2, and I did not change the recipe. The kernel files are identical to main's; other kernels' shares differ on main (for example the MXFP8 fusions), so the gain on main may differ.
- c16 and c32 only (c1-c8 do not use this indexer path; c64 not run); one model, TP4, DSpark, DBO on; 2 runs per arm.
- Validation is gfx950 only, and no Buildkite step runs the test file on gfx950 (I ran it on MI355X). The microbench is not in `benchmarks/kernels/`.
- A 2-way merge for rows up to 2,048 blocks would halve the 131k-213k regression (+8 lines); it is not in this PR.

Not a duplicate: no open PR changes the top-k files or their test file (checked against main at 76c6f3f2a9). #64198 (MXFP4 K/V and index cache) does not touch them. #64264 (NVFP4 kernel warmup at startup) and #64273 (monokernel decode on M3.1) are closed drafts that only carried the same bytes of these files as main. #64448 (decode CP for DSpark 7) is open and edits the indexer module and the CP push kernel, not the top-k kernel, so it is complementary.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Rust Frontend] Fail token-less streams in vllm-bench openai-chat
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Fixes #59722.

The `openai-chat` backend in the Rust `vllm-bench` marked a request as successful whenever the stream ended cleanly, even if no token ever showed up. The completions backend and Python `vllm bench serve` only count it as a success once the first token arrives, so chat was the odd one out.

So a 200 response with no tokens got counted as a success, with `ttft`, `latency` and `output_tokens` all left at their defaults. Thanks to @aron-intframe for pointing out in the issue that this goes beyond Mean TTFT:

- Mean TTFT and Mean E2EL get pulled down, since both are `0` for those requests.
- The `1 + output.itl.len()` fallback in `metrics/calculator.rs` counts each one as a phantom output token, which inflates total output tokens and output throughput.
- They pass every goodput SLO, because TTFT/TPOT/E2EL are all `0`.

The fix gates `success` on the `first_token_received` flag that's already there, and fails the request with the same error as the completions backend and Python. That message now lives in a shared `NO_VALID_CHUNK_ERROR` const so the two backends can't drift apart.

This also lines up with #64626 (thanks @dilberx). That PR stopped counting vLLM's opening role chunk as a token, so the stream vLLM actually sends when it generates nothing (a role chunk, then usage) now reaches this check and fails as it should.

**Heads up for multi-turn:** `multi_turn.rs` branches on `output.success`. Right now a token-less turn gets appended to the history as an empty assistant message and the run keeps going. After this change that turn is reported as failed, like any other failed turn, which is what the completions backend and Python already do.

## Not a duplicate

Claimed in #59722. Other PRs that touch `openai_chat.rs`:

- #55809 adds server queue time / TTFT to the detailed results, which is a different change.
- #59694 (mine, merged) changed the usage-chunk block a few lines up. This branch is rebased on top of it.
- #64626 (merged) decides which chunks count as tokens, and this PR decides what happens when none do, so the two fit together.
- #57519 handles server error events, but only on the Python side.

## Test Plan

Two new tests in `openai_chat::tests`:

- `test_tokenless_stream_is_failed`: the local SSE test server sends zero token chunks, then usage and `[DONE]`.
- `test_role_only_stream_is_failed`: the role chunk plus usage that vLLM sends when nothing is generated. It uses the `run_chat` helper from #64626, and thanks @esmeetu for suggesting it.

Both check that `success == false` and `error == NO_VALID_CHUNK_ERROR`.

```bash
cargo test -p vllm-bench --lib
cargo clippy -p vllm-bench --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all -- --check
```

For the end-to-end check, I used a mock OpenAI-compatible server that returns 200 with only the usage chunk and `[DONE]` for every 8th request, run with `--dataset-name random --random-input-len 100 --random-output-len 8 --num-prompts 32 --max-concurrency 8`.

## Test Result

- `cargo test -p vllm-bench --lib`: 225 passed on current `main`. Clippy and fmt are clean.
- If I revert the fix, both new tests fail.

End-to-end against the mock server. I re-ran the Rust rows after the rebase and got the same counts (28 ok, 4 failed, 224 tokens). The mock doesn't send a role chunk, so that case is covered by the unit test instead.

| client | Successful | Failed | Total generated tokens | Mean TTFT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Python `vllm bench serve` (`openai-chat`) | 28 | 4 | 224 | 212.28 ms |
| Rust `vllm-bench` (`openai`), reference | 28 | 4 | 224 | 203.13 ms |
| Rust `vllm-bench` (`openai-chat`), before | 32 | 0 | 228 | 178.32 ms |
| Rust `vllm-bench` (`openai-chat`), after | 28 | 4 | 224 | 202.93 ms |

In the "before" row you can see the four phantom output tokens (228 vs 224) and the TTFT skew. With the fix, chat matches the completions backend and Python.

commits.pr_title: [Step5] Allow MegaMoE with pipeline parallelism
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Step5 rejects `--moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe` with TP>1 and PP>1 at startup (`Step5 MegaMoE with TP requires sequence parallelism and PP=1`), because its model-level sequence parallelism (SP) is gated on PP=1. Step5 already handles the PP boundary under SP:
- it all-gathers its token shards before returning `IntermediateTensors` from a non-last stage;
- it re-shards them on entry to the next stage.

The default PP transport therefore sees full, TP-identical tensors, and the gate is unnecessary. This PR removes the PP=1 condition from the SP gate and the startup check.

## Claims

- Step5 with MegaMoE, TP>1 and PP>1 starts and matches PP=1 accuracy.
- At PP2×TP2 on B300, output throughput is +13.5% compared with the default MoE backend, which was the only option under PP before.
- PP=1 behavior is unchanged. No other model is affected.

## Validation

Hardware: 8× B300 (SM100) per node, NVLink, MRV2. GSM8K uses the full 1319 questions, 5-shot.

| Step5 config (EP on) | MoE backend | main | This PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| PP1×TP4 (reference, SP on) | MegaMoE | 0.934 | — (path unchanged) |
| PP2×TP2 | default | 0.936 | — |
| PP2×TP2 | MegaMoE | fails at startup | 0.934 |
| PP2×TP4 | MegaMoE | fails at startup | 0.926 |

Throughput, PP2×TP2. Two runs per arm, no other jobs on the node. Each cell lists the two runs' output tok/s, then their mean TPOT in ms:

| Workload (in/out, concurrency) | Default MoE | MegaMoE + SP | Throughput |
|---|---|---|---|
| decode 512/512, c64 | 934.1, 935.6 / 66.5, 66.4 | 1058.6, 1064.5 / 59.0, 58.2 | +13.6% |
| mixed 2048/256, c64 | 814.4, 809.0 / 72.2, 72.6 | 920.5, 921.6 / 63.0, 62.9 | +13.5% |
| prefill 8192/16, c8 | 43.1, 42.9 / 85.9, 85.4 | 43.1, 42.2 / 95.3, 95.3 | −1% |

At PP2×TP4 (EP4) the trade-off differs: prefill throughput is +19% (TTFT −26%) and decode is −15%. The backend choice stays with the user.

Lint: `pre-commit run --files vllm/models/step5/nvidia/model.py vllm/models/step5/nvidia/mega_moe.py` passes on upstream main 79d0899cca.

<details>
<summary>Commands</summary>

```bash
# Fails at startup on main; starts with this PR
vllm serve stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview --max-model-len 131072 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --max-num-seqs 64 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --disable-custom-all-reduce --no-enable-prefix-caching --enable-expert-parallel \
  --moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe --tensor-parallel-size 2 --pipeline-parallel-size 2
# Default-MoE arm: same command without --moe-backend.

python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --port 8000 --max-concurrency 64

vllm bench serve --model stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 512 --random-output-len 512 --num-prompts 512 \
  --max-concurrency 64 --ignore-eos --seed 1
```
</details>

## Details

With TP>1 the PP transport sends 1/t of each `IntermediateTensors` entry from every TP rank and all-gathers it on the receiver. This is correct only when the tensor covers all tokens and is identical on every TP rank. `Step5Model.forward` meets that:
- it calls `sp_all_gather(hidden_states)[: positions.shape[0]]` before the non-last-rank return;
- it calls `sp_shard` on the received `hidden_states` on entry.

That code was already on main but never ran with PP, because SP was off whenever PP>1.

The gather at the boundary adds two TP all-gathers per stage boundary per step. On NVLink this cost is not measurable: an interleaved A/B against a prototype that sends the shards rank-to-rank instead showed no throughput difference beyond run-to-run spread at PP2×TP2 and PP2×TP4.

**CI.** This path needs MegaMoE, which runs only on SM100. The SM100 CI steps use at most 4×B200, which cannot hold the ~650 GB Step5 checkpoint plus KV cache; the 8-GPU H200 steps can hold it but cannot run MegaMoE. Validation was done outside CI as listed above.

AI assistance (Claude) was used to investigate, implement and validate this change. The submitter reviewed every changed line and the validation results.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][Core] Keep per-request token and block id lists out of the cyclic GC
commits.pr_body:
## Overview Keep the per-request Python lists that grow with context length out of CPython's cyclic GC by untracking them at creation (`PyObject_GC_UnTrack`): block id lists, block hashes and token id lists in EngineCore, long lists received by workers, and prompt/output token lists in the API server. The prefix-cache index stores block ids so it holds no GC-tracked objects. Also sends a new request's prompt to MRV2 workers once instead of twice (from #62702). An alternative to the per-block containers of #64700, whose prefix-cache map this reuses. Removes the cause of the EngineCore GC pauses that #63306 works around with `gc.freeze()`, including the young-generation passes reported in RFC #63363, without freezing anything. Overlaps with the GC part of #62702, whose serialization and memory gains are independent and compatible (`gc_untrack` is a no-op on arrays). ## Claims - 256 running requests × 128K-token prompts with prefix caching, real `Scheduler`, Python 3.12: a full GC pass drops from 258 ms (1 KV cache group) / 459 ms (4 groups) to 0.1 ms, with token ids still `list[int]` (no #62702 needed for the GC cost). - No change to the decode step; admission step +6%, chunked-prefill step +1–2%, prefix-cache lookup unchanged. (#64700's containers: admission +40%, chunked-prefill step 3.0–3.3×.) - No behavior change: identical block ids, hashes and scheduling decisions. - A new request's prompt is pickled to MRV2 workers once rather than twice (not separately measured). ## Validation **CPU benchmark, real `Scheduler`** (GB200 Grace, `numactl` node 0, Python 3.12, exclusive node). Extends the #64700 reproducer with admission, chunked-prefill and prefix-lookup timings. All arms on the same base; mean of 2 interleaved rounds (rounds within ~2%); values are 1 / 4 KV cache groups. A fingerprint of block ids and hashes matched across all arms. | | base | #64700 | this PR | |---|---|---|---| | full GC pass, token ids `list[int]` | 258 / 459 ms | 172 / 171 ms | **0.1 / 0.1 ms** | | full GC pass, token ids int32 | 83 / 285 ms | 0.1 / 0.1 ms | 0.1 / 0.1 ms | | decode step (GC off) | 2.16 / 3.46 ms | 2.17 / 3.40 ms | 2.16 / 3.41 ms | | admission step, 256 × 128K (GC off) | 2.21 / 9.46 s | 3.10 / 13.06 s | 2.35 / 10.00 s | | chunked prefill per step, 16 × 128K, 8K chunks | 0.64 / 2.30 ms | 1.95 / 7.57 ms | 0.65 / 2.33 ms | | prefix-cache lookup per 128K request | 4.9 / 16.1 ms | 6.0 / 17.1 ms | 4.9 / 15.7 ms | The benchmarked revision covers the EngineCore lists and the prefix-cache map; the worker, API-server and `reset_prefix_cache` changes came later and are not in these numbers.
reproducer (VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 PYTHONPATH=. python bench_gc2.py <groups> <main|chunked>) ```python # Extended version of the #64700 reproducer: also times the admission step, # prefix-cache lookups and chunked prefill. Run from a vLLM checkout: # VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 PYTHONPATH=. python bench_gc2.py import gc import hashlib import statistics import sys import time from array import array import tests.v1.core.utils as u from vllm.utils.gc_utils import freeze_gc_heap from vllm.v1.kv_cache_interface import KVCacheConfig, KVCacheGroupSpec from vllm.v1.outputs import ModelRunnerOutput NUM_GROUPS = int(sys.argv[1]) MODE = sys.argv[2] PROMPT, BLOCK = 131072, 16 NUM_REQS = 256 if MODE == "main" else 16 def multi_group_config(*, kv_cache_groups, **kw): spec = kv_cache_groups[0].kv_cache_spec groups = [KVCacheGroupSpec([f"layer{i}"], spec) for i in range(NUM_GROUPS)] return KVCacheConfig(kv_cache_groups=groups, **kw) u.KVCacheConfig = multi_group_config sched = u.create_scheduler( max_num_seqs=NUM_REQS, max_num_batched_tokens=NUM_REQS * PROMPT if MODE == "main" else 8192, num_blocks=NUM_GROUPS * (NUM_REQS * (PROMPT + 4096) // BLOCK) + 1024, block_size=BLOCK, max_model_len=PROMPT + 4096, enable_prefix_caching=True, use_v2_model_runner=True, ) freeze_gc_heap() # what EngineCore does after startup reqs = u.create_requests( num_requests=NUM_REQS, num_tokens=PROMPT, block_size=BLOCK, max_tokens=4000 ) for r in reqs: sched.add_request(r) def step(): out = sched.schedule() ids = list(out.num_scheduled_tokens) sampled = [ [7] if sched.requests[rid].num_computed_tokens >= sched.requests[rid].num_prompt_tokens else [] for rid in ids ] sched.update_from_output( out, ModelRunnerOutput( req_ids=ids, req_id_to_index={rid: i for i, rid in enumerate(ids)}, sampled_token_ids=sampled, logprobs=None, prompt_logprobs_dict={}, pooler_output=[], ), ) def full_gc_ms(): ts = [] for _ in range(3): t = time.perf_counter() gc.collect(2) ts.append(time.perf_counter() - t) return min(ts) * 1e3 def fingerprint(): # Same scheduling decisions across arms -> same digest. h = hashlib.sha256() for r in reqs[:8]: for ids in sched.kv_cache_manager.get_block_ids(r.request_id): h.update(array("i", ids).tobytes()) h.update(b"".join(r.block_hashes[:64])) bp = sched.kv_cache_manager.block_pool h.update(str(len(bp.cached_block_hash_to_block)).encode()) return h.hexdigest()[:12] tag = f"groups={NUM_GROUPS} mode={MODE}" gc.disable() if MODE == "chunked": t = time.perf_counter() nsteps = 0 while any(r.num_computed_tokens < r.num_prompt_tokens for r in reqs): step() nsteps += 1 total = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e3 print(f"RESULT {tag} chunked_prefill_total_ms={total:.1f} steps={nsteps} " f"ms_per_step={total / nsteps:.3f} fp={fingerprint()}") sys.exit(0) t = time.perf_counter() step() admit = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e3 gc_list = full_gc_ms() for r in reqs: # token ids as int32, as with #62702 r.prompt_token_ids = array("i", r.prompt_token_ids) r._all_token_ids = r.all_token_ids = array("i", r._all_token_ids) gc_i32 = full_gc_ms() for _ in range(20): step() ts = [] for _ in range(5): t = time.perf_counter() for _ in range(64): step() ts.append((time.perf_counter() - t) / 64 * 1e3) decode = statistics.median(ts) # Prefix-cache lookup for new requests repeating cached prompts. wave2 = u.create_requests( num_requests=32, num_tokens=PROMPT, block_size=BLOCK, max_tokens=4000, req_ids=[f"w2-{i}" for i in range(32)], ) lt, hits = [], 0 for r in wave2: t = time.perf_counter() _, num_hit, *_ = sched.kv_cache_manager.get_computed_blocks(r) lt.append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e3) hits += num_hit print( f"RESULT {tag} admit_step_ms={admit:.1f} full_gc_list_ms={gc_list:.1f} " f"full_gc_int32_ms={gc_i32:.1f} decode_step_ms={decode:.3f} " f"prefix_lookup_ms={statistics.median(lt):.2f} " f"hit_frac={hits / (32 * PROMPT):.3f} fp={fingerprint()}" ) ```
**Tests** (GB200 node, slurm, Python 3.12), on this branch rebased onto current `main`: - `tests/v1/core`, `tests/v1/test_request.py`, `tests/utils_/test_gc_utils.py`, `tests/v1/engine/test_output_processor.py`, `tests/v1/engine/test_logprobs_processor.py`, `tests/tokenizers_/test_detokenize.py`, `tests/entrypoints/openai/responses/test_parsable_context{,_unit}.py`, `tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py`: 2092 passed + 223 passed in the re-run of the server-launching tests (`test_parsable_context.py`, `test_serving_chat.py`, `test_hybrid_prefix_cache_hit_rate.py`, which needed `vllm` on `PATH`). No failures. - With the last commit: `tests/v1/core`, `tests/v1/test_request.py`, `tests/v1/streaming_input`, `tests/v1/engine/test_output_processor.py`: 1301 passed, no failures. - Not run: 34 tests in `test_output_processor.py` that load the gated `meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B` tokenizer (no Hugging Face token on the test nodes); they error at setup in both runs. - New tests: `gc_untrack` / `untracked_list` (`tests/utils_/test_gc_utils.py`), long `NewRequestData` lists untracked after a pickle round trip (`tests/v1/core/test_output.py`), prompt and output token lists untracked in the output processor (`tests/v1/engine/test_output_processor.py`), the prefix-cache map staying untracked across `reset_prefix_cache` (`test_prefix_caching.py`), and `Request.prefill_token_ids` sharing the prompt object (`tests/v1/test_request.py`, from #62702). ## Details **Root cause.** A full collection visits every slot of every tracked container. `freeze_gc_heap()` at startup hides the static heap (including the `KVCacheBlock` pool), but per-request lists are created afterwards and grow with context length, so each full pass visits one slot per token and per block, for every running request. **Changes.** - `vllm/utils/gc_utils.py`: `gc_untrack` (calls `PyObject_GC_UnTrack` through `ctypes.pythonapi`, which holds the GIL; no-op for untracked objects such as `array`), `untracked_list`, and `untrack_long_lists`. - EngineCore: `req_to_blocks` lists (one per KV cache group), `Request.block_hashes`, and `Request` prompt / all / output token id lists. All are only mutated in place. - Workers: `NewRequestData.__setstate__` untracks long lists (≥ 256) on unpickling. MRV2 copies them into its buffers, so they only live for that step; short ones are skipped since the call costs more than a young-generation scan. `CachedRequestData` never carries full block lists under MRV2 (resumed requests are sent as `NewRequestData`). - API server (also calls `freeze_gc_heap()`): the prompt list, which is one object shared from the HTTP request through `RequestState` and each `RequestOutput`; the detokenizer's output token ids and the slow detokenizer's token strings; chat streaming's `generated_token_ids` and the Responses API's accumulated token ids. - Prompt sent once: `Request.prefill_token_ids` returns the `prompt_token_ids` object itself while the request has no output tokens, so `NewRequestData`'s two fields are one object and pickle writes it once (from #62702, co-authored). - Prefix cache: `BlockHashToBlockMap` maps hashes to block ids, keeping keys cached by several blocks in a small side dict, so the main dict holds only bytes and ints (from #64700, co-authored). It is also untracked explicitly, and `reset_prefix_cache` clears it in place rather than replacing it. **Safety.** A reference cycle through an untracked container is never collected, so only containers that cannot be in a cycle are untracked: these lists hold ints, bytes, strs, or `KVCacheBlock`s that never refer back to them, and are freed by reference counting. The prefix-cache dict needs int values for this: an untracked dict holding blocks (which refer to their pool, which refers to the dict) leaks the pool on Python 3.14. **Python versions.** 3.11–3.13 auto-untrack dicts of atomic values, which int values alone exploit; 3.14 does not, hence the explicit untrack, which on 3.14 sticks even across inserts. Checked with standalone probes on 3.11–3.14; the scheduler benchmark ran on 3.12 only. **Tradeoffs and limitations.** - Relies on CPython's `PyObject_GC_UnTrack` via `ctypes`; untested on free-threaded builds. - A list that later code replaces with a new one becomes tracked again, silently losing the benefit (nothing fails). - Untracked lists are invisible to `gc.get_objects()`, so `VLLM_GC_DEBUG` top-object counts omit them. - The API server untracks the prompt list it was handed, which can be the caller's own list (an offline `LLM` prompt list, or the pydantic request list); safe for lists of ints. - Not covered: MRV1's worker-side request state, non-flat logprobs, and the Rust frontend (no Python API server). ---

## Overview

In `tests/distributed/test_pipeline_parallel.py`, skip the multi-node-only cases at collection instead of inside the fresh process that `create_new_process_for_each_test` starts for every case.

## Claims

- The ten `microsoft/Phi-3.5-MoE-instruct` cases of `test_tp_language_generation` are `multi_node_only`. On single-node CI each started a new interpreter and then skipped. All ten now skip in 0.57 s instead of 101.8 s on MI300X.
- Test IDs, the `-k "ray"` selection used by the RayExecutorV2 jobs, and the multi-node run (`VLLM_MULTI_NODE=1`) are unchanged.
- Expected CI saving: about 2 minutes per build in (MI250) Pipeline + Context Parallelism (the ten cases took about 11.5 s each in the vllm/ci build 99098 log) and about 1 minute per run in the RayExecutorV2 jobs, which select the five Phi-MoE `ray` cases.

## Validation

Environment: CI image `rocm/vllm-ci:build-01a19b0e-d62f-4889-8556-b5c2d4478cbf` (vllm/ci build 99098), MI300X. One run per row (n=1). No server is started by these commands.

Commands run:

```bash
pytest -q -rs distributed/test_pipeline_parallel.py -k "test_tp_language_generation and Phi-3.5-MoE"
pytest --collect-only -q distributed/test_pipeline_parallel.py
```

- Not a duplicate: I searched open PRs for "test_pipeline_parallel" and "multi_node_only"; none changes this parametrization. #64784 edits `_compare_tp` in the same file but touches different lines.

commits.pr_title: [Kernel] Accumulate ranks in absolute order in 2-stage custom all-reduce
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

`cross_device_reduce_2stage` rotates the rank pointers, so each partition's owner starts its sum at its own rank. `cross_device_reduce_1stage` sums ranks in absolute order `0..N-1`. Both reduce through the same `packed_reduce`, which accumulates into float32 (`csrc/custom_collective_common.cuh:87`, `:323-330`). When those partial sums round, the two kernels can return different bits for the same all-reduce — and the choice between them is made by message size (`csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh:298-307`: 1-stage below 512 KiB at ≤4 ranks and 256 KiB at ≤8, 2-stage above).

(Line numbers are at main `b49c921a27`, this PR's base; the comment added here shifts the `.cuh` ones after line 47 by 2 on this branch.)

The rotation also makes 2-stage output depend on the total tensor size, even with no switch between kernels. This was independently measured by @curvedinf ([comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57042#issuecomment-5686335910)). `part = size / ngpus` moves the ownership boundaries whenever the size changes (`csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh:38-40`), and each owner starts its sum at its own rank (`:45-48`). In their on-GPU in-vitro run of the unmodified kernels at 4 ranks and fp32, 14.86% of the elements of a 1664×5120 tensor differ bitwise from the same rows of its 2048×5120 parent. Both sizes are above the 512 KiB threshold, so this comes from a chunked-prefill geometry change alone. The 1-stage control on the same data is bit-identical, which pins the cause to the rotation this PR removes.

This PR makes the 2-stage kernel read the rank pointers in absolute order, so both kernels produce identical bits whichever one the heuristic selects, and 2-stage output no longer depends on the tensor size. The direction was proposed by @sfeng33 in the review of #50505; this is that change, split out and self-contained against main. cc @sfeng33

**The change** is one line in `csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh`: `ptrs[i] = (const P*)_dp->ptrs[target]` → `_dp->ptrs[i]`.

Only `ptrs` loses the rotation. `tmps[i]` must keep it: `tmp_out = tmps[0]` has to be the rank's own scratch buffer, and the stage-2 gather indexes `tmps` with the same `(rank + i)` rotation. De-rotating both would make every rank write its stage-1 results into rank 0's scratch region. The code comment records this.

**Why the kernels then agree bit-for-bit.** For every element, both compute `downcast(((up(x0) + up(x1)) + ...) + up(xN-1))` through the same float32 accumulator. There are no partial sums on the 2-stage path: each partition's owner computes the full N-term sum, and stage 2 only copies already-downcast values. Once the order matches, every operation matches.

**Effect outside batch invariance.** This changes 2-stage output bit patterns for all runs, not only under `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`. Before and after, each result sums the same terms through the same float32 accumulator; only the order of the additions differs. How often bits actually change depends on the data and dtype: in the CPU emulation below, plain random fp16/bf16 inputs changed no elements and fp32 inputs changed ~32% (31.28% on GPU in @curvedinf's run, below). No existing test asserts bit-exact 2-stage output: the custom all-reduce tests either run at TP=2, which always selects 1-stage, or force 1-stage (`test_custom_allreduce_chunked`), and the bit-exact all-gather/reduce-scatter tests never dispatch `allreduce()`.

**Prior art, and why this is a separate PR.** #52231 by @mawong-amd already contains this same one-line change, with `ptrs` de-rotated and `tmps` kept rotated. It is part of a 36-file PR adding batch invariance on ROCm, which describes the change as making 2-stage batch-invariant and keeps that path disabled on CUDA pending tuning. This PR splits out only the kernel line, with a 4-rank differential test, so it can be reviewed and land on its own. If #52231 lands first, this PR reduces to the test. cc @mawong-amd

#56358 also targets fixed-order TP reduction, but through an opt-in Python gather-and-sum path (`VLLM_TP_FIXED_ORDER_ALLREDUCE`); it doesn't touch this kernel. Relationship to #50505: complementary. This PR makes kernel *selection* irrelevant to the bits; #50505 keeps *backend* selection (custom vs NCCL) batch-independent. Whichever lands second should drop #50505's force-1-stage gate.

## Test Plan

New test `test_one_and_two_stage_allreduce_bitwise_identical` in `tests/distributed/test_custom_all_reduce.py`. No NVIDIA CI job runs this file: the `:nvidia: (A100) Distributed` step it is declared in is no longer emitted, because the A100 fleet is retired. Its AMD mirror, `:amd: (MI355) Distributed`, still runs it on 4× MI355. The mirror inherits `optional: true`, so it runs only when someone unblocks it (`Run :amd: (MI355) Distributed` in build #93586).

- 4 ranks. It forces each kernel in turn with `VLLM_CUSTOM_ALLREDUCE_ALGO=1stage|2stage` (read on every `allreduce()` call, `csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh:271`) over the same per-rank inputs, and asserts bitwise-identical outputs.
- fp16 / bf16 / fp32 × 4 sizes, from 16,336 B to 4,194,224 B. The sizes straddle the 512 KiB threshold, and three leave an uneven last partition.
- Adversarial inputs: each element holds `+B`, `-B` and small terms below float32's resolution at `B`, in a random rank order. Ordinary random fp16/bf16 data almost never detects a change of order, because its float32 partial sums are almost always exact (see the emulation below).
- Both forced kernels must also return the exact sum on integer inputs. The existing custom all-reduce tests run at TP=2 or force 1-stage, so none of them reaches 2-stage.
- Why 4 ranks: at 2 the rotation only turns `a+b` into `b+a`, which is commutative, so no 2-rank run can tell the orders apart.
- Skips cleanly with fewer than 4 GPUs, without the custom all-reduce ops, or without full NVLink (custom all-reduce disables itself above 2 PCIe-only ranks).

## Test Result

**4-rank GPU differential: run on 4× MI355.** @mawong-amd ran it on 4× MI355 (gfx950, XGMI) with this PR rebased onto main ([review](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57042#pullrequestreview-5454848047)). The test passes on this branch, and against main's kernel it fails with `fp16, 16336 bytes: 2-stage differs from 1-stage in 5113/8168 elements`.

It has not been run on NVIDIA. It needs 4 GPUs with NVLink all-to-all; to reproduce there, the test should **fail** against main's kernel and **pass** on this branch:

```bash
TEST=tests/distributed/test_custom_all_reduce.py
git fetch https://github.com/mosafariuk/vllm.git rankorder-2stage
# main's kernel (this PR's base; a precompiled build is enough, since main's kernel is unchanged):
git checkout b49c921a27083c25c16f308be1326055dbc87bbf && VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install -e .
git checkout d7f127882cd37a5f57f313493a7498688f5457b8 -- "$TEST"
pytest -rA "$TEST" -k one_and_two_stage   # expect FAILED: "... 2-stage differs from 1-stage in N/M elements"
# this branch (kernel change, needs a source build):
git checkout d7f127882cd37a5f57f313493a7498688f5457b8 && uv pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
pytest -rA "$TEST" -k one_and_two_stage   # expect PASSED
```

Other runs:

Independent in-vitro run by @curvedinf on an AMD gfx1100 ([comment with harness and logs](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57042#issuecomment-5686335910)). It used the unmodified kernel headers from main `241e9391e`; `custom_all_reduce.cuh` and `custom_collective_common.cuh` there are byte-identical to this PR's original base `2983fc6286`. Main has since added only an unrelated `mnnvl_multimem_reduce_scatter` declaration to `custom_all_reduce.cuh`. Four logical ranks are staged sequentially on one GPU with the barrier flags pre-armed. That exercises the kernels' arithmetic (pointer order and partition ownership), but not IPC, NVLink, or this PR's pytest test. Inputs are `N(0,1)·(0.1 + 0.05·rank)`:

| comparison, 4 ranks | fp32 | bf16 |
|---|---|---|
| 1-stage vs 2-stage, same 2048×5120 data | 31.28% of elements differ | 0 |
| 2-stage at 1664×5120 vs the same rows at 2048×5120 | 14.86% | 0 |
| control: 1-stage at 1664 vs 2048 | 0 | 0 |

With this PR's line applied to the harness's header copy, all fp32 rows are reported as 0. The attached logs cover the unmodified runs. A CPU emulation of the same geometry, with a different RNG, gives 30.9% and 14.7%. 34.6% of the smaller tensor's elements change owner between the two sizes.

CPU, full test file (run before the rebase; line numbers and skip counts differ at the current head):
```
$ pytest -rA -v tests/distributed/test_custom_all_reduce.py
SKIPPED [4] tests/distributed/test_custom_all_reduce.py:217: Not enough GPUs to run the test.
SKIPPED [1] tests/distributed/test_custom_all_reduce.py:312: Not enough GPUs to run the test.
================== 11 passed, 5 skipped, 14 warnings in 6.35s ==================
```

4× A100-SXM4-40GB without NVLink (`nvidia-smi topo -m` shows every pair as `NODE`), with a wheel built from this branch before the rebase — the skip path on real hardware:
```
is_fully_connected(0..3): False
SKIPPED [1] tests/distributed/test_custom_all_reduce.py:320: Custom all-reduce needs fully connected GPUs above 2 ranks.
================ 1 skipped, 15 deselected, 14 warnings in 2.45s ================
```

CPU emulation of `packed_reduce`'s float32 accumulation (emulated, not GPU). For each element, 1-stage order vs the unpatched 2-stage owner-rotated order, downcast and compared bitwise at 4 ranks:

| inputs | fp16 | bf16 | fp32 |
|---|---|---|---|
| this test's adversarial inputs, all 4 sizes | 62.5–62.6% of elements differ | 62.4–62.5% | 61.8–62.5% |
| plain `randn` | **0** differ | **0** differ | ~32% |

Partition owner 0 differs in 0% of elements, as expected (its order already matches); owners 1–3 differ in ~83%. The plain-`randn` row is why the test uses adversarial inputs. The fp16/bf16 zeros are structural at 4 ranks, not luck. Those terms carry 11 or 8 significant bits, so float32's 24-bit accumulator adds them exactly unless their magnitudes differ by roughly 2^11–2^14 or more. The rare rounding that remains is erased by the downcast: in an emulation with @curvedinf's input distribution, 480 of 10.5M 1-stage bf16 sums round in float32, and 0 bits differ between orders after the downcast. For realistic data the practical impact is on fp32 all-reduces. fp16/bf16 bits change mainly for inputs like this test's cancellation.

`pre-commit run --files csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh tests/distributed/test_custom_all_reduce.py`: all applicable hooks passed (ruff check/format, clang-format, typos, mypy, SPDX).

No model evaluation was run. The change only reorders a float32 accumulation of the same terms, so outputs can differ at the bit level but not in expected accuracy. Happy to run an lm-eval comparison if reviewers want one.

---

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][KV Connector] Mooncake store: register the committed blocks of an extensible KV cache
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

With the extensible KV cache (on by default since #56492), `MooncakeStoreConnector` fails at startup. Its worker splits each layer's view by `cache_config.num_gpu_blocks`, but `extend_kv_cache` creates the connector against the committed views before it updates that value, so `group_kernel_blocks` asserts. The worker now takes the block count from its own `kv_cache_config`, as the rest of the worker already does.

```
mooncake/store/worker.py, in register_kv_caches
    group_kernel_blocks(view, self.num_blocks)
kv_cache_interface.py, in group_kernel_blocks
    assert cache.shape[0] % num_blocks == 0
AssertionError
```

No open PR covers this (searched for Mooncake + extensible KV cache). Related: #56492, #65225, #65137.

## Validation

GLM-5.3-Flash, colocated DEP8 on 8x B200, `MooncakeStoreConnector` with a standalone store (1.3 TB DRAM plus a 6 TiB SSD tier), real MTP 5. Image nightly `e0d00e4b8e` with this change applied:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Startup | `AssertionError` in `group_kernel_blocks` | Serves; KV cache extended to 1920 blocks (105.38 GiB, 15,728,640 tokens per rank) |
| GSM8K, 5-shot | – | 0.9727 (0.975 with `--disable-extensible-kv-cache`) |
| Needle read-back | – | 16/16 on a cold store; 32/32 after 15 minutes of AgentX at concurrency 384, by which time 2.61 TB had spilled to SSD |

Needle read-back: 16 contexts of about 20K tokens with 800 locker codes each. Each context is asked one code on a cold store, then the same code and a new one after the load.

The new unit test fails without the fix and passes with it. The rest of `test_mooncake_store_worker.py`, `test_mooncake_store_connector.py` and `test_mooncake_store_hma_e2e.py` give the same results with and without it.

```bash
pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_worker.py -k register_kv_caches
```

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Fix DFlash draft acceptance of 0 with FULL CUDA graphs
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Fixes #63587. With the default `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` CUDA graphs, the DFlash draft reads a stale kernel block table, so none of its tokens are accepted. This PR maps the draft kernel block tables before the FULL graph replay, the same way `TargetDependentARSpeculator` already does (#57169).

## Claims

- DFlash-family drafts work again under FULL draft CUDA graphs when the KV cache block is split into smaller kernel blocks. Tested with hybrid `Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B` and a DFlash2 draft on B200: acceptance goes from 0.0000 to about 0.185, the same as the PIECEWISE control (0.1863).
- The FULL draft path from #60692 stays on. Throughput is 20.56–21.21 requests/s, against 6.59–6.67 before the fix and 11.57 with PIECEWISE.
- Adds one row to `test_dflash_correctness`. It fails without the fix and passes with it.
- The code change is 8 lines in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dflash/speculator.py`.

## Validation

Setup: 1 x NVIDIA B200. vLLM at `00b6c4c565a8732c131e1f452d4a17803bb0842b` (`0.32.1rc1.dev505+g00b6c4c56`), with and without this patch. Target `Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B` (rev 851bf6e8), draft `nchapman/Qwen3.5-4B-DFlash2` (rev 8d8bb628), both BF16. Every server log shows `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, `Using FlashAttention version 4`, `Setting attention block size to 640 tokens` and `Capturing dflash2 CUDA graphs (FULL)`.

Server:

```
VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"nchapman/Qwen3.5-4B-DFlash2","num_speculative_tokens":15}' \
  --max-num-seqs 24 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --no-enable-prefix-caching --port 8000
```

Wait for `Application startup complete`, then run `python client.py`. The client uses only the standard library. It sends 200 chat requests (concurrency 16, `max_tokens` 256, temperature 0) and prints how much the `vllm:spec_decode_*` counters changed.

<details>
<summary>client.py</summary>

```python
import json, sys, time, urllib.request, concurrent.futures as cf, re
base = "http://localhost:8000"
model = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B"
N, C = 200, 16
topics = ["the water cycle","binary search","the French revolution","how a transformer works","photosynthesis","TCP congestion control","the Roman empire","quicksort","black holes","the stock market"]
def metrics():
    t = urllib.request.urlopen(base + "/metrics").read().decode()
    d = {}
    for k in ["num_drafts_total","num_draft_tokens_total","num_accepted_tokens_total"]:
        m = re.search(r"^vllm:spec_decode_%s(?:\{[^}]*\})? ([0-9.e+]+)" % k, t, re.M)
        d[k] = float(m.group(1)) if m else None
    return d
def one(i):
    body = {"model": model, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Write a detailed explanation of {topics[i%10]} (variant {i}). Include examples."}],
            "max_tokens": 256, "temperature": 0}
    if i == 0: print("REQUEST BODY (example, i=0):", json.dumps(body), flush=True)
    t = time.time()
    r = urllib.request.Request(base + "/v1/chat/completions", json.dumps(body).encode(), {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    resp = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(r, timeout=900))
    print(f"req {i} status 200 {time.time()-t:.2f}s tokens={resp['usage']['completion_tokens']}", flush=True)
    return resp
m0 = metrics(); t0 = time.time()
with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(C) as ex: list(ex.map(one, range(N)))
dt = time.time() - t0; m1 = metrics()
d = {k: m1[k]-m0[k] for k in m0}
print(f"requests/s {N/dt:.2f}")
print("drafts", d["num_drafts_total"], "draft_tokens", d["num_draft_tokens_total"], "accepted", d["num_accepted_tokens_total"])
print(f"acceptance {d['num_accepted_tokens_total']/max(d['num_draft_tokens_total'],1):.4f}")
```

</details>

 | Tree | `cudagraph_mode` | Runs | `acceptance` | requests/s |
 |---|---|---|---|---|
 | base | `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` (default) | 4 | 0.0000 in every run (0 of 765000 draft tokens) | 6.59–6.67 |
 | base | `PIECEWISE` (control: adds `--compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"PIECEWISE"}'`) | 1 | 0.1863 (37889 of 203325) | 11.57 |
 | this PR | `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` (default) | 6 | 0.1850, 0.1853, 0.1845, 0.1849, 0.1856, 0.1845 | 20.56–21.21 |

```
# base
drafts 51000.0 draft_tokens 765000.0 accepted 0.0
acceptance 0.0000
# this PR (run 1 of 6)
drafts 13678.0 draft_tokens 205170.0 accepted 37948.0
acceptance 0.1850
```

Every request returned status 200 in every run. Base: 3 runs were on one server, and 1 was on a fresh server on the same GPU as the patched runs. This PR: each run started a fresh server, 3 by me and 3 in a separate check. The base result also showed in the `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` image at the same commit (0 of 765000 accepted).

Regression test (new row `qwen3.5-4b-dflash2-mrv2`, same models, 15 speculative tokens, 32 sequences, default compilation config, GSM8K):

```
cd tests && python -m pytest -v -s v1/e2e/spec_decode/acceptance_rates/dflash/test_dflash.py -k 'qwen3.5-4b-dflash2'
```

 | Tree | Runs | Result | GSM8K accuracy | acceptance_len |
 |---|---|---|---|---|
 | base | 2 | FAILED: `acceptance_len 1.000 is below 4.095` | 0.845 | 1.00 |
 | this PR | 2 | PASSED | 0.845 | 4.55 |

The thresholds follow the other rows: accuracy 0.8, and acceptance length `4.55 * 0.9`, from the values measured with the fix. `pre-commit run --files` on both changed files passes.

## Details

**Root cause.** Qwen3.5 is a hybrid model (attention plus GDN layers). To make the attention page match the mamba page, the KV cache manager uses 640-token blocks. The draft's FlashAttention 4 backend uses 128-token kernel blocks. So the draft attention group reads its block table from the persistent `AttentionGroup.kernel_block_table` buffer (`vllm/v1/worker/utils.py`), and the captured FULL graph reads that buffer. Only `map_to_kernel_block_table` fills it, and only the eager metadata build calls that (`_with_kernel_block_table`).

Since #60692, `DFlashSpeculator.propose` skips `_build_uniform_attn_metadata` when it replays a FULL graph and every draft backend supports `update_draft_decode_metadata`. The in-graph `_update_draft_decode_metadata` only asks each builder to refresh its own data. It does not map the block table. So after capture, the buffer keeps the rows from the dummy all-zero block table: kernel pages 0..4, which belong to the null block. On every replay the draft reads the null block's K/V instead of the request's. The drafts are unrelated to the context, and the target rejects all of them. The output stays correct because the target checks every token.

A debug print before `run_fullgraph` (not part of this PR) confirmed this. Request 0 owned manager block 83, so its kernel row should be `[415, 416, 417, 418, 419]`, but the buffer held `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]`. With the fix, it held `[415, 416, 417, 418, 419]`.

**Fix.** In the branch where the build is skipped, call `group.map_to_kernel_block_table(self.block_tables.input_block_tables[group.kv_cache_group_id])` for every draft attention group before the replay. This is the same step `TargetDependentARSpeculator._fused_multi_step_decode` takes before its FULL replay. `map_to_kernel_block_table` already handles the kernel block size, the packed stride and the backend, and it returns at once for groups with no split. When the build does run, it maps the table itself, so that path is unchanged. DFlash, DFlash2, DSpark, LiLiCorr and XPress all use this `propose`.

**Other FULL draft replays checked.** `TargetDependentARSpeculator` (MTP, EAGLE, Gemma4) already maps the table before its fused FULL replay. `MultiModuleMTPSpeculator` builds the metadata before `run_fullgraph`. `StandaloneARSpeculator` does not use FULL replay.

**Not chosen.** Mapping inside `_update_draft_decode_metadata` would also map again on every `TargetDependentAR` step, which already maps. Reporting `supports_decode_metadata_update = False` for split groups would turn #60692 off for these models.

**Limitations and notes for reviewers.**

- The issue does not name its checkpoints (a 9B FP8 target and an NVFP4 target, served through Dynamo). I validated with the 4B BF16 pair above and plain `vllm serve`. The issue saw acceptance of 0.004 and 0.0005; here it was exactly 0. The issue's `no KV cache group could be identified as the draft model's` warning did not appear here, and I did not look into it.
- The test row uses a community draft checkpoint, `nchapman/Qwen3.5-4B-DFlash2`, the one used in the issue thread. If CI should use only official checkpoints, the row can point at another hybrid target/draft pair with the same block split.
- CI: the row id contains `dflash2`, so the nightly `spec-decode-dflash2-nightly-b200` step (`-k "dflash2"`) selects it. `-k dflash2` also selects it in non-B200 steps (H100, MI355), and the thresholds were measured only on B200.

commits.pr_title: [CI/Build] Publish nightly EFA image to DockerHub
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Publish the nightly CUDA 13.0 EFA image to DockerHub. Follow-up to #58768, which builds the EFA nightly but leaves it in ECR staging only.

## Claims

- Nightly builds push the EFA image as `vllm/vllm-openai:efa-nightly` and `vllm/vllm-openai:efa-nightly-<commit>` (plus `efa-nightly-x86_64` / `efa-nightly-aarch64`), and keep the last 14 like other nightly variants.
- The image's `VLLM_IMAGE_TAG` / `ai.vllm.image.tag` label for the EFA nightly now matches that published tag (`efa-nightly-<commit>` instead of `nightly-<commit>-efa`).

## Validation

- First nightly after #58768 ([release-v2 #9252](https://buildkite.com/vllm/release-v2/builds/9252)): `build-release-image-{x86,arm64}-efa` and `create-multi-arch-manifest-efa` passed, but DockerHub has no EFA tag for that commit; only `nightly-<sha>` and `cu134-nightly-<sha>` were pushed.
- New `test_nightly_variant_tags_match_published_nightly_tags` fails on `main` (helper emits `nightly-def456-efa`) and passes with this change:
  ```
  uv run --no-project --python 3.12 --with pytest python -m pytest \
    tests/tools/test_docker_build_metadata_args.py --noconftest -q -k "metadata_args or nightly_variant"
  # 36 passed (excluding test_rust_build_cache_excludes_git_metadata, which needs torch locally)
  ```
- `pre-commit` passes on the changed files.
- CI gap: the new publish step only runs in the nightly release pipeline (`NIGHTLY=1`), so the first nightly after merge is the real end-to-end check. It reuses `push-nightly-builds.sh <variant>` and `cleanup-nightly-builds.sh <prefix>` unchanged, which already publish `cu134-nightly` the same way.

## Details

- Tags use the `<variant>-nightly` prefix, not a `-efa` suffix: `cleanup-nightly-builds.sh` selects by prefix, so `nightly-<sha>-efa` would count against (and get deleted with) the default `nightly-` tags. `efa-nightly-` never matches `nightly-`.
- Not covered here: the Rubin CUDA 13.4 aarch64 EFA nightly step fails because that base builds NIXL from source with only the UCX plugin (`BUILD_NIXL=true`), so `Dockerfile.efa`'s LIBFABRIC plugin check rejects it. Rubin EFA images are not published anywhere; that will be a separate fix.
- Docs: published EFA tags are listed in `docs/contributing/dockerfile/dockerfile.md`.
- Not a duplicate: no open PR touches EFA nightly publishing (searched "efa nightly" and "Dockerfile.efa").

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Step3 tool parser: coerce nullable and object/array parameters by schema
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Fixes #65273. `Step3ToolParser._cast_arguments` only coerced a parameter when its schema had a single string `type`, so nullable parameters (`Optional[int]`, `Optional[bool]`, …) and `object`/`array` parameters reached clients as raw strings. It now resolves types with the shared `extract_types_from_schema` + `coerce_to_schema_type` helpers.

Related: #64517 / #64546, fixed for the Muse, MiniCPM5, and Poolside V1 parsers in #64539.

## Claims

- Nullable parameters are coerced to their declared type, whether written as `"type": ["integer", "null"]` or `anyOf`/`oneOf` with `{"type": "null"}` (the form pydantic emits for `Optional[...]`): `"5"` → `5`, `"true"` → `True`, `"null"` → `None`.
- `object` and `array` parameters are parsed as JSON instead of being returned as strings.
- Plain `string`/`integer`/`number`/`boolean`/`null` parameters, untyped parameters, and values that cannot be coerced (e.g. `"many"` for an integer) behave as before.

## Validation

Reproduction script from #65273 (CPU only, no model download):

```
# main
{'count': 5, 'opt_count': '5', 'opt_count_list': '5', 'opt_flag': 'true', 'filters': '{"a": 1}', 'tags': '["x", "y"]'}

# this PR
{'count': 5, 'opt_count': 5, 'opt_count_list': 5, 'opt_flag': True, 'filters': {'a': 1}, 'tags': ['x', 'y']}
```

Tests: added 13 parametrized cases to `tests/tool_parsers/test_step3_tool_parser.py` covering nullable integer/number/boolean/string via `type` lists, `anyOf` and `oneOf`, plus object, array, untyped, and uncoercible values. They construct the parser with a mock tokenizer, so they need no download.

```
pytest tests/tool_parsers/test_step3_tool_parser.py
24 passed, 8 xfailed
```

The 8 xfails are pre-existing markers on this file and are unchanged. `pre-commit` passes on both changed files. Run on CPU (WSL2, Python 3.14).

## Details

**Root cause:** `_cast_arguments` read `prop.get("type")` and dispatched on it with an `if typ == "string" / "integer" / "number" / "boolean" / "null"` chain. A list `type`, an `anyOf`/`oneOf` schema, or `object`/`array` matched no branch, so the value was left as the raw string.

**Fix:** replace the chain with `coerce_to_schema_type(value.strip(), extract_types_from_schema(prop))`, the same helpers `k2_horizon_tool_parser.py` uses. They already handle type lists, `anyOf`/`oneOf`/`allOf`, enum inference, type aliases, and non-finite numbers. The now-unused `contextlib` import is removed.

**Behavior changes inherited from the shared helper** (noting for reviewers):
- Whole `number` values come back as `5` rather than `5.0`. Both are valid JSON numbers.
- `"1"` and `"0"` are accepted for `boolean` parameters, in addition to `true`/`false`.

**Not changed:** the separate issue behind this file's existing xfail markers. Non-streaming extraction only parses calls in the `<｜tool_call_begin｜>function<｜tool_sep｜>…` form. That is out of scope here.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][Spec Decode] Pad DFlash draft inputs on extra programs of the same launch
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

`prepare_dflash_inputs` pads its per-request and per-token output buffers up to `max_num_reqs` / `max_num_tokens` for CUDA-graph replay, and today the last request's program does all of that padding serially. This PR launches 32 extra programs in the same grid and splits the padding loops between them. Related: #58633 targets the same padding loop with a wider padding block; this is an alternative that stays one launch.

## Claims

- `prepare_dflash_inputs` device time drops to ~2.1 µs per call regardless of batch size, from 7.9–8.5 µs at 16K batched tokens and 5.3–5.8 µs at 8K (GB200).
- Host time per call is unchanged vs `main` (still a single launch).
- Outputs are unchanged: every output and padded buffer is bit-identical to `main`.

## Validation

Microbenchmark of `prepare_dflash_inputs` on one GB200 GPU, base `main` 79d0899cca. Verify batch with 8 query tokens per request (1 + 7 speculative steps), `max_num_reqs` 256, block size 64. Device time: CUDA graph of 20 calls, median of 30 replays. Host time: eager call-return, median of ~1,900 calls. "#58633" = that PR's diff applied to the same base.

| max_num_batched_tokens | reqs | device: main / #58633 / this PR (µs) | host: main / #58633 / this PR (µs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16384 | 1 | 8.52 / 8.31 / **2.11** | 32.3 / 34.0 / 33.1 |
| 16384 | 8 | 7.92 / 7.79 / **2.08** | 31.4 / 33.7 / 31.8 |
| 16384 | 32 | 7.89 / 8.17 / **2.12** | 31.9 / 34.2 / 31.7 |
| 8192 | 1 | 5.81 / 5.57 / **2.09** | 31.4 / 33.3 / 31.8 |
| 8192 | 8 | 5.30 / 5.17 / **2.08** | 31.6 / 33.3 / 32.1 |
| 8192 | 32 | 5.28 / 5.17 / **2.09** | 31.8 / 33.5 / 32.3 |

- In every row, all three variants write identical buffers (compared from the same sentinel-filled tensors).
- `pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_prepare_inputs.py`: 6 passed on GB200 (including the compile-once check).
- End to end: in a TP4 DFlash-style draft with 5 draft KV-cache groups (the call runs once per group per step), the padding cost went from ~58 µs to ~20 µs per decode step, about −0.2% to −0.4% of a 5–15 ms step. This is a small end-to-end gain; the claim is the per-call saving.

## Details

- Grid becomes `(num_reqs + 32, num_blocks)`. Programs with `req_idx >= num_reqs` (block 0 only) each take every 32nd padding block of each padding loop; the regular per-request programs no longer pad.
- `num_reqs` is passed as a kernel argument with `do_not_specialize`, since it is no longer `tl.num_programs(0)`.
- The padded ranges and values are the same as before; only which program writes them changes.
- Why not a wider padding block (#58633): on current `main` the padding already uses `BLOCK_SIZE = 128`, so the remaining cost is the single program walking the whole span, which a wider block barely reduces (see table), and #58633 adds ~2 µs host time. Spreading the span over more programs removes it without a second launch, which was the concern raised on #58633's earlier two-kernel version.

Co-authored with @fululi12, whose #58633 identified this padding loop as a hot spot.

---

commits.pr_title: [Perf][Spec Decode] Skip vocab blocks with no target token in the resample kernel
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

In Model Runner V2 verification, `_resample_kernel` now returns early for a vocab block whose target logits are all `-inf` (masked by top-k/top-p or a logits processor): the residual there is `-inf` too, so the draft-logit load and the Gumbel draw are skipped. Sampled tokens are bitwise identical. Part of the rejection-sampling work tracked in #61024; first of a stack (see the end of this description).

## Claims

- Resample kernel on top-p-masked verify rows (K = 3, top-p 0.95, Qwen3-0.6B logits, V = 151,936, GB300): **165.9 → 55.4 µs** (creative-writing rows) and **149.5 → 42.2 µs** (math rows) at 256 requests; 13.7 → 6.8 µs at 16 requests.
- No cost on unmasked rows: the check runs only when some request in the chunk may have masked logits (top-p = 1 rows stay at 165.1 µs; forcing the check on them would cost 173.7 µs, +5%).
- Output is bitwise identical with the skip on or off.

## Validation

```
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_rejection_sampler_utils.py \
    tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_sampler_flags.py tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_rejection_sampler_chunking.py -q
# 127 passed (GB300). Unmodified main, first two files: 111 passed; this adds 4 parametrizations.
```

- `test_skip_masked_vocab_blocks_is_bitwise_identical`: two whole vocab blocks and most of a third masked, with and without draft logits, fp32 and fp64 Gumbel; skip on vs off must match bitwise.
- `test_logits_processing_cache_matches_request_features` gains the expected `may_mask_logits` per request feature; temperature-only is the case that needs processing but never masks.

Kernel times: `_resample_kernel` device time from the torch profiler (10 calls after 3 warm-up), the same inputs through upstream `main` and this branch, loaded side by side; outputs compared on the valid positions only.

| rows (requests × 4) | profile | top-p | main µs | skip on µs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | creative | 0.95 | 13.7 | 6.8 |
| 1,024 | creative | 0.95 | 165.9 | 55.4 |
| 1,024 | math | 0.95 | 149.5 | 42.2 |
| 1,024 | creative | 1.0 | 165.1 | 165.1 (gated off) |

Not measured: end-to-end serving throughput. In a verify-step harness with vLLM's own chain (fp32 copy, temperature, Triton top-p mask, rejection sampling) the same kernel change took a 256-request step from 2,086 to 1,976 µs.

## Details

- **Gate.** The block max costs about 5% of the kernel when nothing is masked, so `rejection_sample` takes `skip_masked_vocab_blocks` (default off) and `RejectionSampler._verify` turns it on when any request in the chunk may have masked logits. `Sampler` records that per request in `may_mask_logits`: min-p, top-k or top-p active, or thinking-budget forcing or a logits processor (counted conservatively, e.g. logit bias). Temperature alone only scales and never sets the flag. No host/device sync: the flag is a NumPy lookup.
- **Why it is exact.** The residual is a subset of the target's support, so an all-`-inf` target block yields an all-`-inf` residual. Such a block never wins the global argmax unless every block is `-inf`, and in that case it reports index 0, which is what the argmax of an all-`-inf` block returns.
- **Not duplicating.** Searched open PRs for "resample kernel skip", "rejection sampler resample", "top-p rejection sampling" and #61024: #41258 (lazy recovery) changes the V1 sampler, #48928 (FlashInfer AIR top-p) replaces the mask itself; neither touches the MRV2 resample kernel.
- **With the on-load path.** #65102 and #65103 carry this commit. There the kernels apply the top-p cutoff to raw logits as they load them, so the raw block is never all `-inf`; their next commit tests the block after the cutoff instead, which is the same tensor on this PR's path.
- **Stack.** 1/4, independent of the rest: (2) #65101 `topp_cutoffs_lse` op, (3) #65102 top-p applied as target logits load, (4) #65103 target log-sum-exp from that op. #65104 (draft log-sum-exp from the drafter) closed: a net loss once the drafter's cost is counted.

AI assistance (Claude) was used to write this change and its tests; the submitter is reviewing every line.
