commits.pr_title: [Perf][Mamba] Use the shared checkpoint exporter for Mamba2 and drop ssd_checkpoint
commits.pr_body:
## Overview Mamba2 prefill checkpoints now use the shared `MambaPrefillCheckpointExporter` (introduced for GDN/KDA in #60050) instead of their own `ssd_checkpoint.py` kernel, which is deleted. Part of the internal prefill checkpoint work tracked in #52959. ## Claims - One checkpoint-store kernel for GDN, KDA and Mamba2 instead of two. Diff: +53 / -157 in `vllm/` (including the deleted 118-line file) and +35 / -17 in tests (the Mamba2 test retarget, plus new Mamba2 and wide-state cases in the exporter test). - Mamba2 checkpoint store time is faster than the removed kernel in 39 of 48 cases, and no TP1/2/4 case is slower. The 3 slower cases are all TP8 (Nano 30B at 1-2 rows, Super at 2 rows), by at most +2.9 µs per step. GDN/KDA are 13-37% faster at 4+ rows on TP1/2. Across 96 cases, 25 are slower than main by at most +15 µs per step, mostly at TP4/8 with 1-2 rows (details and numbers below). - Stops Mamba2 from writing skipped prefill checkpoints into the null block. Under the default sparse retention a non-final prefill chunk that spans two or more Mamba blocks gets a checkpoint offset but a null destination (by design since #59175, so that the export is masked); the removed kernel had no null check and wrote it into block 0, while the shared kernel skips it (reproduced with `check_mamba2_null_block_write.py`, which runs both kernels on a Super TP1 row whose column is null). Latent: no reader of block 0 was found (details under "Behavior of the swap"). ## Validation Hardware: one B200, torch 2.14.0+cu130. All outputs are bitwise equal to the baseline kernel before timing. Tests (all pass): ``` pytest tests/kernels/mamba/test_mamba2_checkpoint_state.py tests/kernels/mamba/test_checkpoint_exporter.py tests/kernels/mamba/test_gdn_prefill_flashinfer.py tests/kernels/mamba/test_mamba_mixer2.py tests/v1/attention/test_mamba2_prefill_checkpoints.py tests/v1/attention/test_gdn_metadata_builder.py tests/models/kimi_k3/test_kda.py tests/models/kimi_k3/test_prefix_cache.py tests/models/kimi_k3/test_kda_metadata.py tests/models/glm5next/test_kda_recurrent.py -v pytest tests/v1/e2e/general/test_mamba_prefix_cache.py -k mrv2_async_flashinfer -v ``` `tests/kernels/mamba` runs in CI (`.buildkite/test_areas/kernels.yaml`). No CI test exercises the Mamba2 mixer's internal checkpoints end to end (the kernel is covered by the unit test above), so that path was checked only by the Nemotron serving run below. The test changes are pointing `test_store_selects_the_checkpoint_from_all_chunk_states` at the shared exporter, and adding a `mamba2` caller and a wide recurrent state shape to `test_checkpoint_exporter.py`. The wide shape launches programs past the conv window, so the guard is covered for correctness (not speed). With `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error`, serving Nemotron 3.5 Super at TP1 (4224-token Mamba block) under the traffic below triggered no host-device sync from the exporter; afterwards the server was healthy and prefix-cache hits were recorded: ``` VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error vllm serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4 --trust-remote-code 2>&1 | tee serve.log & M=nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4; PORT=8000 B="vllm bench serve --model $M --port $PORT --seed 0 --num-warmups 4" # 1) one long prompt at a time (1 checkpoint row per step) $B --dataset-name random --random-input-len 8192 --random-output-len 32 \ --num-prompts 16 --max-concurrency 1 # 2) bursts of 2.7k-token prompts (below the Mamba block, so no checkpoints) $B --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2700 --random-output-len 32 \ --num-prompts 120 --request-rate inf --max-concurrency 6 # 3) repeated long prefixes (checkpoint exports, then prefix-cache hits) $B --dataset-name prefix_repetition --prefix-repetition-prefix-len 6144 \ --prefix-repetition-suffix-len 1024 --prefix-repetition-num-prefixes 4 \ --prefix-repetition-output-len 32 --num-prompts 64 --request-rate inf # 4) mixed lengths, 600-11400 tokens (up to 3 checkpoint rows per step) $B --dataset-name random --random-input-len 6000 --random-range-ratio 0.9 \ --random-output-len 32 --num-prompts 64 --request-rate inf curl -s localhost:$PORT/health -o /dev/null -w "health: %{http_code}\n" grep -i -E "traceback|synchron|error" serve.log | head curl -s localhost:$PORT/metrics | grep -E "^vllm:prefix_cache_(queries|hits)" ``` GSM8K (`python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --num-shots 50`, 1319 questions, greedy) on the same server without `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK`. Every prompt starts with the same 50-shot prefix, longer than the 4224-token Mamba block, so the first prompts export checkpoints inside it and the rest resume from them (prefix-cache hit rate about 86% on both servers). Two runs per server: | | run 1 | run 2 | |---|---|---| | main (`24324ef0f6`) | 0.928 | 0.926 | | this PR | 0.926 | 0.926 | The two servers differ by at most 3 questions, within run-to-run variation. The two assertions added to `export()` (see "Behavior of the swap") were profiled in a real Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B step that exports a checkpoint in all 23 Mamba layers: one 4177-token prompt, one more than the 4176-token Mamba block, with fresh tokens every step (`profile_mamba2_checkpoint_step.py`, attached, 30 profiled steps per run). They add about 1.4 µs of host time per `export()` call (75.1 vs 73.7 µs median, inflated by the profiler). The GPU idle time right before each store kernel is unchanged: 34.8 vs 36.0 µs median, within the 33-55 µs spread between steps. Benchmarks (microbenchmark scripts that are not part of this PR, attached). Shapes are per-rank states derived from the models' Hugging Face configs. Each arm is timed over 3 rounds in rotating order with fresh buffers; a second copy of the baseline is the noise control, and the `noise` column (mostly ≤0.03) is the floor a ratio has to clear. `step` = per-layer delta × layer count. Each attached output comes from one command, run from the repo root with the attached scripts saved under `benchmarks/kernels/`: ``` python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_mamba_prefill_checkpoint.py # out_benchmark.log python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_mamba_prefill_checkpoint.py --block-sweep # out_sweep_benchmark.log python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_mamba_checkpoint_exporter_callers.py --block-sweep # out_sweep_callers.log python benchmarks/kernels/scratch_mamba_checkpoint_ablation.py # out_ablation_sass.log python benchmarks/kernels/check_mamba2_null_block_write.py # check_mamba2_null_block_write.log ``` **What "rows" means.** A row is a request in the step that exports a checkpoint: its final prefill chunk spans more than one Mamba block, so the checkpoint falls inside this chunk (`is_mamba_prefill_checkpoint_valid`). Decodes and other prefills add no rows. 1 row is one long prompt finishing in the step; several rows are a burst of mid-length prompts finishing together. A step holds at most about `max_num_batched_tokens / mamba_block_size` rows. Super at TP1 has a 4224-token block, so at most 3 rows at the default 16k budget. The block size is set so an attention page is at least as large as a Mamba page, so it shrinks with TP once the attention KV heads are replicated and the per-rank Mamba state keeps shrinking; higher TP therefore allows more rows per step (not measured here). The kernel only reads 3 conv tokens and one state row per request, so lengths do not affect its time, only the row count does. Mamba2, new exporter vs the removed SSD store (`out_benchmark.log`): | shape | rows | SSD µs | new µs | ratio | step µs | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Super (128 heads) TP1 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 4.70 / 6.43 / 9.22 / 12.26 | 4.13 / 5.60 / 8.26 / 11.04 | 0.88 / 0.87 / 0.90 / 0.90 | -23 / -33 / -38 / -49 | | Super TP4 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.49 / 4.00 / 4.83 / 5.73 | 3.14 / 3.49 / 4.19 / 4.77 | 0.90 / 0.87 / 0.87 / 0.83 | -14 / -20 / -26 / -38 | | Super TP8 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.17 / 3.36 / 3.94 / 4.22 | 3.17 / 3.39 / 3.74 / 4.26 | 1.00 / 1.01 / 0.95 / 1.01 | 0 / +1 / -8 / +1 | | Nano 30B TP1 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.97 / 4.77 / 6.30 / 7.74 | 3.52 / 4.26 / 5.44 / 6.91 | 0.89 / 0.89 / 0.86 / 0.89 | -10 / -12 / -20 / -19 | | Nano 30B TP8 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.10 / 3.36 / 3.46 / 3.68 | 3.23 / 3.46 / 3.42 / 3.58 | 1.04 / 1.03 / 0.99 / 0.97 | +3 / +2 / -1 / -2 | Across all 48 Mamba2 cases 39 are faster, 6 are within noise and 3 are slower: Nano 30B TP8 at 1 and 2 rows (+3 and +2 µs per step) and Super TP8 at 2 rows (+1). GDN/KDA, the exporter at 512 vs main's kernel (`out_sweep_callers.log`): | shape | rows | main µs | new µs | ratio | step µs | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Kimi K3 (KDA) TP1 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 6.18 / 9.92 / 17.41 / 24.86 | 4.83 / 6.91 / 11.30 / 15.81 | 0.78 / 0.70 / 0.65 / 0.64 | -93 / -208 / -422 / -625 | | Kimi K3 TP8 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.04 / 3.36 / 4.35 / 5.28 | 3.14 / 3.42 / 4.10 / 4.51 | 1.03 / 1.02 / 0.94 / 0.85 | +7 / +4 / -18 / -53 | | Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (GDN) TP1 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 3.71 / 5.09 / 7.65 / 10.24 | 3.62 / 4.16 / 5.47 / 6.98 | 0.97 / 0.82 / 0.71 / 0.68 | -3 / -28 / -65 / -98 | | Qwen3.5-35B-A3B TP8 | 1 / 2 / 4 / 6 | 2.91 / 3.04 / 3.17 / 3.42 | 3.26 / 3.13 / 3.30 / 3.39 | 1.12 / 1.03 / 1.04 / 0.99 | +11 / +3 / +4 / -1 | Across the 96 GDN/KDA cases (all six models, TP1/2/4/8, 1/2/4/6 rows) 63 are faster, 8 are within noise and 25 are slower: ratio up to 1.144 and up to +15.0 µs per step (both Qwen3-Next-80B TP8, 1 row), per-layer cost +0.06 to +0.42 µs. 21 of the 25 are TP4/8 and 21 are at 1-2 rows; the four at 4+ rows are all TP8 (ratio at most 1.05). At 4+ rows on TP1/2 all 24 cases are 13-37% faster. The slower cases are ~3 µs launches, where the same case moved by up to 0.4 µs between two runs of this benchmark (more than the in-run noise floor), so individual verdicts there are not stable; the counts and the TP1/2 results are. Not validated: end-to-end serving throughput (microbenchmarks only), how often real traffic reaches 4+ checkpoint rows in a step (3 at most for Super at TP1; higher TP allows more, but was not measured), and any hardware other than B200. ## Details **Why this swap makes sense now.** Before #60050 the two checkpoint-store kernels were not interchangeable: the shared one read each checkpoint's recurrent state from row `i` of the prefill output, while Mamba2's SSD store picked it out of all chunk states through `checkpoint_chunk_idx`. #60050 added `HAS_RECURRENT_ROWS` (`recurrent_rows`) to the shared kernel, which is exactly that selection. Since then the two kernels are basically identical: they differ in launch configuration (block size 1024 vs 256 on main), in the null-block and short-offset masks described under "Behavior of the swap" (the shared kernel already has them), and in how the conv window is addressed (the removed kernel took `x` as `(dim, tokens)`; the shared one takes `raw_qkv` as `(tokens, width)`, and the mixer now passes `x.transpose(0, 1)`). This PR sets the shared kernel's block size to 512 and makes its strides runtime arguments, so Mamba2 can use it without losing time and the duplicate can go. **Why the kernel changed.** Three changes to `store_cache_checkpoints_kernel`, each measured separately (the callers benchmark's `cx`, `guard` and `wide` arms each take one change out of the shipped kernel; `scratch_mamba_checkpoint_ablation.py` is a replica kernel that toggles one change at a time, with SASS diffs in `out_ablation_sass.log`): - **Block size 256 -> 512 (one value for all callers).** The removed Mamba2 kernel used 1024-wide blocks, and at 256 the shared kernel was 1.19-1.27x slower than it at 4-6 rows on large states (Super and Nano 4B at TP1), so Mamba2 would have regressed. 512 has a better worst case than 1024: 1024 is slower than the old kernel in 11 of the 24 TP4/TP8 cases, by up to about +12 µs per step, and it is ahead of 512 in only 7 of 48 cases (by 1-6%, mostly TP1/2 at 4+ rows). GDN/KDA share the kernel and get 512 as well. Keeping them at 256 was measured and is worse: with the conv guard below, 44 of 96 GDN/KDA cases were slower than main (up to ratio 1.19, +20 µs per step, both at Qwen3-Next-80B TP8 1 row), against 25 at 512 (up to ratio 1.14). A larger block means fewer programs, so the guard's fixed cost matters less. (The 256 and 1024 figures come from the block-size sweeps `out_sweep_benchmark.log` and `out_sweep_callers.log`, which time 256, 512 and 1024 side by side. `out_sweep_callers.log` is also the source of the GDN/KDA table; `out_sweep_benchmark.log` is a separate run from the Mamba2 table, so its 512 counts differ by a case or two.) - **Strides as runtime arguments, not `tl.constexpr`.** Specializing the 8 strides costs about 6% on average (`cx/cur` column of the callers benchmark: 0.97-1.20, mean 1.06 over the 144 Mamba2/GDN/KDA shapes), most at 1-2 rows (mean 1.08 and 1.07) and least on large states (TP1 at 4-6 rows: mean 1.015). The SASS has 192 vs 184 static instructions (216 vs 192 at TP8 shapes), with more IADD3/IMAD where runtime strides use LEA, and an identical sequence of global memory ops. On the conv-only Qwen4Exp PLE shape the two are within 2% (`cx/cur` 0.98-1.01). - **Skip the conv window in programs that don't cover it.** The conv section used to run, fully masked off, in every program. Guarding it on `program_id(1) * BLOCK_SIZE < WIDTH * STATE_LEN` cuts the time by 15-22% on large states in the ablation (for example 14.2 -> 11.1 µs at Super TP1, 6 rows) and is about neutral on small ones (-5% to +3% at Super TP4/TP8 and Nano 30B TP8). In the callers benchmark, removing it (`wide` arm) makes TP1 shapes at 4-6 rows 13-29% slower (mean 22%). **Tradeoff of the conv guard.** The guard is what makes the Mamba2 swap faster than the removed kernel. Removing it (`wide` arm: the shipped kernel without the guard) measured, by rows (mean over the 12 shapes per model kind; positive means removing it is slower): | rows | GDN | KDA | Mamba2 | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 0% | +1% | -1% | | 2 | +6% | +2% | +4% | | 4 | +10% | +8% | +10% | | 6 | +14% | +12% | +15% | So the guard is about neutral on average at 1 row and wins from 2 rows up, by up to about 255 µs per step on TP1/2 (Kimi K3 TP1, 6 rows; Super TP1 at 6 rows about 125 µs). It loses on a few launch-bound shapes: 15 of the 72 1-2 row cases are 3% or more faster without it (13 of them TP4/8), by at most +0.5 µs per layer (+19 µs per step, Super TP8 2 rows). Without it Mamba2 would be slower than the removed kernel at TP1 with 2+ rows (Super TP1 about 1.03x at 2 rows and 1.15x at 6, from the ablation). On GDN/KDA's 1-2 row TP4/8 cases (2.6% slower than main on average) the guard accounts for about 1 point: removing it makes them 1.2% faster, while going back to 256 or to constexpr strides alone makes them 6% and 9% slower. The benchmarks' main kernel predates #63761's int64 cast; the `guard` arm (the shipped kernel with an int32 index) shows the cast is free (-2.4% to +2.0% per case), so the comparisons with main still hold. **Behavior of the swap.** The shared kernel also skips null destination blocks, which the removed kernel did not check, and for an offset shorter than the conv window it skips the conv window but still stores the recurrent state. The manager would cache such a block as a valid checkpoint, so `export()` now asserts that every nonzero offset covers the conv window, and that `recurrent_rows` has one entry per checkpoint row. Both are host-side checks with no device sync. Neither can fire today: a valid checkpoint's offset is at least `hash_block_size` (`query_start + hash_block_size <= checkpoint_position`), above the 3-token Mamba2 conv window, and every caller sizes recurrent_rows per checkpoint row. The null-block skip is reachable. Under the default sparse retention (`prefix_cache_retention_interval=0`) the manager reserves a checkpoint block only for the chunk that ends the prefill, and leaves the column null for earlier chunks so that the export is masked (#59175, `test_checkpoint_reservation_matches_worker`). An earlier chunk that spans two or more Mamba blocks still gets an offset, and the removed kernel wrote that checkpoint into the null block (block 0); the shared kernel skips it. `check_mamba2_null_block_write.py` reproduces this with Super TP1's geometry (a 12672-token first chunk, checkpoint offset 8448 in column 1): the removed store writes the row's checkpoint into block 0 and the shared exporter leaves it untouched, while a row with a real block is written identically by both. No reader of that write was found: Mamba's decode conv and SSU kernels skip `NULL_BLOCK_ID` rows, and cache groups overlay the same memory, so it also lands in attention's block 0, which only the FA4 restricted-sliding-window gap path assumes is zero (not used by full-attention hybrids such as Nemotron). That needs a prompt longer than the token budget and a budget of at least two Mamba blocks (Super TP1: prompts over 16k tokens at the default budget). The `mamba2` case in `test_checkpoint_exporter.py` covers the skip. Mamba2 passes the pre-conv activations through `x.transpose(0, 1)`, the same view the removed kernel read. **Considered: keeping main's launch shape for GDN/KDA.** A per-caller option that keeps GDN/KDA on 256-wide blocks without the guard, with only the runtime strides, is the callers benchmark's `wide256` arm. It is slower than main in 69 of 96 GDN/KDA cases (up to 1.04x, +58 µs per step at Kimi K3 TP1 with 6 rows) and gives up the 13-37% gains at 4+ rows on TP1/2. On the 1-2 row TP4/8 cases it would be 0.9% slower than main on average instead of 2.6%. So all callers share 512 and the guard. **Limitations.** Measured on B200 only; microbenchmarks, not serving. The shared kernel is also used by the ROCm Kimi-K3 KDA exporter (conv half only, `vllm/models/kimi_k3/amd/ops/kda_checkpoint.py`), so the 512 block size and conv guard apply there too; `tests/models/kimi_k3/test_amd_kda_checkpoint.py` covers it but needs gfx950 and was not run. The Qwen4Exp PLE short conv (#61601: conv-only with a token map, one layer) shares the kernel too. It is 2-6% slower than main at 1, 2 and 6 rows and within noise at 4, at most +0.19 µs per step, which comes from the 512 block size (at 256 the shipped kernel is up to 6% faster on that shape); its conv window spans every program, so the guard skips nothing there. **Related PRs.** No open PR does this swap (searched 2026-10-26: issue #52959 and open PRs that cite it, `ssd_checkpoint`, `store_cache_checkpoints_kernel`, `MambaPrefillCheckpointExporter`, "Mamba2 prefill checkpoint"). #61601 (Qwen4Exp PLE checkpoints) and #61497 (Mamba2 SSD host overhead) are merged, and this PR is rebased on them. #59175 is where the manager leaves a non-final chunk's checkpoint column null for the exporter to skip (see "Behavior of the swap"). Open PRs near this code: #60659 (GDN Triton/FLA and AITER checkpoints) and #61951 (ROCm GLM-5.3-Flash KDA on Triton) add new `export()` callers without changing the exporter, so they pick up these kernel changes; #61501 (opt-in FlashInfer SSD prefill scan, draft) edits `conv_ssm_forward` next to the Mamba2 export but keeps checkpointed prefills on the Triton scan; #61466 (per-layer checkpoint alignment) edits `mamba_mixer2.py`'s imports and spec override; #60888 (checkpoints at or before the initial-state column, draft) changes the scheduler and manager rules, not the exporter, and like #59175 expects checkpoints into null columns to be skipped; #62232 (Mamba2 prefill checkpoints on CPU) adds a CPU path to `store_prefill_checkpoint`, which this PR deletes, and a test to `test_mamba2_checkpoint_state.py`; whichever lands second moves that path into `MambaPrefillCheckpointExporter.export()`, which, like the removed kernel, always launches Triton (Mamba2 checkpoints on CPU are broken on main too, #62153).
Scripts and outputs

[benchmark_mamba_checkpoint_exporter_callers.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33964545/benchmark_mamba_checkpoint_exporter_callers.py) [benchmark_mamba_prefill_checkpoint.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33964546/benchmark_mamba_prefill_checkpoint.py) [check_mamba2_null_block_write.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33964550/check_mamba2_null_block_write.log) [check_mamba2_null_block_write.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33964552/check_mamba2_null_block_write.py) [mamba_checkpoint_bench_utils.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33964553/mamba_checkpoint_bench_utils.py) [out_ablation_sass.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33964556/out_ablation_sass.log) [out_benchmark.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33964557/out_benchmark.log) [out_sweep_benchmark.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33964558/out_sweep_benchmark.log) [out_sweep_callers.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33964559/out_sweep_callers.log) [scratch_mamba_checkpoint_ablation.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33964560/scratch_mamba_checkpoint_ablation.py) [profile_mamba2_checkpoint_step.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34316357/profile_mamba2_checkpoint_step.py) [profile_mamba2_checkpoint_step.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34316397/profile_mamba2_checkpoint_step.log)

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][HiSparse] Release temporary device KV bindings after graph profiling
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Release HiSparse's temporary device KV bindings after CUDA-graph memory profiling, while preserving the engine-scoped registered host pool for the real KV cache.

## Claims

- Live attention handles and runtimes no longer retain the throwaway KV slab and its per-binding tables after profiling cleanup.
- Cleanup is idempotent. Rebinding preserves host registration and clears stale hot-cache tags before the new backing is consumed.
- No throughput, accuracy, or reproduced model OOM improvement is claimed.

## Validation

### Review follow-up (2026-11-04)

- Both the runtime and attention handle now use `_reset_binding_state()` from construction and unbinding. Persistent index-group/draft membership is retained.
- Removed the `runtimes` argument from `release_pinned_state()`. Connector shutdown/error paths detach their attention handles; the Host release helper retains its existing drain, unregistration and shared-region cleanup responsibilities.
- Also fixed an adjacent partial-initialization failure path: if KV binding fails before initialization returns, already-bound context handles are detached before the Host-pool reference is dropped.
- Removed redundant handle deduplication and the extra bind-time Hot-state reset. Real model capture retains ownership of the existing connector reset; the throwaway profiling capture uses a no-op connector.
- Applicable pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` passed. Four source-isolated CPU lifecycle checks passed (2.52 s), covering storage detachment, repeated cleanup, shutdown and partial-binding rollback. These checks use real CPU tensors/handles with external device services substituted; they are not full-package or device tests.
- Full-package pytest collection was blocked by missing `tblib`. Fresh CUDA/model validation of this follow-up has not been run. Device/model results from the initial submission below remain historical and do not validate this revision.

### Review follow-up (2026-11-03)

- `release_pinned_state()` now calls the same `HiSparseRuntime.unbind_cache()` used by profiling cleanup. Final shutdown retains its existing synchronization, Host unregistration, and shared-region cleanup; profiling cleanup retains the registered Host pool.
- Added a HiSparse-op availability skip guard to the Host-pool reuse test. Its teardown also exercises `release_pinned_state()` on the already-unbound real runtime.
- Narrowed the device regression to binding a temporary 64 MiB backing with a real runtime/attention handle, then checking that profiling cleanup drops the views and releases the allocation. Removed the unrelated gather, rebind, and graph-replay checks from this test; Host-pool reuse remains covered separately.
- Local pre-commit checks and `git diff --check` passed for the follow-up. The Dockerfile graph hook was checked separately through Git Bash; actionlint had no applicable workflow files.
- The device/model results below are historical results from the initial submission, not a rerun of this follow-up. Updated GPU tests have not been rerun locally.

Functional validation completed in the current container; the human submitter reviewed the change and approved submission.

- Current H200 container, frozen main 24e80c261428cc45200b28f77fd0e2fdc36a56a8 plus existing PR63801 changes; unchanged matching native libraries.
- New storage-lifetime regression before this fix: 1 failed, at the retained-view weak-reference assertion (2.94 s).
- The same regression after this fix: 1 passed (2.80 s).
- Compute Sanitizer memcheck: 1 passed, ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors.
- Adjacent eviction, MTP multi-step, and invalidation contracts: 7 passed.
- Real GLM-5.2-FP8 TP8/MTP3 startup, gpu_memory_utilization=0.9, CUDA graph memory profiling enabled: passed through profiling capture, teardown, real KV initialization, final capture, and API readiness. Available KV cache memory: 31.11 GiB. Four concurrent greedy requests succeeded (103/128/128/70 output tokens); no request errors or pre-cleanup ERROR lines. This is a short serving smoke, not accuracy or performance evaluation.
- Existing host-pool cleanup test migrated from fake runtime objects to real runtime/handle/pool objects; worker HiSparse subset: 15 passed. Original fake-object test failure is preserved.
- Final committed tests: 2 passed (3.47 s) after adopting torch.accelerator memory queries and explicit type-narrowing assertions.
- Repository pre-commit checks passed, including pinned Ruff, typos, mypy (Python 3.11), Buildkite keys, test tethering, and API checks. actionlint was skipped because no GitHub Actions workflow changed; Dockerfile graph check was run successfully via Git Bash (Windows lacks /bin/bash for its direct shebang). CI YAML parsing and git diff --check also passed.
- The standalone startup wrapper failed during intentional cleanup with pidfd EINVAL, after all requests completed. The original failed state and post-termination EngineDeadError logs are preserved. An independent audit verified no surviving task processes and all eight GPUs at 0 MiB/0% utilization; the model was not rerun to replace this evidence.
- Evidence archive (retained locally): profiling-cache-release-current-v2-evidence.tar.gz, SHA256 2dc1cbdb80d271bcf37e265bb498641db3e57a8a87c6b901fab37ecb97d9cdd2; 63 files hash-verified. Original downloaded evidence had 56 individually verified files; v2 adds final committed tests and contribution checks.

The contributed patch is isolated against main 5d55ef1590c92213e3893dc8e8712f7f2e0bc508. Latest-main native validation was cancelled in favor of validating the fix directly in the user's current container. No CUDA source or package dependency is changed by this patch. NPU and ROCm hardware were not validated.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction commands</summary>

Run from the configured vLLM checkout:

```bash
PYTHONPATH="$PWD" CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py::test_hisparse_profiling_releases_device_storage \
  tests/v1/worker/test_attn_utils.py::test_profiling_cleanup_keeps_host_pool_for_real_kv_cache -v

compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --report-api-errors extended --error-exitcode 42 \
  .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py::test_hisparse_profiling_releases_device_storage -v -s

.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/worker/test_attn_utils.py \
  -k 'hisparse or profiling_cleanup' -v

.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py -v \
  -k 'test_hisparse_resident_rows_bypass_hot_lru or test_hisparse_swap_in_preserves_rows_across_eviction or test_hisparse_multi_step_swaps_match_independent or test_hisparse_multi_step_writes_request_major_output or test_hisparse_newest_write_and_recycled_slot_invalidation or test_hisparse_invalidation_covers_every_index_group'
```

The current device regression binds a 64 MiB temporary backing with a real attention handle and runtime, then checks dead view weak references and the fall in allocated device memory after profiling cleanup. The separate worker test checks Host-pool reuse. The earlier, broader regression also checked rebinding and graph replay; its historical validation is recorded above.

</details>

## Details

The profiling teardown clears the runner's normal caches, but model layers still own HiSparseCacheHandle objects. Their PagedCacheView and Runtime.hot keep the temporary device backing alive. release_pinned_state(..., []) removes only some runtime aliases; it does not detach those handle-owned device views.

Separate per-binding detachment from final host-pool shutdown. Keep the permanent index group, streams, and shared workspaces; drop only storage and metadata associated with the old KV binding. Group leaders reset the existing hot state when binding new storage.

Duplicate-work review: #61668 is the merged host-pool reuse change and leaves these device aliases attached. The inspected open ROCm PR #60358 addresses other cleanup/registration behavior, without this device-binding detachment. Searches for HiSparse profiling release and the exact cleanup function found no open PR addressing this fix as of 2026-11-01.

AI assistance was used for code analysis, implementation, and validation. The human submitter reviewed the change and validation results and approved submission.

commits.pr_title: [HiSparse] Support the extensible KV cache
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Lets HiSparse run on the extensible KV cache (#56492), which previously excluded it. HiSparse's device pool is reserved and grown like any other KV cache. Its host pool stays outside it.

## Claims

- HiSparse uses the extensible KV cache by default.
- At default flags, GPU+host KV capacity grows by 16% and throughput matches `main`. GSM8K under heavy host offload also matches `main`.
- HiSparse with NIXL P/D and with the Mooncake store connector works on the extensible cache.
- Fixes two warmup crashes that removing the gate exposed:
  - the FlashInfer HiSparse autotune read hot blocks that had not been committed;
  - context-prefill warmup overflowed the hot group's fixed-size block-table rows.

## Validation

All runs on B200 with `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1`, against base 3b6eeb0606.

**Default flags.** GLM-5.3-NVFP4, TP4, no `--gpu-memory-utilization`. Two runs each, server restarted for every point.
```
vllm serve RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-NVFP4 -tp 4 --max-model-len 17408 --max-num-seqs 256 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 64 \
  --attention-config '{"hisparse_config":{}}' \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"HiSparseConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"host_pool_gib":64}}'
vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-input-len 16384 --random-output-len 1024 \
  --num-prompts 2c --max-concurrency c --ignore-eos --seed 42
```

| | GPU+host KV tokens | c=16 tok/s | c=16 TPOT | c=64 tok/s | c=64 TPOT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `main` | 1,313,935 | 661 / 666 | 20.3 / 20.1 ms | 949 / 944 | 54.3 / 54.7 ms |
| PR | 1,529,536 | 668 / 664 | 20.1 / 20.2 ms | 956 / 962 | 53.9 / 53.5 ms |

- The PR's log shows `Extended KV cache to 367616 blocks (63.11 GiB)`.
- At c=64, HiSparse stats show heavy host traffic in both variants.

**Accuracy.** GSM8K: 1319 questions, 5-shot, concurrency 32. The same server at `--max-model-len 8192 --max-num-seqs 32 --kv-cache-dtype bfloat16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.625` and `host_pool_gib` 32.
- PR: `Extended KV cache to 6208 blocks`, scores 0.904 and 0.912.
- `main` with `--num-gpu-blocks-override 6208`: 0.923 and 0.914.
- Both ran with 12.8k tokens of KV capacity against about 48k demanded, with about 14M hot-buffer misses and 61–65 GB H2D per stats interval.

**P/D.** Tiny DeepSeek-V3.2 with dummy weights, one prefiller and one decoder. The decoder is sized only by `--gpu-memory-utilization`.
- **NIXL:** the decoder runs `MultiConnector[HiSparseConnector, NixlConnector]`. Greedy outputs match HiSparse without P/D (5/5 prompts, 48/48 tokens) with a 1.26M-block pool and with a 768-block pool, where imports land in host memory. Without the post-extend cache-dict fix, the handshake fails: `RuntimeError: Engine ... holds KV layer 'model.layers.0.self_attn.attn', which has no counterpart here.`
- **Mooncake store:** `MultiConnector[HiSparseConnector, MooncakeStoreConnector]` starts and serves requests. Without the fix, startup fails: `ValueError: Missing transferable KV caches for layers: [...]`.

**Warmup crashes on `main`.** Run the GSM8K command on `main` with only the gate removed:
- `cudaErrorIllegalAddress` in `FlashInferMLASparseImpl.autotune_hisparse_decode`;
- with autotune disabled, `Block table write ... exceeds row capacity (128 > 64)`.

**Tests**, all passing:

| File | Passed |
|---|---|
| `tests/v1/e2e/general/test_hisparse.py` | 6/6 |
| `tests/v1/worker/test_extensible_kv_cache.py` | 20/20 |
| `tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_planning.py` | 66/66 |
| `tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_warmup_blocks.py` | 36/36 |
| `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_worker.py` | 248/248 |
| `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector_hma.py` | 98/98 |

One more NIXL HMA case needs a gated checkpoint that could not be downloaded.

New tests:
- **`test_hisparse_extensible_kv_cache`:** greedy outputs and the post-extend `kv_caches_by_layer` (layers, dtypes, devices, shapes, storage sizes) must equal a fixed-size cache of the same block count. It fails with either warmup fix reverted, and before the resident/hot rebind (resident entries spanned the whole reservation). CI runs it on H200, which does not use the FlashInfer autotune, so only SM100 guards the autotune fix.
- **`test_shrink_kv_cache_configs_leaves_host_resident_tensors`:** fails on `main`, where the measured shrink rescales the host pool's tensor.

The NIXL/Mooncake registration itself has no permanent test: there is no HiSparse P/D CI job.

## Details

- **Host-resident tensors stay out of the extensible paths.** `ExtensibleKVCache`, `committed_views`/`committed_kv_cache_tensors` and `shrink_kv_cache_configs` skip `host_resident` tensors. `host_resident` is an existing generic field.
- **The post-extend cache dict matches the fixed path's.** The runner keeps the dict `init_kv_cache` returned (`kv_caches_by_layer`); `extend_kv_cache` swaps in the committed views and passes it to `runner.kv_caches` and the connectors. Host layers keep their views and HiSparse's hot slabs stay out. `committed_views` gives layers laid out over the raw buffer (`has_layer_views=False`) the committed prefix, and `rebind_hisparse_device_caches` rebinds HiSparse's resident and hot views over it, so they span the committed blocks rather than the reservation. CUDA graphs captured before extend stay valid: the base address does not move.
- **Autotune:** the HiSparse autotune commits `cdiv(topk, hot_block_size)` blocks before tuning.
- **Warmup:** clamps reservations to the spec's block-table row length (`max_num_blocks_per_req`), which bounds HiSparse's fixed-size hot rows. Mamba is exempt: in non-align modes `MambaManager` can hold more blocks than its row length.
- **Considered:** feature-owned `if hisparse:` branches in the model runner and `extend_kv_cache`. That is more code, and it still needs the same planning changes.
- **Not covered:** sleep/wake with HiSparse on the extensible cache.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Keep the extensible tensor's PyCapsule_New prototype private
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

The extensible tensor's DLPack helper configures the process-wide `ctypes.pythonapi.PyCapsule_New`. FlashInfer's MNNVL helpers (`flashinfer.comm.dlpack_utils`) reset that same object's `restype` to `c_void_p`. This PR binds a private `PYFUNCTYPE` prototype instead, so other libraries can't change it. Follow-up to #56492.

## Claims

- Fixes `RuntimeError: from_dlpack received an invalid capsule` in `ExtensibleTensor` views (e.g. `allocate_kv_cache` → `full_view`) when a FlashInfer MNNVL / symmetric-memory buffer was created earlier in the process.
- No behavior change otherwise: the same C function is called with the same signature.

## Validation

- New test `test_views_survive_shared_pycapsule_new_restype_change` in `tests/utils_/test_extensible_tensor.py` sets `ctypes.pythonapi.PyCapsule_New.restype = c_void_p` (what FlashInfer does), then takes a view. It runs in its own spawned process like the rest of the file, so the global change doesn't leak into other tests.
  - Without the fix: fails with `RuntimeError: from_dlpack received an invalid capsule ...`.
  - With the fix: passes.
- `pytest tests/utils_/test_extensible_tensor.py` on GB200: 11 passed.
- End to end: a TP4 model that allocates a FlashInfer MNNVL buffer during weight loading failed in `initialize_kv_cache` on all ranks with the error above. With this change it loads and runs.
- `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` pass.

## Details

Root cause: `ctypes.pythonapi.PyCapsule_New` is one shared `_FuncPtr`, so its `restype` / `argtypes` are global mutable state and the last writer wins. FlashInfer's `create_dlpack_capsule` sets `restype = c_void_p`, after which our call returns an int address instead of a capsule and `torch.from_dlpack` rejects it. `ctypes.PYFUNCTYPE(...)(("PyCapsule_New", ctypes.pythonapi))` creates a separate function object bound to the same symbol, so it is unaffected.

Not a duplicate: no open PR touches `extensible_tensor.py` or this error.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Mistral] Carry token ids in stream state for byte-fallback tokens
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Fix streaming derender for Tekken-based Mistral tokenizers, where a byte-fallback token in the decode window breaks the client-carried `stream_state`.

The `/v1/responses` corruption originally reported here was fixed by #65118; this PR only covers the derender endpoints.

## Claims

- Streaming `/v1/completions/derender` and `/v1/chat/completions/derender` keep working when the decode window contains a byte-fallback token instead of rejecting the request.
- With a parser configured, chat derender for `MistralTokenizer` now uses the request's `skip_special_tokens`, matching serving after #65118.


## Validation

### Unit test

```shell
python -m pytest tests/entrypoints/scale_out/derender/test_derender_stream.py -v

# 124 passed, 1 xfailed in 76.12s
```

### E2E test

#### Server:

```shell
vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B \
  --config-format mistral \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --decode-context-parallel-size 8 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --reasoning-parser mistral \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser mistral \
  --load-format mistral
```

#### Client:

**req.json**

```json
{
  "model": "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B",
  "stream": false,
  "max_output_tokens": 100,
  "tools": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "name": "get_weather",
      "description": "Get current weather for a location",
      "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"location": {"type": "string"}, "unit": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["location"]
      }
    }
  ],
  "input": [
    {"role": "user", "content": "서울의 날씨가 어때?"},
    {"type": "function_call", "call_id": "udM7soqYx", "name": "get_weather", "arguments": "{\"location\":\"서울\",\"unit\":\"celsius\"}"},
    {"type": "function_call_output", "call_id": "udM7soqYx", "output": "서울의 현재 날씨: 22°C, 맑음, 습도 60%"}
  ]
}
```

**Request**

```shell
curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/responses -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d@/tmp/req.json | jq .output[0].content
```

#### Result:

- main: `[{"text": "사용자가 \"서울의 날씨가 어���?\"라고 물어��고, get_weather 함수를 호출해서 ...`
- PR: `[{"text": "사용자가 \"서울의 날씨가 어때?\"라고 물어봤고, get_weather 함수를 호출해서 ...`

## Details

- Root cause: `MistralTokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens` returns raw `bytes` for byte-fallback tokens. This happens with `skip_special_tokens=True` too, so it already affects `main`. Streaming derender stored those pieces in `DerenderStreamState.prev_tokens: list[str]`, which goes through JSON between chunks. An incomplete UTF-8 piece can't be carried there.

commits.pr_title: [Frontend] Add granite_toolcall_parser for Granite 4.2 tool calling
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Granite 4.2 emits tool calls in an XML format:

```
<tool_call>
<function=func_name>
<parameter=key>value</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
```

This PR adds a dedicated `granite_toolcall_parser` so Granite 4.2 ships with its own
tool-call parser name.

```bash
vllm serve ibm-granite/granite-4.2-8b \
    --tool-call-parser granite_toolcall_parser \
    --enable-auto-tool-choice
```

## Design

`GraniteToolCallParser` is a thin subclass of the existing `GraniteThinkingParser`. Granite 4.2
already drives both `<think>`/`</think>` reasoning and `<tool_call>` XML tool calls through a
single engine, so the subclass inherits the grammar, argument converter and streaming logic
unchanged and is exposed as a standalone `--tool-call-parser`.

- **No duplicated grammar** — the tool-call extraction is inherited, so future fixes to the shared
  parser engine flow in automatically.
- **Works standalone** — it extracts tool calls correctly whether or not
  `--reasoning-parser granite_thinking_parser` is also configured, and with any reasoning parser.
- **Both thinking modes** — behaves identically with `enable_thinking` on and off.

Changes:

- `vllm/parser/granite_toolcall.py` — `GraniteToolCallParser(GraniteThinkingParser)`
- `vllm/tool_parsers/granite_toolcall_parser.py` — tool-parser adapter shim
- `vllm/parser/engine/registered_adapters.py` — generate the adapters
- `vllm/tool_parsers/__init__.py` — register the `granite_toolcall_parser` key
- `docs/features/tool_calling.md` — document the Granite 4.2 row
- `tests/tool_parsers/test_granite_toolcall_parser.py` — parity test suite

## Test Plan

`tests/tool_parsers/test_granite_toolcall_parser.py` runs a shared corpus of model outputs through
both `granite_toolcall_parser` and the in-tree `qwen3_coder` parser (which handles the same XML
format) and asserts byte-identical results. Coverage:

- single / parallel / no-call / reasoning-then-call outputs
- every JSON argument type (int, float, bool, null, string, array, object)
- empty arguments, escaped strings, multiline values, whitespace inside tags
- malformed/partial inputs (missing closing tags, missing `>` on the function name, unclosed
  function names, consecutive calls without a closing tag)
- each case run in non-streaming, per-token streaming, and random-chunk streaming
- each case run with `enable_thinking` both `True` and `False`
- a standalone test confirming extraction works with no reasoning parser configured

## Test Result

```
tests/tool_parsers/test_granite_toolcall_parser.py  212 passed
tests/tool_parsers/test_qwen3coder_tool_parser.py    60 passed
```

commits.pr_title: [CI] Pin existing dependency hashes and enforce immutable references
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Pin archive hashes for the dependencies already present in the five compiled requirement files and enforce immutable GitHub Actions references. This initializes hash pinning and its checks; automatic dependency updates remain in #59667.

## Claims

- Add SHA-256 archive hashes to all **1,458 existing requirement entries**, preserving every package version from current main. All five pre-commit compile hooks emit hashes without upgrading pins.
- Add a check rejecting tags, branches, and short commits in external Actions/reusable workflows; require image digests for Docker actions. Pin the recipe reusable workflow to its current main commit.
- Keep hashed requirement consumers working: remove complete continued Torch requirements, filter whole CPU requirements, preserve complete fastsafetensors requirements and enforce source hashes in both remaining ROCm rebuilds, emit hashes during CUDA nightly/arm64 recompilation, and require hashes in the documentation install.

## Validation

- `.venv/bin/python -m pytest --confcutdir=tests/tools tests/tools/test_dependency_pins.py -q`: **15 passed**. The four ROCm cases execute each Dockerfile’s extraction/install command against a local sdist: valid hashes install successfully; incorrect hashes fail verification. These tests are wired into the existing Buildkite CPU test step, with both remaining ROCm Dockerfiles included in its source dependencies.
- `pre-commit run --files .buildkite/test_areas/misc.yaml .github/workflows/recipes.yml .pre-commit-config.yaml .readthedocs.yaml docker/Dockerfile docker/Dockerfile.cpu docs/contributing/README.md docs/contributing/ci/dependency_hashes.md requirements/docs.txt requirements/test/{cpu,cuda,rocm,xpu}.txt tests/tools/test_dependency_pins.py tools/pre_commit/check_github_actions_pins.py tools/use_existing_torch.py`: passed, including all five compile hooks, actionlint, mypy, formatting, and test-to-CI coverage checks. The compile hooks leave the hashed files unchanged.
- `.venv/bin/python tools/pre_commit/check_github_actions_pins.py .github/workflows/*.yml`: passed for every workflow.
- `uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --target /tmp/vllm-standalone-hash-docs-install --python-platform x86_64-manylinux_2_28 --python-version 3.12 --require-hashes --only-binary :all: -r requirements/docs.txt`: passed for the full **55-package** documentation lock in a fresh target.
- Automated comparison: every current-main package version is preserved and every emitted requirement has SHA-256 hashes. Local archive validation accepted a correct hash and rejected a wrong hash, both with `--require-hashes` and uv's default verification. CPU x86_64/aarch64 filtering preserved every retained requirement/hash entry. `git diff --check` passed.

<details>
<summary>Torch-removal regression: failure before the fix</summary>

```bash
baseline=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$baseline/tools" "$baseline/tests/tools"
git show upstream/main:tools/use_existing_torch.py > "$baseline/tools/use_existing_torch.py"
cp tests/tools/test_dependency_pins.py "$baseline/tests/tools/"
.venv/bin/python -m pytest --confcutdir="$baseline/tests/tools" "$baseline/tests/tools/test_dependency_pins.py" -k use_existing_torch -q
```

Observed on the unmodified helper:

```text
FAILED test_use_existing_torch_removes_complete_requirements[True-False]
FAILED test_use_existing_torch_removes_complete_requirements[True-True]
2 failed, 2 passed, 6 deselected
```

Both hashed cases retain orphaned Torch hash lines. With the fix, the full new suite reports `10 passed`.

</details>

Review fix for [the ROCm fastsafetensors regression](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/64241#discussion_r4418136828): the line-oriented extraction retained a trailing backslash, producing an invalid quoted pip requirement. Each remaining ROCm Dockerfile now extracts the entire continued requirement into a file and rebuilds from it with `--require-hashes --no-deps --no-binary fastsafetensors`. The actual `fastsafetensors-0.3.3.tar.gz` source hash is retained.

- After merging main at `6de8c7ba51`, running the new tests with both remaining Dockerfiles restored from that main commit (`.venv/bin/python -m pytest --confcutdir=tests/tools tests/tools/test_dependency_pins.py -k rocm -q --tb=short`) reports **4 failed, 10 deselected**. The valid-hash cases fail with an invalid requirement ending in a backslash; the invalid-hash cases fail because pip rejects the requirement before checking its hash.
- After the fix, the full test command above reports **14 passed**. `pre-commit run --files docker/Dockerfile.rocm docker/Dockerfile.rocm_gfx1250 tests/tools/test_dependency_pins.py .buildkite/test_areas/misc.yaml` and `git diff --check` pass. Tests use a local pure-Python sdist to verify extraction and pip source-install/hash behavior; they do not compile the ROCm C++ extension.

Merge-conflict resolution: merged main at `6de8c7ba51`, retained its replacement ROCm Dockerfile and deletion of `Dockerfile.rocm_72`, and adapted source-rebuild coverage to both remaining images. Regenerated the four test locks with the existing compile hooks; all **1,458 requirement pins** across the five compiled files exactly match main, and every requirement retains SHA-256 hashes. All five compile hooks pass without modifying their output.

Review fix for the docs version parser (`3f3978e44d`): read the first token of each pinned requirement so continuation backslashes do not enter mocked package versions. The regression test executes the actual version-loading block and verifies all **374 entries** remain present and parse as versions. The CPU CI step now tracks the generator and CUDA lock as source dependencies. The hash-coverage documentation explicitly lists NCCL overrides, handwritten requirements, direct Dockerfile installs, and build dependencies. NCCL version alignment remains follow-up work; this PR preserves existing package versions.

- Before the parser fix, `.venv/bin/python -m pytest --confcutdir=tests/tools tests/tools/test_dependency_pins.py -k docs_mock -q --tb=short` reports **1 failed, 14 deselected**, with `packaging.version.InvalidVersion: Invalid version: '2025.11.29 \\'`.
- After the fix, `.venv/bin/python -m pytest --confcutdir=tests/tools tests/tools/test_dependency_pins.py -q --tb=short` reports **15 passed**.
- `pre-commit run --files .buildkite/test_areas/misc.yaml docs/mkdocs/gen_files/generate_argparse.py docs/contributing/ci/dependency_hashes.md tests/tools/test_dependency_pins.py` and `git diff --check`: passed.
- `uv pip install --require-hashes -r requirements/docs.txt`: passed for all 55 packages. `.venv/bin/python -m mkdocs build --strict`: **passed**, including CLI generation and the full site (128.81 seconds).

**Pending:** full Linux CPU/GPU container builds and hosted documentation/CI runs. Model evaluations are not applicable: package versions and model code are unchanged. Human review remains required before merge.

## Details

This PR supplies hash initialization, compile/check enforcement, install compatibility, and contributor documentation. It contains no scheduled updater, publishing workflow, or Dependabot grouping changes. Merge this prerequisite before the automatic updater in #59667, whose helper requires hash-generating compile hooks.

uv verifies supplied hashes in existing test-image installs. Hash coverage is limited to archives named in the five compiled files; handwritten lint/build/bootstrap dependencies, separately built wheels, and packages deliberately excluded from the ROCm lock remain outside it. Hashing a source archive does not hash its build dependencies, so mixed installs do not globally require hashes. The documentation install uses a complete lock and explicitly requires them.

Contributor documentation is linked from the contributor index at `docs/contributing/ci/dependency_hashes.md`. Local documentation discovery passed; hosted preview validation remains pending.

**Duplicate-work check:** this extracts the pinning changes from #59667, where they are removed. No other open PR found initializes these five hashed files and adds these checks. #38500 pins setup-uv in a different workflow, which this PR does not modify; #64010 restores already-version-locked CI jobs; #63574 raises dependency floors.

commits.pr_title: [Quantization] Remove QuTLASS and fp_quant, run QuIP NVFP4 on Humming
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Removes QuTLASS and the deprecated `fp_quant` method, and runs compressed-tensors NVFP4 checkpoints with a Hadamard input transform (QuIP) on Humming. Supersedes #61671, and makes #51112 moot.

## Claims

- QuIP NVFP4 checkpoints load and generate again. At `main` they crash at startup on SM100+.
- The checkpoint's declared FP4 activation is honored, with no fallback to A16 on this path.
- Input transforms always receive unquantized activations, which also fixes the generic transform path.
- The `_qutlass_C` build dependency, the `fp_quant` method, and about 1,800 lines of code are gone.

**Breaking:** `fp_quant` checkpoints no longer load. They already failed to load on `main`, and the method has been deprecated since #31688.

## Validation

B300 (SM103), humming-kernels 0.1.18. FP-Quant numbers below are from a scratch prototype, since that path is removed here; the QuIP row was re-run on this branch.

**Tests**

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `pytest tests/models/quantization/test_nvfp4.py -k 'quip or hadamard_fp4_routing'` | 8 passed |
| `pytest tests/quantization/test_compressed_tensors.py -k transforms_perplexity` | 3 passed |
| QuIP generation with `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error` | clean |
| `pre-commit` on changed files | passed |

Reproducer on `main`: `LLM(model="nm-testing/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-quipv16-nvfp4")` fails during startup with `'QuantizedActivation' object has no attribute 'shape'`.

**GSM8K** (600 questions, 5-shot, greedy, %)

| Checkpoint | QuTLASS* | Humming A4 | Humming A16 + Hadamard |
|---|---|---|---|
| Llama-3.2-1B QuIP NVFP4 (float: 32.3) | 18.8 | 17.3–20.5 (this branch) | 22.8 |
| Qwen3-1.7B FP-Quant RTN NVFP4 (float: 66.8) | 23.5 | 21.3 | 45.2 |
| Qwen3-1.7B FP-Quant QAT NVFP4 | 55.0 | 52.0 | 62.0 |
| Qwen3-1.7B FP-Quant RTN MXFP4 | 16.3 | 15.3 | 26.7 |

\* `main` cannot run these, so the baseline needed small harness patches for the two root causes below. FP-Quant rows ran in eager mode.

A4 vs QuTLASS is a statistical tie (paired p = 0.13–0.93), though lower in every prototype row. Run-to-run noise is large: two passes in one process scored 17.3 and 20.5, with 196/600 identical outputs.

**GEMM GPU time** (µs, graph replay, real `down_proj` weights, N=2048, K=6144, warm L2, not hand-tuned)

| M | QuTLASS + cutlass | QuTLASS + FlashInfer | Humming A4 | Humming A16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 17.9 | 7.7 | 9.7 | 9.8 |
| 1024 | 36.8 | 24.1 | 15.9 | 41.4 |
| 8192 | 164.9 | 146.4 | 75.8 | 240.6 |

NVFP4 shown. Graph replay was used because CUPTI failed in this environment (`cupti-python` 13.3.1).

## Details

**Root causes on `main`**
- `fp_quant`: checkpoints contain `backward_hadamard_matrix`, which `FPQuantLinearMethod` never registers, so loading fails.
- QuIP: since #44260 NVFP4 layers expose `input_quant_key`, so producers pass a `QuantizedActivation`, which the transform methods cannot handle. Per #61671, SM12x also fails because QuTLASS wheels contain only `sm_100` code.
- Neither was caught because the job holding the QuIP perplexity test is commented out. The new tests are in `test_nvfp4.py`, whose Blackwell job does run.

**Routing:** Humming is used for W4A4, SM100+, a `hadamard` input transform with `head_dim` in 16–128, no output transform, and backend `auto` or `humming`. Everything else uses the generic transform path. Humming's block size 16–256 output matched the dense Sylvester matrix to bf16 rounding.

**What is lost**
- QuEST for MXFP4. None of the 36 public `fp_quant` models use it.
- Bit-exact output against QuTLASS, since scale rounding differs.
- Fused handling of non-Sylvester dense transforms. They use the generic path, which is slower and was not tested here.
- About 2 µs at M=1–16 versus the CT FlashInfer path.

**Not validated:** SM120, and TP>1 (`HadamardTransform` still raises `NotImplementedError`). `Humming float4e2m1 activation is slow on SM103` still logs, though A4 was the fastest option at M ≥ 1024. Plain NVFP4 on `--linear-backend humming` still falls back to A16 on SM10x and is unchanged here.

Not a duplicate: open PRs #61671 and #51112 fix QuTLASS rather than remove it.

commits.pr_title: [Perf][HiSparse] Prefetch speculative groups with bounded copy workers
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Extend HiSparse's existing shared-index group prefetch to multi-token speculative verification, including MTP, and bound the CUDA compact-gather launch as verification expands the batch.

Related: #60072. This is separate from the platform-interface PR #62592. It composes with #60103; slot-invalidation fusion, padding-mask fusion and the all-resident resolver optimization remain in that PR and are not duplicated here.

## Claims

- Eligible pure-decode verification batches can stage follower layers' historical KV on the existing group copy stream, with a separate completion event for each layer.
- Prefetch eligibility is separate from the single-token resident-write and host-mirror policy. Mixed/prefill batches keep per-layer staging.
- Compact gather launches at most 64 thread blocks. Additional rows are processed by the existing workers; batches of at most 64 rows retain their column parallelism.
- Add native payload/graph regression cases and a reusable gather benchmark. Scoped H200 serving and profiling results are reported below; no model accuracy or acceptance improvement is claimed.

## Performance results

Measured on 8 x NVIDIA H200 with GLM-5.2-FP8, TP=8, MTP=3 and the V2 model runner. Both arms were rebuilt from frozen main `a1cfd2c1b584c4ac197db9cc9ac84a6d973d39df`; the candidate adds this PR's changes at `bb84fb5e976f941e9e2b8586f79930be64408a74`. Source/native-library pairs were checked. The table uses the original PR implementation.

Runtime: Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, driver 595.58.03; EvalScope 1.14.1 for unprofiled serving measurements.

- Workload: 65,536 input tokens, forced 4,096 or 8,192 output tokens, concurrency 32, 32 requests per case; temperature 0, ignore EOS. Frozen GSM8K-derived long prompts are a synthetic performance workload, not a natural long-reasoning accuracy evaluation. Request bodies match between arms and actual input/output lengths were audited.
- Both arms: `kv_cache_dtype=fp8_ds_mla`, 32 GiB GPU KV cache per rank, 128 GiB shared host pool, `max_model_len=73728`, `max_num_batched_tokens=8192`, `max_num_seqs=32`, prefix caching disabled, seed 42; FLASHMLA_SPARSE / DEEPSEEK_V32_INDEXER.
- Each initial process ran a separate C32 64K/128 warmup (excluded), then 4K output, 8K output and an 8K repeat. A separate PR process restart repeated warmup -> 4K -> 8K. The restart rows reuse the original main process's corresponding first measurements; they are not additional independent main restarts.
- TPOT is the mean of per-request `(latency - TTFT) / (output_tokens - 1)`, not inter-chunk latency. TTFT includes queueing.

All arrows below are **main -> PR**. Throughput is aggregate output tokens/s; TPOT and TTFT are client means.

| Output / run | Output tok/s | Change | TPOT (ms/token) | Change | TTFT (s) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4K, first | 487.7481 -> 494.6458 | +1.41% | 38.14 -> 37.08 | -2.78% | 107.739 -> 107.676 |
| 8K, first | 780.2473 -> 802.4179 | +2.84% | 26.80 -> 25.35 | -5.41% | 107.713 -> 107.733 |
| 8K, same-process repeat | 782.5196 -> 800.9244 | +2.35% | 26.59 -> 25.50 | -4.10% | 107.541 -> 107.610 |
| 4K, PR restart | 487.7481 -> 495.4115 | +1.57% | 38.14 -> 36.87 | -3.33% | 107.739 -> 107.992 |
| 8K, PR restart | 780.2473 -> 803.6892 | +3.00% | 26.80 -> 25.43 | -5.11% | 107.713 -> 107.901 |

The 32 GiB series completed main 96/96, first PR process 96/96 and restarted PR process 64/64 measured requests, with **zero preemptions in both arms**. Earlier 24 GiB runs had capacity-driven preemptions; increasing capacity is a separate tuning change and its gain is not attributed to this PR.

These observations support a modest benefit for this workload: 8K-output throughput +2.35% to +3.00%, mean TPOT -4.10% to -5.41%, with essentially unchanged mean TTFT. They are not confidence intervals or a general performance guarantee. Host NUMA placement was not pinned; generated continuations and MTP acceptance can differ across processes. No accuracy or acceptance-rate improvement is claimed.

### Profiling

A separate Torch-profiler diagnostic run at 24 GiB GPU KV capacity selected pure-decode steps with 26 requests / 104 verification rows: 24 main steps versus 23 PR steps, excluding one mixed-prefill PR step. Values are medians across rank-level medians, not end-to-end serving results.

| Diagnostic metric | Main | PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| GPU pure-decode envelope per step | 63.0585 ms | 54.8721 ms |
| Total gather duration per step | 14.9948 ms | 16.3471 ms |
| Exposed / non-overlapped gather duration | 14.9948 ms | 5.3232 ms |
| Gather overlap fraction | 0% | 67.44% |

The trace supports the intended copy/compute overlap: exposed gather time falls about 64.5%, despite total gather duration increasing. The selected GPU interval is about 13.0% shorter; **this is not a 13% end-to-end speedup**. Tokens and cache hit/miss state may differ. HiSparse traffic counters publish every 2,000 worker calls, so their per-case deltas are not used to attribute transfer-volume changes.

#### Trace timeline: before and after

![HiSparse main versus PR: actual GPU trace timelines and 20–24 ms zoom](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhenwenqi2024/vllm/974d68aa2b97c604003a42163f3257d926f7c606/pr63801/overlap-before-after.png)

The figure is rendered from original GPU event timestamps and durations, grouping events into per-category interval unions. **Left: main. Right: main + this PR.** Orange shows HiSparse gather kernels reading mapped host KV; blue shows other GPU activity; purple is the measured time intersection of the two tracks. In the magnified main panel, gather occupies gaps between other GPU work. In the PR panel, gather runs concurrently with other kernels; the original events include sparse MLA attention, fused MoE and GEMM kernels in these overlapping intervals.

Both panels show **rank 0, 26 requests / 104 verification rows, 24 GiB GPU KV**. To select a representative example, each arm uses the pure-decode step nearest its own rank's median GPU envelope: main step 22 and PR step 21 (zero-based profiler indices). Each panel starts at its own first GPU event; the lower panels show the same relative 20–24 ms window in the separate executions.

| Metric in the displayed step | Main | PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| GPU envelope | 63.0919 ms | 54.8733 ms |
| Gather duration (interval union) | 15.0741 ms | 16.6993 ms |
| Gather overlapped with other GPU activity | 0 ms | 10.9321 ms |
| Gather without other GPU activity | 15.0741 ms | 5.7672 ms |
| Gather overlap fraction | 0% | 65.46% |

The gather duration itself increases in this example, while much of it executes alongside other GPU work. **65.46% is this single rank/step's overlap; 67.44% in the table above is the summary across rank-level medians.** Generated tokens and cache states can differ between executions. A time intersection is not a direct measurement of critical-path savings, and this 24 GiB diagnostic is separate from the unprofiled 32 GiB serving results.

## GSM8K accuracy and MTP acceptance

Full real-weight regression on the same 8 x H200, GLM-5.2-FP8, TP8/MTP3, V2 runner and 32 GiB KV configuration above, comparing frozen main `a1cfd2c1` with main + original PR `bb84fb5e`.

Protocol: EvalScope 1.14.1 / GSM8K adapter v1.1, standard `main/test` **all 1,319 questions**, first four training examples in fixed order, thinking enabled with `reasoning_effort=max`, temperature 0, top_p 1, seed 42, concurrency 32, `max_tokens=16384`, normal EOS, non-streaming, no retries. This is a custom greedy regression, not a reproduction of the official GLM model-card score. Dataset: `openai/grade-school-math@3101c7d5072418e28b9008a6636bde82a006892c`; test SHA256 `3730d312f6e3440559ace48831e51066acaca737f6eabec99bccb9e4b3c39d14`. The complete request bodies and model metadata hashes matched across arms.

| Metric | Main | Main + PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Unique questions / scored | 1,319 / 1,319 | 1,319 / 1,319 |
| Correct | 1,285 | 1,282 |
| Accuracy, all questions | 97.4223% | 97.1948% |
| Output-budget failures, scored zero | 14 | 8 |
| HTTP errors / missing / duplicate questions | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
| Accepted / proposed draft tokens | 781,084 / 910,050 | 705,864 / 831,003 |
| Speculative steps | 303,350 | 277,001 |
| True draft-token acceptance | 85.8287% | 84.9412% |
| Mean acceptance length, including bonus token | 3.5749 | 3.5482 |
| Position 1 / 2 / 3 unconditional acceptance | 94.6313% / 86.1961% / 76.6586% | 94.3011% / 85.3723% / 75.1503% |
| Preemptions | 0 | 0 |

Accuracy changed by **-0.2274 percentage points (three fewer correct answers)**: 11 main-correct answers became wrong, and eight main-wrong answers became correct. All eight gains came from baseline output-budget failures; four of the 11 losses were PR output-budget failures. Every budget failure reached 16,384 tokens with reasoning but no final answer and remained a zero in the full denominator. This single pass does not establish accuracy equivalence or isolate the cause of the differences; no accuracy improvement is claimed.

Acceptance is `sum(accepted) / sum(proposed)`; mean acceptance length is `1 + sum(accepted) / sum(steps)`. All per-request counters, histograms and three position counts reconciled exactly with isolated Prometheus deltas. The table includes the budget failures and excludes the preceding 20-question smoke runs. It does not use EvalScope's streaming-chunk acceptance estimate.

As a secondary diagnostic, excluding the union of either arm's truncated questions leaves the **same 1,300 questions** in both arms: acceptance is 83.8127% -> 83.9579%. This illustrates sensitivity of the token-weighted aggregate to generated continuation lengths; it is not the primary metric or evidence of an acceptance improvement.

Raw responses, per-question reviews/reports, request hashes, metrics snapshots, source-patch hash and native-library identities were archived and audited. The baseline was re-audited without regenerating answers or changing scores after correcting the harness's classification of scored budget failures; the initial failed audit remains preserved. The model/PR implementation and frozen generation protocol were unchanged.

`DATASET_DIR` contains the frozen official train/test JSONL files and the local `main` split mapping; `OUT` is a fresh directory for each variant. Port 18593 is the local raw-response audit proxy forwarding to the model on 18592.


</details>

These are standard short GSM8K prompts, not inputs padded to 64K. They do not alone validate long-history offload misses or establish performance gains; the separate 64K performance and byte-level device tests above address different aspects.

## Validation

### Rebase validation (2026-10-29)

Rebased the original PR commit `bb84fb5e976` onto main `914d61fc538a84e8487cb16fe8241a70f6f4bf9e`; the updated head is `fc1fd11a1d306ab5f7b2d00e12107d3076e188af`. The only textual conflict was two tests added at the same location in `tests/v1/worker/test_utils.py`. Both main's resident-gather stride/payload test and this PR's bounded-decode prefetch test were preserved unchanged, including their parametrization. A per-file comparison verified that all added/removed lines in the seven-file PR patch are identical to the original patch; only surrounding context changed.

- On the isolated rebased Python source, `python -m pytest -q tests/v1/worker/test_utils.py -k 'hisparse_resident_gather_preserves_stride_and_payload or hisparse_group_prefetch_requires_bounded_decode_only'`: **10 passed, 55 deselected**. These are CPU tests run with the existing CUDA environment's import dependencies, not a rebuild or device validation of the new base.
- Applicable pre-commit checks passed: Ruff check/format, mypy, typos, Markdown formatting, Buildkite keys/test tethering, SPDX/import/config checks, boolean-context/remote-code checks, filenames and Docker ignore rules. The test-tethering check used UTF-8 on Windows. The Windows clang-format launcher failed, so the exact rebased CUDA source was checked on Linux with **clang-format 21.1.2 `--style=file --dry-run --Werror csrc/hisparse_kernels.cu`**, which passed. Python syntax and `git diff --check` also passed.

The performance, profiling, device-test and GSM8K measurements reported above/below remain results for frozen main `a1cfd2c1` plus the original PR `bb84fb5e`; they have **not** been rerun on the new main base.

Linux/CUDA native builds and H200 device checks have now run:

- `.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/v1/worker/test_utils.py -k hisparse`: main **45 passed**, PR **53 passed** (12 deselected each).
- Attention HiSparse selection: **53 main / 67 PR passed using out-of-tree compatibility copies** that repaired stale fixtures while preserving assertions. The unmodified baseline selection had 6 fixture failures / 47 passes; this is not a claim that the unmodified checked-in attention suite passed.
- Supplemental `validation/test_pr63801_device_stress.py`: **2 main / 2 PR passed**, eager and CUDA Graph replay, exact independent CPU byte-level golden comparisons; 656-byte rows, top-k 2048, four layers, up to 32 requests x 4 verification rows with changing active counts. PR Compute Sanitizer memcheck: **2 passed, 0 errors**.
- Supplemental `validation/test_pr63801_stream_consumption.py`: **2 main / 2 PR passed**, eager and CUDA Graph, immediate compute-stream consumption of each layer while follower prefetch proceeds, 64K history and an explicit logical-index readiness event. PR memcheck independently on GPU 0 and GPU 1: **2 passed, 0 errors on each**. These supplemental local tests are not checked-in full-model accuracy tests.

The standard reduced-model E2E suite (`tests/v1/e2e/general/test_hisparse.py`), real-weight accuracy under long-history offload misses, repeated accuracy runs and a broader concurrency / MTP-on-off sweep remain outstanding. The completed standard GSM8K regression above and byte-level device checks do not replace these.

Previously recorded local checks: the isolated CPU harness passed 10 contract cases (stand-in runtime owner); Ruff, syntax, whitespace, markdownlint, typos, SPDX/import checks, Buildkite test tethering and isolated Python 3.11 mypy passed. LLVM 21.1.2 WASM formatting produced identical CUDA source bytes; the native Windows formatter hook was skipped because its launcher failed. These are local results, not a claim of upstream CI success.

## Details

Group prefetch already exists for single-token decode. This extends its eligibility without adding a backend support flag, stream, buffer or CPU readback. Current verification KV remains resident and is written by each layer before its attention; only historical host misses are staged early.

The compact gather previously targeted 64 blocks but launched one block per row once the row count exceeded 64. For example, 32 requests with four verification rows produced a 128-block copy grid. Workers now loop over those rows within a 64-block launch. Miss-count clamping, invalid entries, out-of-range source zeroing and padded hot-page strides keep their existing behavior. Tests cover row counts around the boundary, empty plans, payload bytes and replay with updated inputs.

The launch bound may trade dense-copy bandwidth for compute overlap, as illustrated by the diagnostic trace above. A block-count bound does not reserve particular SMs.

An open-PR search found no equivalent speculative-group-prefetch or bounded-gather change. #60103 handles separate existing launch/resolver overhead; #61263 changes residency hash probing.

AI assistance was used for implementation, tests, performance/accuracy analysis and preparation of this update. Human review and the remaining validation items above are still outstanding.
